prompt: For years I dreaded the idea of having kids, and now that I have them I feel completely differently. Write a personal essay about that change: what I got wrong beforehand, what I got right, and how honest I can be about it given that parenthood probably rewires your brain.
Write a short essay on how people actually lose money once they have it, and whether the same pattern applies to how we waste time.

You've spent years doing office hours with early-stage startups. Write an essay about the question you find more useful than "how can this company make more money": how could it become more powerful? Cover the different forms that takes and what limits it.

If a university genuinely wanted more of its students to go on to start successful startups, what should it do, and what should it avoid? Write it up as an essay, from the perspective of someone who funds those students right after they graduate.

You've been invited to speak to a student debating society full of future politicians, and a prominent politician recently claimed nobody can earn a billion dollars without cheating. Write the talk: explain how people actually become billionaires through startups, and what someone young would need to do to get there.

Politicians keep talking about a "small" 1% wealth tax. How does a wealth tax rate compare to an income tax rate? Write a short, clear piece explaining how to convert between the two and why it matters.

An essay has to tell readers something they don't already know. Write a short reflective essay on the different reasons readers might not know something, and what that implies about who an essayist ends up writing for.

I want a long essay on how the Swiss luxury watch industry survived the quartz crisis by turning itself into a business of brand, and what that history reveals about the relationship between branding, design, and quality.

Is there any real connection between writing that sounds good and writing whose ideas are right? It seems like those should be independent, like a car's speed and its paint color. Write an essay working out whether they are.

Write an essay taking on the big childlike question: what should one do with one's life? Not a self-help listicle, an actual attempt at an answer from first principles, and consider why older traditions answered it the way they did.
Now that AI can write for people at school and at work, what happens to the ability to write? Give me a short, punchy essay with a prediction and say whether it matters.

"Follow your passion" gets argued about endlessly. I'd like an essay that actually maps out when you should work on what interests you most and when you shouldn't, rather than giving a yes-or-no answer.

You run a startup accelerator. Lately a lot of successful founders have told you that the standard advice for scaling a company, hire good people and give them room, nearly wrecked their businesses. Write an essay about why that advice might be wrong for founders and what the alternative could look like.

Write an essay on persistence versus obstinacy. Is there a real behavioral difference between the stubbornness that leads to success and the kind that leads nowhere, or do we just label people after the fact depending on whether they turned out to be right?

You co-founded Y Combinator and funded Reddit in the very first batch. Write a personal piece about Reddit's founders and how the company got started, and what it says about the match between founders and the companies they build.

I've been asked to give a talk to a room of 14 and 15 year olds about what they should be doing now if they might want to start a big tech company someday. Write the talk. Keep it concrete and in language teenagers will follow.
What would the best possible essay be like? Take that question seriously and follow it wherever it leads, including into how essays actually get written.

We were all raised on 'you get out what you put in.' I'm increasingly convinced that's false and that rewards for performance are wildly nonlinear in most areas that matter. Write an essay on where these outsized returns come from and what an ambitious person should do about it.
Short essay idea: if we met intelligent aliens, which truths beyond math and physics would we probably share with them, and why might asking that be a useful exercise for philosophy?
You co-founded Y Combinator and have advised hundreds of startups through it. Write a reflective essay on what you've learned from your own 'users', the founders you've funded.
Write an essay about what happens to your ideas when you try to put them into words. Is it possible to have fully formed ideas about something you've never written about?
Is there really such a thing as good taste, or is it all just preference? I'm giving a talk to a student debating society and want a short, rigorous argument for one side. Write it as an essay.
Plenty of very smart people never discover anything new. Write an essay on the gap between intelligence and having new ideas, and what else goes into the latter.

My kid came home excited to keep working on a story nobody assigned him. It got me thinking about how different that kind of work is from schoolwork or a job. Write an essay about working on projects of your own: what makes them different, where the boundary lies, and how adults can keep doing it.

People picture nerds as meek, but some of the most competitive people I know are nerds. Write an essay about this fierce type of nerd: what they're like, why it works for them, and some advice for young people who recognize themselves in it.
Write an essay on how we should react when a serious expert proposes an idea that sounds absurd, and why so many people are quick to dismiss new ideas.
Debates about the death penalty usually focus on morality and deterrence. Write a short, forceful essay (as of around 2021) arguing that the real issue is something more practical.
Compare the Forbes 400 lists from the early 1980s and from 2020. How has the way people get very rich in America changed, and why? Write it up as an essay, written from the vantage point of 2021.
Write a short blog post on why you try to write in plain words and simple sentences.

You and your partner have been judging startup founders for years, and you have a private vocabulary for the qualities you look for. Write an essay about one of those words: earnestness. Why would an old-fashioned virtue like that matter so much in a place like Silicon Valley?

Politicians keep saying the only way to become a billionaire is by exploiting people. You spent years at Y Combinator trying to pick the founders who would get enormously rich. Write an essay that uses what you actually looked for in YC interviews to answer that claim, and give founders honest advice on how to do well in the interview along the way.

Airbnb just went public, and you funded them back in 2008 when nobody else would. Write a short piece for future founders about what was special about the Airbnb founders and how they got the company off the ground during Y Combinator.

Write an essay on independent-mindedness: which kinds of work require thinking differently from your peers, whether people can tell where they fall on that spectrum, and whether it's possible to make yourself more independent-minded.

We're usually taught that an essay should be persuasive. I'd like a more ambitious standard. Write an essay on what it means for writing to be genuinely useful, how a writer can actually achieve that, what it costs you, and how someone should start.

Founders are often caught off guard by the attention they get as their companies grow, including people who seem obsessed with hating them. Write an essay about haters: what they are, where they come from, and how someone who becomes famous should deal with them.
Write a short essay on political moderates. Is being a moderate just cowardice or fence-sitting, or is there more than one way to end up in the middle?

Write an essay about what school really teaches people, beyond the subject matter of any class, and how that lesson follows them into adult life and work. You've spent years advising young startup founders fresh out of college, so draw on what you saw there.
You grew up in Pittsburgh and now live in Silicon Valley, and you've been asked to give a talk in Pittsburgh. Write the talk: what would it actually take for Pittsburgh to become a startup hub?
Everyone says life is short. Is it actually, or is that just a complaint about it being finite? And if it is short, what should that change about how we live? Write an essay on this.
Is there any way for an outsider to tell whether a selection process (hiring, admissions, VC funding) is biased, without access to data on who applied? Write a short piece explaining how.
A founder tells you he's worried he's too soft-hearted to succeed and gives too much away for free. Write a short essay on whether startup founders can afford to be nice.
Should a US startup that doesn't own the .com of its name change its name? Write a short, opinionated essay for founders.
Write a short essay about Ron Conway, and what his career suggests about whether being genuinely good pays off for investors.
Someone from a big company's corporate development team wants to meet with our young, fast-growing startup. Write an essay for founders in this position: should they take the meeting?
Tech companies keep lobbying for easier immigration for programmers, and critics say we should just train more Americans instead. Write a short, punchy essay taking a side in that argument.

Experts are often confidently wrong when the ground shifts under them. Write an essay on how someone with deep experience in a field can keep their beliefs from going stale in a world that keeps changing.

Write an essay for startup founders about a dangerous situation: you've got money in the bank and several months of runway, but you're burning cash, growth is flat, and the plan is to raise another round. What's really going on, and what should they do?

I've noticed that almost none of the really successful people I know are mean, even though the internet makes it obvious how much meanness there is. Is that a coincidence? Write an essay exploring whether meanness and success are actually related.

You're giving a guest lecture to a room of college students who are curious about startups. Write it up as an essay: what should they know now, before they ever start one, and what should they actually be doing in college if they think they might want to found a company someday?

Why do investors pile into some startups and ignore others, and why does the first check seem so much harder to get than the rest? Explain the dynamics of investor herd behavior for a founder about to raise a seed round.

You've advised hundreds of early-stage startups. Write an essay on the laborious, manual, seemingly unscalable things founders need to do at the very beginning to get a company off the ground, and why they resist doing them.

It's mid-2013 and you run Y Combinator. You've been asked to give a talk to a room full of investors about where startup investing is heading over the next decade. Write the talk as an essay: what forces are changing the business, and what should investors do about them?

What actually makes a company a startup, as opposed to just a new small business? Write an essay that gets to the bottom of it and follows the idea through to how it explains founders, investors and acquirers.

I'm a decent writer but a mediocre public speaker, and everyone tells me I should work on my speaking. Write an essay comparing writing and speaking: how much do ideas matter in each, and what are talks actually good for?

Y Combinator just turned seven. As one of its founders, write a short piece telling the story of how it actually got started, including the parts that were luck and the parts you didn't understand at the time.

The record labels keep saying file sharing is theft. Is it? Write a short essay about what actually makes something property, and what that means for people who sell music and movies now that copying is free.
You advise early-stage founders. Write a short essay on why the founders who are hard to talk to tend to be the ones whose startups fail, and what that has to do with resourcefulness.

Why do so many hackers who start companies end up building trivial things when there are huge, painful problems sitting in plain sight? Write an essay about it, aimed at programmers looking for a startup idea.
Startups per capita varies wildly from city to city. Write an essay explaining what it is about places like Silicon Valley that makes startups succeed there and not elsewhere.

Patent reform keeps stalling in Congress. Is there anything the tech industry could do on its own, without waiting for the government, to stop big companies from using patents to crush small competitors? Write it up as a short essay.

It's late 2010. A founder you funded is raising a series A, and the VCs are telling him founders basically never keep control of the board after an A round. Write an essay on whether that's still true and where things are heading.
Write a short essay about what iPhones and iPads really are, what we should call them, and what that implies about which everyday objects they'll end up replacing. Assume it's 2010.
A business magazine has asked you, as someone who funds very early-stage startups, for a short piece on the qualities you look for in founders. Use examples from companies you've backed.
Why have startups started raising angel rounds on convertible notes instead of fixed-size equity rounds? Write an essay explaining what's going on and what it means for founders and investors.
You worked at Yahoo in the late 90s after they acquired your startup. Write an essay about what actually went wrong there, and what lessons today's software companies should take from it.

It's 2010, VCs are starting to write smaller checks and a new breed of 'super-angels' has appeared. You fund very early startups. Write an essay predicting how startup funding is going to change over the next several years and why.

I keep noticing that more and more things in my life feel 'addictive' -- the internet, games, food. Is the world actually getting more addictive, and if so what should a person do about it? Write me an essay.
Write an essay about the thoughts that occupy your mind when you're not trying to think about anything, like in the shower, and why they matter so much for getting good work done.
I'm 22, I want to start a startup, and I have no idea what to work on. Write a short essay on how to come up with a good startup idea.

It's late 2009 and developers are increasingly furious about the iPhone App Store's approval process. Write an essay on why this matters more to Apple than Apple seems to think, and what it might lead to.
Newspapers, record labels and book publishers all complain that people won't pay for content anymore. Write an essay on whether that framing is even right, and what happens to publishing next.
Why are listicles ('7 things...', '10 ways...') so popular? I'd like a proper essay on the format: what it does for readers and writers, and what it costs.
Investors say determination is the best predictor of startup success. Write an essay that tries to take determination apart: what is it made of, and which parts can a person actually develop?

Someone who had worked for years as an architect just spent nine months fully immersed in our startup accelerator. I asked her what surprised her most about the startup world. Write a short essay built around her answers, with your own commentary on each, and end with whatever her outsider's view says about startup culture compared to the rest of the world.

The phrase "ramen profitable" is getting thrown around a lot now. Write an essay that pins down what it actually means, why it matters so much for an early-stage startup, what it does not mean, and whether it has a downside.
Why do programmers hate meetings so much more than everyone else seems to? Write it up properly as an essay, ideally one I could send to the non-engineers who keep booking time on my calendar.

Suppose startups really are a new economic phase on the scale of the Industrial Revolution, and also suppose they only thrive in a few specialized hubs, the way movies cluster in LA. What happens if both are true? Write an essay working through it.
If you had to describe what makes a good startup founder in as few words as possible, what would you say? Write a short essay that hunts for the right phrase and then explores what follows from it.

I sold my company a few years ago and keep meaning to start angel investing, but it seems mysterious and I don't know where to begin. Write me a guide: the mechanics, how to pick companies, how to find deals, and how to be the kind of investor founders actually want.

For years people talked about computers and TV "converging." Write an essay on how that contest actually played out, why it went the way it did, and what it means for TV networks and anyone thinking of competing with them.

Our city council keeps talking about becoming "the next Silicon Valley" by funding local startups. Could a city actually buy its way into becoming a startup hub? Write an essay thinking through what it would really take and what it would cost.

If you could only give startup founders a dozen or so pieces of advice, one sentence each, what would they be? Write it up with a short explanation under each, and tell me which one you'd keep if you could only keep one.
Why do online discussions about politics and religion always turn into useless flame wars, when threads about baking or programming don't? Write a short essay on what's really going on.

It's December 2008 and the markets have just crashed. You run an early-stage startup investment firm and see a lot of founders up close. Write an essay on whether this recession could hurt venture capitalists more than it hurts the people starting startups.

For most of history, the biggest organizations were the ones that won. Is that still true? Write an essay on the shift away from large organizations toward small independent groups, and what it means for which societies will thrive.

Write an essay about the procedures and approval steps that companies pile up as they grow, meant to protect against mistakes. What do they actually cost, and who pays? I'm especially curious how this affects programmers.

Everyone's saying the economy is about to get really bad. I've been planning to quit my job and start a tech startup with a friend. Should a recession change my plans? Write it up as a short essay for would-be founders.

Some people argue founders should build companies that make money and live off the revenue, rather than aiming to build something valuable and sell it. Write an essay thinking through what the ideal version of the 'live off the revenues' plan would actually look like.
Write a personal essay about procrastination and the internet: why it's so much harder to avoid distraction on a computer than it used to be, and something concrete you've tried to fight it.

You've funded a lot of startups and watched many of them go through fundraising. Write a practical guide for founders on how to survive the process of raising money, not how to pitch, but how to keep it from killing the company.
Give a talk-style essay to an audience of startup founders on whether being genuinely good to users and the world is a sound business strategy, not just a nice sentiment.

Someone recently argued that the reason there aren't more Googles is that promising startups sell out to acquirers too early. You've spent a few years funding very early startups and working closely with VCs. Write an essay giving your own answer to why there aren't more Googles.

Write a personal essay about your heroes: the people (and maybe things) whose example actually shapes how you decide what to do. Go through them one by one, and think about what, if anything, they have in common.

I've noticed that programmers who start their own companies seem more alive than the ones working at big firms, even though they're more stressed. Write an essay on whether a normal job at a large company is actually unnatural for humans, and what that implies for people deciding where to work.

You run a program that funds startups at the very earliest stage, when they're often just the founders. People describe what you do as "seed funding," and you've started to feel that's misleading. Write an essay figuring out what a very early stage investor actually does and why it's a different kind of thing from venture capital.

Several things you've made (a software company, a startup funding firm, a programming language, your essays) got the same dismissive reaction at first: too flimsy, too lightweight. Write an essay about the design philosophy behind them and why it tends to provoke that reaction.

After a talk in London where you said startups would do better in Silicon Valley, an organizer got up to rebut you. Write an essay making the case properly: should startups move to a startup hub, and when shouldn't they?

It's 2007 and you're giving the keynote at a conference for web developers. Starting a web startup has become dramatically cheaper. Write the talk as an essay: what does that cheapness imply about where web startups are headed, for founders, investors, acquirers and even colleges?

Growing up, getting into a good college felt like the meaning of life. Now you judge thousands of young founders a year and see quickly how they turn out. Write an essay on whether it really matters where you go to college.

You're speaking at the final dinner of a summer startup program, to a room of founders who've just built their first versions. You expect maybe half their companies to survive. Write the talk: how do startups die, and how can they avoid it?
Write an essay about what it means for a programmer to really have a program loaded in their head, what helps or hurts that state, and what it implies about how companies organize software work.

My apartment is full of things I picked up because they were cheap or free, and I can't seem to stop. Write me a personal essay about our relationship to stuff: why we accumulate it, what it actually costs us, and whether our attitudes have kept up with how cheap things have become.

Explain, for startup founders, a simple way to decide whether trading equity for something (investment, a key hire, a partnership) is actually worth it. Work through the math with concrete examples, including how to think about salary when sizing an early employee's stock grant.

Write a short essay offering an unconventional explanation for why mid-twentieth-century union manufacturing jobs paid so well, and why those jobs have faded. You've spent years watching fast-growing startups up close; draw on that if it helps.

What is the actual difference between being wise and being smart? I've never seen a satisfying answer. Write a long essay working it out, and consider whether the two might be pulling apart in the modern world.

Is taste really just personal preference, or can some art actually be better than other art? I was taught growing up that it's all subjective, and the older I get and the more I try to make things myself, the less I believe it. Write an essay working through the question honestly.
Write a short personal essay about imitation: everyone learns by copying someone, but how do you make sure you're copying the right things? Draw on your own mistakes if you can.

Lots of governments say they want to build their own Silicon Valley. Write an essay on what it is about the United States that makes startups form there so readily, which of those advantages other countries could copy or beat, and what they'd have to change to do it.
Suppose a city wanted to become the next Silicon Valley. Is that even possible, and if so what would it really take? Write an essay working out what actually causes a technology hub to form.

You fund early-stage software startups and keep having to advise founders about patents. Write an essay taking on the question of whether software patents are evil: what's actually wrong with the system, how startups should deal with patents in practice, and whether patents help or hurt innovation.

Everyone says "do what you love," but almost nobody seems to manage it, and the advice itself feels too glib to be useful. Write an essay that takes it seriously: why is it so hard to find work you love, what gets in the way, and how should someone actually go about it?

Write an essay arguing that procrastination isn't always a vice. I'm interested in the distinction between the kinds of things people put off and what they do instead, and what that means for someone who wants to do ambitious work.

It's late 2005 and everyone in tech is throwing around the phrase "Web 2.0." You've been skeptical of it, and you run a firm that funds early-stage web startups. Write an essay working out whether the term actually means anything, and if so, what.

Writing in 2005, a few years after the dot-com bust: startups have become dramatically cheaper to start, IPOs have dried up after Sarbanes-Oxley, and big companies are starting to buy startups early. Write an essay on the pressures this puts on the venture capital business and what VCs ought to do about it.

People keep asking how you come up with good startup ideas, and most of them seem convinced it's nearly impossible. Write an essay on where startup ideas actually come from and what conditions make someone likely to have them.

Write an essay examining what it would actually mean, mechanically, to reduce economic inequality, and what side effects that might have on risk-taking and new companies. Follow the argument wherever it goes.
Short essay, please: our parents climbed the corporate ladder, and my generation would rather build something in a startup and sell it. Is that shift as big a change as it looks, financially?

Open source software and blogging both seem to beat paid professionals at their own game. Write an essay on what the forces behind them should teach businesses about work, offices, and how companies are organized.

I'm giving a talk to computer science undergrads. Write me an essay arguing about whether talented young programmers should take a job at a big company or start their own company, and how the economics of hiring and acquisitions bear on that choice.

It's early 2005 and you've noticed that the serious programmers you know are buying Powerbooks. Write a short essay about why hackers are moving to the Mac, what the Mac once meant to people like you, and why a company should care what such a small group of users thinks.

Several computer science undergrads have emailed you asking what they should do in college. Write an essay answering them: how to get good at programming, what else is worth studying, how to think about jobs, and whether grad school is worth it.

Founders complain constantly that venture capitalists are slow, paranoid, meddling and arrogant. Write an essay that looks for a structural explanation for why VCs behave the way they do, rather than just blaming the people. Draw on your own experience raising money for and selling a startup in the late 90s.

Write a talk for high school students: the things you and your friends wish someone had told you when you were that age. Speak to them directly, and be honest about school, college admissions, ambition and how to figure out what to work on.

Why is America so good at making some things, like software and movies, and so bad at others, like cars and cities? Write an essay exploring whether those strengths and weaknesses might come from the same national trait, aimed at readers outside the US.

Right after the 2004 US presidential election, pundits are explaining the result as a shift in the country's politics. Write a provocative essay proposing a simpler explanation for who wins presidential elections, testing it against the elections of the TV era.

It's 2004. You worked at Yahoo through the dot-com bubble and watched it burst. Everyone now treats anything that was fashionable in 1999 as discredited. Write an essay arguing about which of the bubble's ideas were actually right and will matter in the long run.

The five-paragraph essay we all learned in school feels like it has almost nothing to do with real essays. Write a piece on what an essay actually is, where the school version came from, and how you go about writing a real one.

People get angry about the gap between rich and poor in a way they never do about the gap between a chess grandmaster and a club player. Write an essay on why making money gets treated differently from every other skill, and whether a growing income gap in a modern economy is actually a bad sign.

Write an essay about the word "hacker": what it really means among programmers, why hackers have such a disobedient streak, and why outsiders like lawmakers should care what hackers think about things like copyright law and civil liberties.

Every era has had opinions you could get in serious trouble for voicing, and plenty of them later looked perfectly reasonable. Write an essay about how someone today might work out which of our own taboos future generations will find ridiculous, and what a sensible person should do once they find one.

Spam filters are entirely defensive: they just sort mail and throw the junk away. Write a short piece arguing for a filter that hits back at the spammer, and think through how it would work, how to keep it from being abused, and whether it could actually change the economics of spam.

I studied computer science and then went to art school, and people keep asking me why. Write an essay arguing that programming is closer to painting than to science or engineering, and what follows from that for how hackers should work and make a living.
Write an essay speculating about what programming languages will look like a hundred years from now, and why thinking about that is useful for choosing or designing a language today.

I design programming languages, but I don't think of it as research. Write an essay, adapted from a talk to language researchers, on what changes when you treat a programming language as a design problem rather than a research topic.

People say taste is subjective, yet everyone who designs things seems to get better at it over time. Write an essay on whether there's such a thing as good taste, and if so, what good design actually has in common across fields like math, painting, architecture and software.

You co-founded Viaweb and wrote its software in Lisp, and you think it gave you a real edge over competitors. Eric Raymond's 'How to Become a Hacker' says Lisp is worth learning even if you never actually use it. Write an essay on why, if some languages really are more powerful than others, most programmers don't switch to them, and what a startup should make of that.
Explain the difference between top-down and bottom-up program design, especially as Lisp programmers practice it, and why the bottom-up approach pays off.

A friend who's been building a Postgres rewrite with coding agents keeps telling me we should be more ambitious with the software we build. I half agree, but most AI-built projects I see are junk. Write a blog post taking his line seriously: what has actually changed about what one programmer can build now, drawing on your own experiments, and why people aren't taking advantage of it.

Write an essay on why some people seem to see software bugs everywhere while most people, including the teams that ship the software, don't notice them at all. Draw on your own experience, and say why it matters for programmers in particular.

You've spent a career on performance work (CPU microcode, search indexes) and lately you've been pointing coding agents at optimization problems: a regex engine, a board game AI, your own ripgrep usage. Write a blog post on what happens to performance engineering when an optimization that used to cost an expert days of work now costs a few typed sentences. Draw on your own experiments, and keep it informal.

People keep saying content moderation on big platforms would be easy if the moderators just used common sense. I think that's wrong, but I want to make the case with something more than vibes. Write an essay on why large platforms can't come up with moderation rules that people agree on, using David Turner's "No Vehicles in the Park" game as a starting point.

Every time a long Twitter thread or a YouTube video gets shared on Hacker News, the top comment is someone asking why it isn't a blog post. Write a blog post on why people actually choose to publish on platforms that seem worse for the reader. You can admit you'd personally prefer the blog post.

You're an engineer at a fast-growing mobile money company in Africa that has scaled a long way on a pretty boring stack. Conference talks are all about microservices and sophisticated architectures. Write a post making the case for simple architectures, drawing on what your team has actually done, including the places where you couldn't stay simple and the choices you'd reconsider.

Someone at a party told me that if a product could be better, a competitor would already have built the better version, so markets basically guarantee things work about as well as they can. That doesn't match my experience buying anything, as a consumer or as a company. Write an essay on why it's so hard to buy products and services that actually work well, and what that means for the build vs. buy decision.

You're a senior engineer who has spent years watching how big tech companies hire and promote people, and you've long been a baseball stats nerd on the side. Write an essay on how organizations misjudge talent: what goes wrong when people trust their gut about who is good, and what that implies for hiring and promotion in software.

Write an essay arguing against the habit, common in big companies and in philanthropy alike, of treating people as interchangeable units: headcount on a roadmap, budget lines, interventions judged only by a simple metric. Draw on what you've seen in tech orgs, and push on why organizations keep doing it anyway.

There's a popular view in software circles that when people behave badly you should never blame discipline or attitude, only fix the incentives and the process. I think that's overcorrected. Write an essay on how much company culture actually matters, next to incentives and process, for things like speed, debugging, quality and ownership, and what it means for someone choosing where to work.

I want a personal essay on being willing to look stupid: why it pays off over a lifetime, in learning, at work, with doctors, with everyday decisions, and where it actually costs you something. Use your own experiences, lots of concrete examples.

Programmers love telling each other what to learn: compilers, functional programming, Lisp, whatever made them better. I'm skeptical of most of that advice. Write an essay on how someone should actually decide which skills to spend years getting good at, drawing on your own experience in hardware and software.

A lot of programmers online say working faster doesn't matter: pick the right problem, typing speed is irrelevant, go live your life. Write a blog post making the case for deliberately working on your own productivity and velocity, and take those objections seriously.

You work in infrastructure at a large tech company, and people are always surprised it employs specialists in things like the OS kernel and the JVM. Write an essay on why mid-to-large companies should keep deep in-house expertise in areas that don't look core to their business, and what that means for buy-vs-build decisions.

Someone once asked me, a bit dismissively, why I'd bother measuring things when I could be building something instead. Write an essay arguing for the value of measurement and benchmarking, with real examples of what changed after someone measured.

Fred Brooks's 'No Silver Bullet' still gets quoted constantly to argue that most of the difficulty in programming is essential and that tools and languages can only buy us a small constant factor. I'm skeptical. Write an essay taking that argument on, looking back at it with the benefit of everything that's happened in software since 1986.

Do car makers actually build safe cars, or do they just build cars that score well on the crash tests everyone knows about? One way to find out is to look at what happened when the IIHS introduced new tests, like the driver-side small overlap test in 2012 and the passenger-side version in 2018. Write up an analysis along those lines: which manufacturers held up, what that suggests, and what caveats someone should keep in mind before reading too much into crash test scores.

A lot of engineers think distributed tracing only pays off at Google or Facebook scale. You worked on tracing infrastructure at Twitter, where it was neglected for years before it turned into something clearly worth funding. Write a post explaining what was wrong with the original setup and what relatively simple changes made tracing valuable.

Most corporate engineering blogs are bland, yet a handful of companies manage to run ones engineers actually want to read. I'd like an essay on what separates the two, looking at how posts actually get written and approved inside these companies rather than at writing tips.

Unix tools like ls now have dozens of flags, which seems to fly in the face of 'do one thing and do it well.' Write an essay about the growth of command line options over the decades: why it happened, whether it's actually bad, and what it says about the Unix philosophy itself.

I have a slightly contrarian hunch that being in the top 5% at most things is much easier than people assume, and that the reason most people plateau isn't talent. Write an essay making the case properly, with concrete examples from games and from real-world skills like programming, writing, or public speaking.

Big tech companies justify mandatory algorithms interviews by saying that at their scale they can't afford engineers who write inefficient code. You've spent years doing performance work at these companies. Write an essay on whether that rationale holds up against what actually happens on the job.

People argue endlessly in Overwatch forums about whether women get treated worse in online games, and the threads never settle anything. Suppose you actually ran the experiment yourself: played a few hundred games under a masculine username and a few hundred under a feminine one, logged every chat comment, and categorized them. Write up the experiment and what you found, including an honest account of how the result could be wrong.

Apps I use every day keep moving buttons and changing shortcuts, and I keep doing the wrong thing by accident. Write an essay on whether software UIs should be held to the same backwards-compatibility standards we expect from APIs and operating systems.

I needed a random permutation with exactly one cycle and ended up at Sattolo's algorithm, but every explanation I found leans on Stirling numbers or cycle notation. Can you write up why it works, starting from Fisher-Yates, for a programmer with no combinatorics background? Include code.

There's an old, much-repeated claim that Apple's research proved the mouse is faster than the keyboard and that keyboard users are fooling themselves. Write a blog post that looks at where that claim actually comes from, whether the evidence holds up, and what you find when you time some everyday editing tasks yourself.

Joel Spolsky famously argued that great developers are basically never on the job market, so the resume pile is mostly people nobody else wanted. Write an essay pushing on that claim. Is developer hiring really a 'market for lemons' in Akerlof's sense, and if hiring managers keep saying they can't find good people, what's actually going on?

Every time a big tech company comes up online, someone says 'what do all those thousands of engineers even do? I could build that in a weekend.' Write a blog post on why that intuition is wrong (or whether it is).

A friend with over a decade of solid engineering experience keeps getting bounced at the resume screen by startups that say they 'only hire the best'. Write an essay about how tech companies filter candidates on pedigree and trendiness, what that costs them, and what they could do instead.

You spent years at a company building x86-compatible chips. Write a blog post about the serious Intel CPU bugs that surfaced at the end of 2015 and what they suggest about where hardware reliability is heading, especially now that so much runs in the cloud.

I keep noticing that practices that horrify new hires at tech companies are treated as completely normal by everyone who's been there a while. Write an essay about why this happens in software organizations, what other fields have learned about it, and what it would take to change it.

Everyone in tech seems to repeat that if you're a good programmer you should join a startup: more money, more interesting work, you learn more. I'm skeptical. Write an essay that actually checks those claims one at a time against a job at a big company, with real numbers where you can get them.

Why do desktop apps like email clients corrupt their data files so often, when big web services almost never lose anything? Write a technical blog post on what it really takes to write a file safely, how filesystems behave under crashes and disk errors, and what the research literature says.

A well-known programming blogger argued that ECC memory isn't worth paying for: early Google didn't use it, most RAM errors are hard errors you can catch with memtest, modern RAM is reliable, and if it mattered it would be in every machine. Write a response that takes those arguments one at a time and explains whether ECC is worth it, for servers and for ordinary desktops.

It's 2015. Write a blog post about how changes in the relative speed of hardware components (disks, SSDs, NVRAM, networks) should change the way we architect systems, not just how we optimize code. Focus on storage and what falling network latency means for it, both inside the datacenter and for consumers.

Distributed systems are usually designed to survive machines dying. What happens when a machine doesn't die but just gets really slow, like a NIC running at a thousandth of its speed or a degraded disk? Write up how systems like Hadoop, HDFS and Cassandra cope with that, why it can be worse than a crash, and whether we should care.

You've spent a lot of time reading internal postmortems at big tech companies. Write an essay on the recurring patterns you see in what causes really bad outages, and what you'd do differently because of it.
People keep telling me it's insane that Google and Facebook put all their code in one giant repository. Write a post making the case for why a monorepo might actually be a reasonable choice.

So many popular ideas get passed around as "backed by science", in pop psychology and in programming arguments alike. Write an essay that actually checks a few of these against the studies people cite, and then asks why the misreadings spread and whether ordinary people can realistically check sources themselves.

Everyone arguing about whether AI will replace customer service workers seems to compare AI to an ideal human. I want a blog post that takes a different angle: what is the human service people actually get today, and what does that imply about when automation wins? Use your own experiences dealing with bureaucracies if it helps.

People often insist a backdoor in a CPU is basically impossible. From a hardware engineer's point of view, how hard would it actually be to build one? Walk through what it could do, how it would be triggered, and how it could get onto the chip.

I run a fairly niche technical blog (low-level programming, hardware stuff) and a small ad network just emailed asking to put an ad on it. Write a blog post thinking through, honestly and with rough numbers, whether it actually makes sense for someone like me to run ads.

It's late 2014 and you've spent a good while using Julia for scripts and data analysis, and even tried contributing fixes to the core language. Write a candid review of the language from that experience, focusing less on the hype and more on what it's actually like to depend on it and contribute to it.

My impression is that open source projects have broken builds and failing tests far more often than codebases at companies. Is that real, and if so, why does it happen and why should maintainers care? Write a short essay on it.

We're reading 'Out of the Tar Pit' in my reading group. The paper leans on Dijkstra's line that testing can show the presence of bugs but never their absence, and argues informal reasoning matters more than testing. Write a short response essay: do you buy that, especially from the perspective of someone who has built genuinely complex systems?

I hit software bugs in big-name apps basically every day, stuff that clearly slipped past testing. You've worked in both chip design and software. Write a blog post about a cheap, underused way big software companies could catch more of these bugs, and what software people could learn from how hardware gets verified.
Why don't engineering and CS programs teach debugging as an actual skill? Write an essay about it, drawing on your own experience as a student and as a TA.

Hey, it's David. Last time we talked I mentioned I'm taking calc III and linear algebra, and a friend told me it's pointless because Wolfram Alpha can do all of that now. You reacted pretty strongly. I'm hoping to move from academia into a programming job. Could you think it over properly and write me back a letter: do programmers actually need math, and was it worth taking those classes?

Software startups are often founded by people fresh out of school, but young teams building CPUs almost always seem to fail. Write an essay on why experience matters so much more in hardware than software.

Write a post about how link aggregators like Hacker News and reddit decide what reaches the front page, what's wrong with the way new submissions get exposure, and how you might fix it. If there's been real-world feedback on the idea, deal with it honestly.

You're a hardware engineer. Write a blog post about why so many newcomers write Verilog that's completely wrong, what it is about the language that causes this, and whether any of the alternative hardware description languages are likely to catch on.

For a decade you ran your own small software businesses, then four years ago you joined a payments company that has been growing extremely fast the whole time. Write a reflective essay on what that experience has taught you: what hypergrowth actually does to an organization and the people in it, how your own work changed, and where your old mental model of the company turned out to be wrong.

I keep hearing about Japan's furusato nouzei 'hometown tax' donation system but can't find a good English explanation of it. Write me a blog post explaining why it exists, how it works in practice, and how the incentives played out once cities started competing for donations (as of around 2018).

I just pulled my credit report and there's an account on it I never opened. Collectors may be next. You've dealt with credit bureaus and banks a lot. Write me a practical guide to how this system actually works and how an ordinary person gets a fraudulent account taken off their record without hiring a lawyer.

People on Twitter are sharing their salaries publicly this week. You've had an unusual tech career: a Japanese salaryman job, a consulting practice, a few small software businesses. Write a candid post that makes the case for talking openly about pay and puts your own numbers on the table, with whatever lessons you think younger engineers should take from them.

Heartbleed spread through the whole industry in about a day and got hundreds of thousands of people patching. Write a blog post for open source developers about what that says about marketing, and why the OSS world should take it more seriously than it does.

It's late January 2013. Rails has just shipped two emergency patches for remote code execution bugs, and rubygems.org was compromised too. You run a couple of small software businesses and you spent your nights patching. Write a blog post for startup founders, including ones who don't use Rails, about what this means for them and what they should be doing right now.

Write up a pricing case study for SaaS founders. The company is a server monitoring service that charged per server plus per website (roughly $11/server, cheaper at volume, $2/website), and its typical customer has about 7 servers. They A/B tested that against a grid of three or four plans starting at $99/month, segmented by users and support level. Trial signups were 150 vs 113 out of ~2,150 visitors each, cards added 23 vs 18, and new monthly revenue $420 vs $876. Explain why the old model was a mistake, what the results mean (including how far to trust them), and what other founders should take from it.

I run a small software business and I've always avoided email marketing. It feels spammy, and I figure my blog and Twitter reach people well enough. Make the case, properly and with specifics, for why I might be wrong.

Most of the engineers I know take the first offer they get and are weirdly proud of not haggling. Write an essay, aimed at them, on why salary negotiation matters so much, how the employer actually sees it, and at what point in the hiring process it should happen.

Write the career advice post you wish someone had handed you as a young software engineer fresh out of college: the stuff about how the industry and business actually work that no CS degree or career center covers. Be blunt and practical.
You quit a grinding corporate job to run your own small software business, and it changed how you think about work, money, negotiation and confidence. Write a personal essay about those changes.
Write an essay arguing that how a startup gets its customers deserves as much innovation as the product itself. Aim it at technical founders who assume the product will sell itself.

A few months ago I quit my job to run my own small software business from Japan. Write a candid blog post about the hardest adjustment to self-employment, which for me turns out to be something I didn't expect.

I sell a small piece of software to elementary school teachers, and my sales swing wildly over the course of the year. Most software founders I talk to seem to have never thought about seasonality at all. Write a blog post on dealing with market seasonality in a software business: understanding it, surviving the slow months, using them well, explaining the dips to outsiders, and preparing for the busy season.

You've sold a bingo card program to teachers for four years, first as a downloadable Java app and for the last year also as a web app, with one price covering both. You've just launched an A/B test where half your visitors see a site on which the downloadable version never existed. Write the blog post explaining why you're doing it, how you're avoiding hurting existing customers, and what you hope it does for the business.

I'm a solo founder running a web app with paying customers and no ops team. Write a thorough guide to keeping a small company's website reliable: where failures really come from, how to prevent and contain them, how to find out fast when something breaks, and how to learn from outages, without letting the pager wreck my life.

You've been running a small software business that sells to teachers for a few years, mostly in spare hours around a brutal Japanese salaryman job, and you're about to quit to go full time. Write a long, practical blog post for programmers who want to run a business on the side with only a few hours a week: what actually lets you pull it off?

There's another round of hand-wringing about how few women there are in Silicon Valley startups. You're a bootstrapped software founder living in Japan whose customers are mostly women. Write a frank, contrarian blog post about the debate and what the Valley might be getting wrong.

I run a one-person software business and I waste way too much time bouncing between analytics, my payment processor and email. Write a blog post about designing an internal dashboard for a small software company: what belongs on it, what doesn't, and why.

You sell a small piece of software to teachers and recently ran an in-app user survey that about forty customers filled out. Write a blog post on what you learned from it, both about running surveys and about your customers, aimed at other small software vendors.

It's early 2010, publishers are fighting Amazon over e-book pricing and delaying Kindle editions to protect hardcover sales. As a voracious reader who now buys almost everything on a Kindle, write a funny, pointed set of open letters to the parties involved.

Small software companies keep asking me how to 'do SEO', and I'm tired of giving everyone a fragment of an answer. Write the long-form piece I can point them to: not page-level tweaks like title tags, but the strategic decisions a startup should make about search, given that it has little money, a brand-new domain, and engineers who are a bit squeamish about the whole subject.

I'm a programmer running a one-person software business. My instinct whenever sales are slow is to build another feature. Write an essay arguing for a different use of engineering time: how a developer can point their programming skills at marketing instead, with concrete kinds of things worth building.

I run a small software business on the side while holding a demanding day job, and I keep hearing that the only way to win is to outwork your competitors. I think that's wrong. Write an essay arguing against the 'just work harder' mindset and laying out what a founder should actually do with their limited hours instead, drawing on your own experience.

You've been selling a downloadable desktop app for a few years and recently launched a web version of the same product. Write a blog post about which one you'd build if you were starting over, and why, using what your own numbers have shown you.

I run a small one-person software business selling a desktop app to consumers, and people keep telling me I'm doomed because there are free open source programs that do the same thing. Write a blog post for other small software sellers about whether and how you can actually compete with free open source alternatives in the consumer market.

Write a research blog post exploring what topology can tell us about what neural networks are doing when they classify data. Focus on low-dimensional networks where you can actually see what's happening, and work out what this implies about network width and architecture.

Explain backpropagation from the ground up using computational graphs, so that someone who knows basic calculus understands why it's so much faster than the naive approach and when forward-mode differentiation would be better instead.

I'm in the second year of a PhD and keep hearing that what separates good researchers is 'research taste', the ability to pick good problems. Nobody tells you how to actually get better at it. Can you write something practical on how to deliberately develop research taste, including the common ways people go wrong?

Write a short essay from the point of view of someone who studies the internals of artificial neural networks, on the ways their job is easier than a neuroscientist's, and what follows from that for how interpretability research should be done.

People talk a lot about analogies between physics and deep learning. I want a rough, exploratory blog post on the less-discussed analogies to biology, especially ones that might be useful for interpretability work. Speculative is fine, just be honest about where the analogies strain.

You've been part of many large ML research collaborations and have seen a few fall apart over hurt feelings about credit. Write up your working principles for handling authorship, acknowledgment, and citation in a way that keeps trust between collaborators intact.

You've built a research career without an undergrad degree or a PhD, and teenagers keep emailing to ask whether they should skip university. Write the essay you wish you could send them: how to think about the decision, and the costs and pressures that come with not going, including the ones nobody warns you about.

Jhanas get described as an 'advanced' meditation practice, which suggests you need years of sitting before you can reach them. You worked with a jhana retreat company on data from about 80 first-time participants. Write up whether meditation experience actually predicts who gets into the jhanas, what you found, the caveats, and what you think might matter instead.

People in tech love to say things like 'there are only 50 people in the world who can do this job,' while consultancies talk about hiring 'top talent.' Are those the same idea? Write an essay on how different kinds of companies think about talent scarcity, and what that does to their cultures.

More and more people I know say they won't have kids because of climate change, AI risk, or because the money would do more good elsewhere. I'm about to start a family myself, and I don't find the usual 'it's natural, just have kids' response convincing as an answer to that. Write a personal essay that takes these social-movement arguments against having children seriously and tries to work out what's really underneath them.

Write an essay on how ideologies in tech, effective altruism being the clearest case, turn into working machinery that moves money and people toward real outcomes. What are the parts of that machinery, how does it compare to the big philanthropic foundations of the 20th century, and should we want more of these things or fewer? Assume a reader who knows tech but isn't an EA.

Everyone is excited about the 'creator economy' and the new tools that let people make a living publishing online. I have mixed feelings about it. Write a reflective essay on what it actually means to be a 'creator' and whether the constant pressure to keep producing serves culture or just fills it up.

I work in tech and, like most people around me, I've been pretty cynical about universities. Someone told me I should look at what Arizona State has done under Michael Crow before writing academia off. Can you write a long blog post walking through ASU's reform model, how it's organized, what it changed, and whether the results hold up or it's mostly marketing? Write it from the point of view of a tech person who is interested in research but wary of academia.

Write a short essay on not voting as a deliberate political act. Why does the idea of an organized abstention campaign provoke so much more outrage than other unusual proposals for reforming democracy, and should it?

You've spent about five years researching one niche topic outside academia, funded by a foundation, then a job at the company at the center of it, then a research role, and you're about to finish a book. Friends keep saying it was basically a PhD. Write a reflective essay on how you actually did it, phase by phase, what you'd tell someone considering independent research instead of a doctorate, and how the PhD itself might be reimagined.

I live in San Francisco and my whole social life has turned into trading ideas: what are you reading, what are you thinking about. It's started to feel like work. Write a personal essay about that fatigue, and about the appeal of deliberately being basic as a way out.

Write an essay about whether it's ethical to publicize small hidden communities, both physical places like an undiscovered town and online subcultures that would rather stay obscure. When does sharing a discovery become exploiting it?

GitHub just launched Sponsors, and the standard take is that individual donations are small potatoes and the real money for open source is in companies. Write a blog post that pushes back: what would a standalone case for developer-to-developer sponsorship look like? Feel free to borrow from how Twitch streamers make money.

Write a speculative essay that treats ideas, not people, as the real actors in culture: creators as hosts that ideas use. What does that lens say about reputation, about why audiences trap successful artists in their old work, and about how a creator might keep some freedom?

You ran a personal microgrant program for two years, read thousands of applications, and are now putting it on hiatus. People keep asking you how to start one. Write the cheat sheet: the practical logistics and the lessons about making a program actually matter.

I want a blog post about why people support creators they follow, through newsletters, Patreon and the like, and why the perks and reward tiers that crowdfunding inherited may be the wrong model. Start from personal experience running a newsletter if that helps.

People keep asking me whether open source maintainers could get paid if projects just switched to commercial or more restrictive licenses. I'm skeptical but haven't put my reasons in order. Write a short blog post laying out the case, both practical and philosophical.
Write an essay about why acting shamelessly seems to work so well in public life now, when social punishment used to keep people in line. Feel free to start from a game or some everyday analogy.

I've been reading Jane Jacobs' The Death and Life of Great American Cities and keep thinking it says something about social media. Write a long essay using her ideas about public and private life in cities to think through how we live online.
Write a reflective essay on whether humans are best understood as animals or as something closer to gods, and what follows if we might be alone in the universe.

For about two years you've run a small no-strings microgrant program out of your own pocket, sending a few thousand dollars at a time to individuals around the world. Write a reflective post on what you've learned about personal giving, what you got wrong, and where you want to take it next.

Platforms like Slack and Facebook run developer funds that take equity in the apps built on them. Write a short blog post arguing about whether platforms should instead give their own equity to third-party developers.

I run a small side project giving out $1,000 no-strings grants, funded by sponsors, and I've been going back and forth on whether to publicize who gets the grants and who funds them. Publicity would help it grow, but something about it bothers me. Write a blog post working through that tension, and what it says about doing good on the internet more generally.

Write an essay making the case for independent research: people who study things seriously without a university or academic post behind them. Look at the history, the downsides, and whether it's realistic today.

I just watched a documentary about indie App Store developers and kept thinking about open source maintainers. Write an essay comparing the two groups: what they have in common, how the platforms they depend on shape their economics, and where they differ.

Can you write up the main ideas in Elinor Ostrom's Governing the Commons for someone who works on open source infrastructure? I want to know what she actually argued, why it matters, and why it never caught on the way the tragedy of the commons did.

Write an essay on online outrage through the lens of Albert Hirschman's exit vs. voice. What would it mean for people to be able to 'exit' platforms like Facebook and Twitter, and should platforms design for it?

Developers' skills are in huge demand, yet code they write on their own, especially open source, earns almost nothing. Write an essay on the ways developers have made money over the years and where that might be heading.

Everyone in crypto is proposing new governance models, but they nearly all boil down to some form of voting. Write a post questioning that: what's wrong with voting as a governance mechanism, especially for decentralized communities, and what could replace it?

Write a personal essay, in the first person, about why someone who has experienced harassment at work might stay silent about it for years, and why the usual media coverage of these stories can make that silence worse rather than better.

Apple just refused the FBI's order to help unlock the San Bernardino shooter's iPhone, and most people I know in tech are cheering. I am too, but something about the reaction bugs me. Write a short essay on how the tech world decides whom to trust with power, companies or governments.

People are up in arms that Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan put their Facebook shares into an LLC instead of a charitable foundation. Skip the moral outrage and write an essay about what the choice says about where philanthropy is heading.

The Atlantic ran a piece arguing programmers should stop calling themselves 'engineers' because they don't carry the public responsibility that civil engineers do. Write a response essay. Take the argument seriously, but tell me where you think it goes wrong.

I just got back from a startup conference for female founders, and it felt different from the usual 'women in tech' events in a way I'm still trying to put into words. Write a blog post reflecting on an event like that and what it suggests about how we organize conversations around inclusion.

Everyone in startups is talking about radical transparency right now: open salaries, public fundraising numbers, all of it. Write a blog post on the other side of that coin. What does privacy actually do for us?
Udemy vs Skillshare, Uber vs Lyft: the same teachers, drivers and customers use all of them. Write up some thinking on what peer-to-peer businesses end up looking like once they reach scale.

Whenever someone raises concerns about big data and targeted advertising, the answer is 'you can't fight progress.' Write an essay questioning that line, using history to think about whether societies ever do choose to hold back on a technology.

Satire about TV-addicted, ad-dazed consumers is starting to feel dated, and 'people staring at their phones' already feels like yesterday's critique. Write an essay guessing at what the cultural critics of ten years from now will skewer about how we live online today.

Investors keep talking about using data to predict which startups will succeed. Write an essay about the pitfalls of predicting the future from historical data when the thing you're measuring keeps changing underneath you.
Foundations have started talking about 'innovation funding' and comparing themselves to venture capitalists. Write a piece on what philanthropic funders and VCs could each learn from the other.

Last week I wrote about funding structures that line up innovation with business, and the most common reply was 'isn't that what B Corps are for?' Write a follow-up post on why 'doing good' shouldn't be defined by tax status or labels.

Wikipedia runs on donations and has no ads. Facebook went public and built an advertising machine on user data. Write an essay asking what would have happened if Facebook had gone the nonprofit route, and what that means for how we fund audience companies with no obvious way to make money.

Write a blog post with your first impressions after a few months of learning Django for a small website, from the point of view of someone who's never really used a full web framework before. Keep it casual and honest about what you like and what still bugs you.

I'm not a C programmer, but every so often I need to compile some C or C++ program from source, and when `make` fails (especially on my Mac) I'm lost. Can you write a practical guide to what's actually going on and how to get things to build?
I run a handful of tiny hobby web services and I want them to mostly stay up while spending close to zero time on operations. Write a blog post on how you'd monitor small, low-stakes sites like that.

Write up your notes on using bubblewrap to run containers that start much faster than Docker, as an unprivileged user, for a small hobby project on a tiny server. Be candid about the weird problems you hit along the way and what's going on under the hood.

Someone just emailed me about how real regex engines like RE2 work and I realized what I learned in my automata class doesn't match reality. Write a casual blog post working through how regular expressions are actually implemented, including this 'derivatives of regular expressions' idea I keep hearing about.

I've always been intimidated by tcpdump - the output looks like gibberish. Write a friendly blog post for developers on how to actually get useful answers out of it (and related tools) when debugging real problems.

I just heard a talk about Roaring Bitmaps. Write a blog post explaining why fast integer sets matter, how bitmaps work as sets, and what modern CPUs have to do with designing data structures like this.

Write an enthusiastic blog post about the Coz causal profiling paper: why profiling multithreaded programs is hard and what clever trick the paper uses to get around it. Write it as someone who doesn't usually read papers and got hooked.

My little Go web service keeps getting OOM killed on a tiny VM, and most of its memory goes to an in-memory IP-to-ASN lookup table. Write a blog post about the process of trying to shrink that memory usage: what you tried, what didn't work, and what you learned along the way.

You run a small educational DNS playground website whose hand-rolled DNS server had lots of correctness bugs, and you just rebuilt it on top of PowerDNS. Write a blog post about the migration and the challenges you ran into along the way.

I built a side project that mounts a git repo as a filesystem where every commit is a folder, using NFS instead of FUSE on Mac. Write a blog post explaining the idea, why it might be useful, and the technical problems I hit building it.

A friend learning to program asked for ideas for small, fun projects they could finish in an evening. Write a blog post about the tiny personal programs you've written for yourself and why you love doing them.

You've just built a website where people can experiment with DNS on a real subdomain and watch queries arrive live. Write a long blog post on why you made it, how the experiments were designed, what user testing taught you, and the interesting parts of building the backend.

People talk about the "current branch" in git as if it were one obvious thing. Is it actually well defined? Write a blog post that tests the different ways you might answer "what branch am I on" across a range of real situations and reports what you find.
A lot of git users say they don't really understand what HEAD is. Write a clear explainer on how HEAD works in git, aimed at someone who uses git every day but has never looked under the hood.

Write a practical guide to the situation where your local git branch and the remote branch have diverged: how to tell that's what's happening, and the different ways to deal with it depending on what you want.
Give me a tour of what's actually inside the .git directory: what each important file or folder is, what it contains, and how it relates to the git concepts I use day to day.

I'm trying to figure out the best way to explain what a git commit actually is to people learning git. Is it a diff? A snapshot? Something else? Write a blog post working through how people think about commits versus how git really stores them, and whether the 'wrong' way of thinking about it actually matters.

Lots of people say git branches are counterintuitive. Write a post comparing the intuitive picture most people have of a branch (an offshoot of main) with how git actually defines and stores branches, and where the intuition holds up and where it breaks down. Use a small example repo with real commands.

I always assumed git cherry-pick just computes the diff of a commit and applies it as a patch. Is that actually what it does? Write a blog post digging into how cherry-pick and revert work under the hood, with small examples I could try myself.

I use git rebase all the time and don't have problems with it, but a lot of people I talk to say they hate it. Write a post cataloguing what actually goes wrong for people with rebase in practice, along with workarounds where they exist, so I can be more careful about recommending it to newcomers.

Git's vocabulary is notoriously confusing: HEAD, detached HEAD, fast-forward, tree-ish, the index, remote-tracking branches and so on. Write a long blog post going through the git terms people find most confusing and explaining what each one really means, being honest about the ones that are genuinely badly named.

Everyone knows git keeps your history in the .git directory, but where exactly are the old versions of a file stored in there? Write a hands-on blog post that investigates this with a real repository and a few very short Python scripts, so a curious programmer could follow along.

DNS has barely changed in 30+ years and every website depends on it, yet plenty of experienced programmers I know still can't confidently debug a DNS problem, and it took me years too. Write a blog post digging into why it's so hard to learn, and what could make it easier.

Why does dig print example.com with a dot at the end, and why do some DNS libraries refuse a domain without one? I know it's something about 'fully qualified' names but I want to understand why the trailing dot actually matters. Write it up as a blog post.

I'm learning how DNS works and keep tripping over the words 'nameserver' and 'DNS resolver', which seem to mean different things in different docs. Write a short explainer that untangles this terminology for a beginner.

"It's always DNS" is a running joke for a reason. Write a blog post cataloguing the real-world ways DNS breaks systems in practice, especially the failures that don't look like DNS problems at first. Keep it concrete and practical, no lecture on how to fix each one.

Most people just use their registrar's DNS and their ISP's resolver. Write a friendly, practical post on why someone might run their own DNS servers instead, both authoritative nameservers and resolvers, and what the fact that DNS is decentralized actually buys you.

Everyone says to wait 24-48 hours for DNS to "propagate" after a change. Write a blog post about what's really going on when you're waiting on a DNS update, why it can be slow, and whether the word "propagation" gives people the right mental model.

I know ANSI escape codes are how terminals do colours and cursor movement, but I have no idea who defines them or whether there's an actual standard. Write a post that maps out the standards landscape for escape codes (ECMA-48, xterm, terminfo and so on) and whether they'll ever be as reliable as web standards.

Write a complete, step-by-step guide to adding a directory to your PATH that covers bash, zsh and fish, how to find the right config file and the right directory, and the common gotchas people hit when it still doesn't work afterwards.

Someone told me they wish a modern terminal experience just came out of the box. Write a reflective post on what a "modern" terminal setup actually involves, how you get there yourself, and why it's harder than experienced users tend to admit.

There's no real standard for how terminal programs should behave, yet most of them act pretty consistently. Write a post laying out the unwritten conventions terminal programs tend to follow, why they exist, and where they get broken.

Write a blog post about why shell pipelines sometimes seem to get "stuck" and print nothing, aimed at people who use the terminal every day but never quite understood it, including the practical ways to work around it.

I've used the terminal for years and I still get tripped up editing a command I've already typed: shortcuts work in one program and not another, arrow keys sometimes print garbage. Can you write a blog post explaining why entering text in the terminal is so inconsistent, and give some practical tips along the way?

When you press a key in a terminal (a letter, Ctrl+C, Escape, Home), what bytes actually get sent, and to whom? Write an exploratory blog post that works this out by experimenting, for programmers who use terminals every day without knowing how they work.

I want to write toy implementations of networking protocols like TCP in Python, with no libraries. The first hurdle is just sending and receiving raw packets without the OS getting in the way. Write a tutorial-style blog post on how to do that on Linux.

Write a blog post that walks through building a toy remote login server in Go: like a tiny ssh with no security at all, purely to learn how terminals work. Explain the server and client step by step, including the bits of Linux terminal machinery you have to understand along the way.

Some huge websites still don't support IPv6 and seem to get on fine. So why do people bother adding IPv6 support to their servers? Write a blog post working through the question, including how IPv4-only sites keep working for people who've been pushed onto IPv6.

A friend just asked me how to put a single HTML page on the internet, and I realised I'd make it way too complicated. Write a short, friendly blog post on the simplest way to do it, for someone who just wants to play with HTML and CSS.

I barely know C++ but I've been contributing to a big C++ codebase (a network proxy), and I finally get why destructors matter beyond freeing memory. Write a blog post explaining it through a concrete example from a proxy, aimed at people who come from garbage-collected languages.

I'm running an internal workshop on IP addresses for my team. Write up some friendly blog-style notes on what's in an IP packet and what actually decides where a packet goes on a Linux machine, with real commands people can try. IPv4 only is fine.

What actually is a network interface on Linux? Don't give me a textbook definition; poke at it with some experiments (network namespaces, tcpdump, the route table) and write up what you figure out, blog-post style.

iptables scares me, and Kubernetes keeps generating piles of rules I can't read. Write a beginner-friendly blog post on the basics: how to see what rules you have and how to decode one of those cryptic NAT rules.
Write a short, enthusiastic blog post about using Linux's tc to add fake network latency to your laptop or a test server, including anything surprising you notice when you browse the web that way.
How big can a network packet actually be? Write a casual explainer that starts from UDP and works through why big packets don't always make it across the internet.

I've used HTTPS forever but have no idea what's inside an SSL certificate. Can you write a hands-on blog post that pulls a real site's certificate with openssl, takes it apart, and explains signing and how the whole trust system is kept honest?
People shrug off lost UDP packets with "well, that's UDP." Write a blog post about where UDP packets actually get dropped on a Linux machine and how you can tell it's happening.
