When one server hosts a bunch of websites, how does an HTTP request end up at the right one? And how does that work once HTTPS is involved? Write it up as a personal, curious blog post with commands people can try.

I just heard a talk where someone said writing your own TCP stack made their web framework several times faster. So why does almost everyone use the Linux kernel's TCP stack anyway? Write a blog post exploring that question.
I just joined an infrastructure team and always assumed CDNs were purely about caching static files. Write a blog post on what else people put their sites behind a CDN for, including the downsides.

My site is down or crawling and someone on the team always says 'it's probably DNS.' How do you actually figure out whether a problem is caused by DNS? Write it up as a practical blog post, with some real debugging stories if you have them.

Every networking tutorial I open starts with the 7-layer OSI model and I can't figure out how it lines up with what actually runs on the internet (TCP, IP, Ethernet, DNS...). Can you write a blog post for beginners about how the OSI model relates to TCP/IP, and whether I really need to learn it?

Running strace inside a Docker container fails with 'ptrace: Operation not permitted', and adding --cap-add=SYS_PTRACE makes it work. I don't just want the fix, I want to know why. Write up an investigation of what's really going on, walking through the hypotheses you'd test along the way.
A friend who's new to tech asked me 'what is a server, actually?' and I fumbled the answer. Write a blog post exploring what people really mean by the word 'server', with concrete examples.
How do Docker containers avoid copying a huge image every time you start one? Write a hands-on explainer of overlay filesystems that I could follow along with on my own Linux machine.

I added myself to a new group on Linux and still got 'Permission denied' on a file owned by that group. Write a blog post explaining how users and groups actually work for processes on Linux, aimed at someone who thought they already understood it.

I keep seeing epoll_wait when I strace programs and I only vaguely know what select, poll and epoll are for. I've just started reading The Linux Programming Interface. Write a blog post explaining these three system calls, how they differ, and why servers care.
Write a friendly explainer of what actually happens on Linux when one program starts another, for programmers who've never looked under the hood, and why the details might matter when debugging.

I've used gdb for years as a kind of magic C REPL without knowing what it's doing underneath. Can you write a hands-on blog post that walks through how gdb actually finds a variable, reads its memory and knows what the struct fields are? Use a real running program (say, the Ruby interpreter) and show the commands.

I said online that Unix signals scare me a bit and a few experienced people told me that's silly, signals are well understood. Write a blog post where you think this through honestly: what signals are, what can actually go wrong with them, which serious programs rely on them, and whether being scared is reasonable.

Write a blog post about trying to parallelize a slow job on the JVM with a thread pool and discovering it's much harder than the one-liner it is in Python. Tell it as the story of what went wrong, what you learned about how thread pools work underneath, and what it says about abstractions.

People talk about "the stack" like it's some sacred fundamental object: stack overflows, stack smashing, setting the stack size. Every language has a call stack, so why is there one capital-S Stack? Write a curious, concrete blog post that gets to the bottom of it, down to the assembly.

I just lost a day at work to a bug caused by Ruby's Timeout. Write a blog post explaining how Timeout works under the hood, why it's dangerous, and how other languages have dealt with the same idea of killing a thread from the outside.
Write a blog post arguing that ordinary application programmers should understand a little bit about TCP. Ground it in a real debugging story rather than theory.

I want to understand how SQLite stores data on disk. Write a blog post about building a small test database, looking at the raw file, and hacking the SQLite source so it tells you which pages it reads when you run a query. Keep it exploratory and fun.

Compiled binaries feel like impenetrable blobs to me. Write a beginner-friendly tour of what's inside a Linux ELF executable, using a tiny hello-world C program and standard tools, so that by the end symbols, sections and segments make sense.

You once wrote a toy TCP stack in Python just to fetch a single web page. Write a blog post about how that went: the plan, the surprises, what broke, and what you learned about networking along the way.

Why is a byte 8 bits? Is that a historical accident or is there something genuinely best about 8? I'm not a computer historian, so write it as an honest investigation: lay out the plausible reasons, say which ones you find convincing and where you're unsure.

Everyone knows 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004 in Python, and everyone hand-waves it with 'floats are inexact'. But that doesn't explain why you get that particular number rather than the float closest to 0.3. Can you work through the actual arithmetic, step by step, with Python you can run to check each step? A blog post in a curious, learning-out-loud voice is fine.

Write a blog post collecting real-world examples of bugs caused by integers: overflow, signedness, byte order, that kind of thing. For each one, show a small program that reproduces it in a language like Go, Java, C, or JavaScript, explain what's actually happening at the bit level, and say what you can do about it where you know.

I keep hearing abstract warnings about floating point (addition isn't associative, big and small numbers don't mix, etc.) but I'd like concrete stories of floats actually breaking real programs. Write a post that goes through a handful of real-world floating point bugs, reproduces some of them with small programs, and explains why each one happens and how you might avoid it.

I write frontend JavaScript with no build system, and I keep getting stuck because library setup instructions all assume webpack or vite. Write the guide you'd want: what kinds of JS files a library might ship, how to figure out which ones a given library actually provides, and how to load each kind in the browser without a bundler. Use real libraries as examples.

Write a blog post about whether to use a JavaScript build system for small personal web projects. I'm interested in the honest tradeoffs for someone who builds lots of tiny sites and touches them once every few years, not advice for big frontend teams.

I'm not a frontend developer, just someone who builds little side-project sites, and I've always reached for jQuery or Vue. Write a short, friendly blog post about trying plain JavaScript with no library for a small project, and the handful of built-in browser APIs that made it easier than expected.

You're an infrastructure engineer who has spent a few months running Kubernetes clusters. Write a blog post on why Kubernetes is actually interesting, for someone who doesn't get the hype, and try to do it without leaning on buzzwords like 'cloud native' or 'orchestration'. Be honest about what's hard, too.

Write a blog post about a recent production mystery: build machines that kept swapping and getting processes OOM-killed even though they seemed to have plenty of free memory. Walk through how you figured it out and what it taught you about Linux memory.

Container networking documentation is mostly terrible. Write a plain-language explainer of how 'every container gets its own IP address' actually works on a cluster of cloud machines, building up from the networking basics a developer would need.
What actually is a container? I want a friendly, hands-on blog post explaining the Linux kernel features underneath, with a few commands a reader can try themselves.

You write zines and blog posts for people teaching themselves technical topics, and you've been prototyping a quiz-like tool to help them figure out what they don't know yet. Write a blog post about how the design evolved and what you learned from people's reactions along the way.

I'm moving toward teaching programming and want to start writing practice exercises. Before I do, help me think it through: what actually makes a programming exercise good, as opposed to one people abandon after ten minutes? Write it as a blog post.

Someone asked me how I cope with writing technical blog posts in public when internet commenters can be so rude. I don't want to just say 'don't read the comments.' Write a blog post from the perspective of a long-time technical blogger about practical ways to get more useful comments and fewer annoying ones.

Most programmers I know learned 'backwards': they built things with frameworks first and only later found out what was underneath. Write an essay about how to teach people who learned that way, aimed at someone who writes technical tutorials.
When I write programming tutorials my code examples always feel fake and contrived. Write a blog post about how to come up with good examples for explaining programming concepts.
You draw popular comics explaining programming concepts. A friend asks how you do it, and you suspect the honest answer has little to do with drawing. Write it up as a blog post.

People keep emailing to ask if they can hire you to document their open source project with comics. You don't take commissions, but you'd like to give them something more useful than 'no'. Write a blog post with practical advice for them.

In what situations does teaching technical topics with comics actually help, and is 'some people are visual learners' a good enough answer? Write a reflective blog post from the perspective of someone who makes programming zines.

You've been posting simple hand-drawn comics about Linux every day, and a commenter called them childish and asked why anyone likes them when Wikipedia exists. Write a short blog post answering that honestly.

I help organize a small tech conference, and our committee keeps arguing about whether to review talk proposals anonymously. Some say it's fairer, others worry it costs time and hurts new speakers. Write a blog post that goes through the question honestly: what anonymous review does and doesn't buy you, and whether it's worth it.

I run a tiny one-person business selling educational stuff for programmers, and I've always hated the idea of email marketing because I don't want to be the source of anyone's spam. Write a blog post from the point of view of someone who got past that: what did you believe about marketing email that turned out to be wrong, and how do you do it now in a way that feels decent?

You've started selling programming zines on the side, and most of your sales come from posting comics on Twitter. Write a candid, early-stage blog post working through marketing: what it's actually for, which common internet marketing tactics you'd use or avoid, and how to tell people about your work without being annoying.

Most of what working programmers learn from (blog posts, conference talks, docs, meetups) is free to read. Somebody is paying for it, though. Write a blog post that maps out who funds developer education and what each kind of funder gets out of it, and think about what that means for where you choose to learn from.

I keep seeing those apps that repaint your photo in the style of a famous painting. I'm a programmer but pretty new to neural networks. Can you write a blog post working out how neural style transfer actually works, going from the original paper's math rather than vague intuition?

Write a short blog post for people new to machine learning: even though ML is powerful and fun, what are some basic reasons to stay skeptical of what a model tells you? Write it from the perspective of someone who builds ML systems at work.

You do machine learning at a tech company and have spent a couple of years uneasy about using big models (random forests and the like) that nobody can really explain. Write a blog post about why black-box models bothered you and what you've found actually helps you see inside them.

I was a pure math major and machine learning's 'well, it works in practice' attitude drives me up the wall. Write me an explainer on the bias-variance tradeoff that is honest about which parts are actual theorems and which are heuristics, and that shows what it buys you when building models.

I tried a Kaggle competition, landed nowhere near the leaderboard, and now I'm wondering if I'm just bad at machine learning. You do ML as your actual job. Can you write a blog post about how real-world machine learning work compares to Kaggle?
Everyone treats being on call as pure misery. Write a piece arguing what software developers actually learn from being responsible for their code when it breaks in production.

I've used bash for years but only by copy-pasting. Can you write a friendly guide to the basics and the weird quirks of bash as a programming language (variables, loops, ifs, quoting, return codes) plus the safety settings people should put at the top of their scripts?

I've seen 'devops' on job postings for years and honestly have no idea what it's supposed to mean beyond 'uses Chef and Puppet'. Write a blog post figuring out what devops actually is and why someone might find it exciting.

Write a post for software developers who have never thought about operations: what is it, how does your understanding of it tend to evolve, and how can an ordinary developer start getting better at it?
How do you even begin capacity planning for a web app that gets sudden spikes in traffic? Write up what a working engineer knows about it, without pretending to be an expert.
Write a short blog post in praise of log files as a debugging tool for performance problems, compared with dashboards and graphs.
There's a line between healthy caution and fear that stops you from making necessary changes to code. Write a blog post about how fear makes programmers worse and what teams can do about it.

Write a blog post encouraging engineers to tell a colleague's manager when that colleague does great work, especially as a way to support people from underrepresented groups. Cover when it matters, how to do it well, and what can go wrong.

I'm an engineer at a mid-sized tech company and I'd like to make our hiring a bit fairer without starting a huge political fight. Write a short blog post making the case for one small, practical change engineers can push for in how their company runs technical interviews.

You just finished a three-month funded sabbatical from your software job to work full-time on an open source profiler. Write a reflective blog post about how that came together, what made it possible, and what you'd tell other developers considering something similar.

Perf review season is coming and I have to write peer reviews for coworkers I think are great. Everything I write comes out as 'X is awesome, love working with them.' Can you write a blog post on how to write positive feedback in a review that's actually useful to the person and to their managers?

I've been at my job for about three years and I'm starting to wonder what I've actually accomplished. Write a blog post about sitting down and writing out your whole career at a company so far: how you might do it and what you get out of it.

Write an essay, from the point of view of a working software engineer who gets plenty of recruiter emails, on why some job pitches get a reply and others don't, and what that suggests about how teams should think about recruiting.
React or Angular, nginx or Apache, Python or Ruby: I get stuck agonizing over which tool is the best every time. Write a blog post about a less paralyzing way to make technical choices.
I'm an individual engineer on a small team, so what I personally ship matters a lot. Write a blog post, personal rather than preachy, about the habits that actually help you get things done at work.

When I started programming I assumed someone would just tell me what to build. Now I have a lot of autonomy and honestly struggle to pick what's worth months of my time. Write an honest essay about how a software engineer decides what to work on.
Write a short, informal blog post on the different routes you can take when you face a hard programming problem and no software solves it yet.

Write a guide for software engineers weighing an offer from a private startup that includes stock options. I don't want a full textbook treatment. I want to understand what can go wrong, especially if I leave before an IPO, the math I should do, and what I should ask before signing.

Someone just emailed me asking how to learn to program. I'd like to write a short, honest blog post about how long it really took me, for beginners who feel behind because of all the 'learn to code in 12 weeks' talk.

I'm a regular software engineer, not a manager, and I keep hearing that culture is set from the top. Write a blog post about whether individual engineers can actually change how things work at their company, drawing on concrete examples, and what tends to help when you try.
Write a casual blog post about what a team member (not the manager) can do to make their team a great one to work on. Base it on a conversation with a friend who's good at this.

I've always found writing design documents kind of pointless and get grumpy when asked to. Write a blog post from the perspective of an engineer who used to feel that way and has slowly started finding them useful: what changed, and how to get real value out of them.
Write a short blog post about reading the source code of the libraries you use when the docs don't answer your question, and about when that approach stops working.

You've worked remotely from Montreal for a San Francisco company for four years, and lots of people have asked you what it's really like. Write a long blog post answering the common worries: loneliness, communication, staying in the loop, and whether your career can grow while remote.

A lot of people tell me they'd like to start a technical blog but don't know what to write about that anyone would find useful. Write an essay on one good answer to that: using the things you've personally struggled with as the source of posts.

Write a blog post about how to measure whether a personal blog is successful if you don't care about maximizing page views. Write it as someone who has blogged for a few years and gets a lot out of it.
You've kept a technical blog going for years while lots of people start one and quit after three posts. Write up the handful of principles that actually keep you publishing, in your own voice.
Write a casual blog post about migrating your personal blog from Jekyll to Hugo: why you bothered, how you actually did it without understanding your old setup, and whether it was worth it.

Someone emailed asking for advice on starting a tech blog, with a bunch of specific questions: what you get out of it, how you started, how long posts take, how you pick topics, whether it's scary. Answer them as a blog post.
Write a short, encouraging post for programmers who are terrified of public speaking, explaining why they should submit a conference talk anyway and how to think about preparing one.

When I ask a senior engineer something I often get a long explanation of stuff I already know or stuff that's irrelevant. Write a practical essay on how to ask questions so you actually get useful answers.

Growth mindset is fine, but attitude alone doesn't get you through learning something genuinely hard. Write an essay on the concrete learning skills a programmer can practice to teach themselves difficult technical topics.

Everyone says to grow as a programmer you need side projects, conference talks and books in your evenings. I don't want to do extra work after hours. Write a post about how to keep learning and get really good mostly during the workday.
Write an essay arguing that asking good questions is a learnable skill, with the kinds of questions that tend to unlock interesting knowledge from people who know more than you.

On every engineering team I've been on, crucial knowledge ends up stuck in one or two people's heads for years. Why does that happen, and what actually helps spread expertise around? Write it up as a blog post.
I'm a new programmer and I avoid asking questions because I'm afraid of looking dumb. Write a short essay making the case for asking anyway, from someone who learned this the hard way.

I've read the lifetimes chapter of the Rust book and sort of get it in principle, but I still get confused by really basic stuff, like why a struct holding a `&u8` won't compile. Write a blog post, from one learner to others, working out what a reference in Rust actually is and how it relates to Box, Vec and String.

I know roughly what strace is but never reach for it. What kinds of real-world problems do people actually solve with it? Write me a blog post that sorts the common uses into categories, with concrete examples.
Write a hands-on getting-started guide to ftrace for someone who already uses strace and perf but has never traced kernel functions. Explain what it's for and walk through actually using it.
Write a short blog post about using ltrace to track down a memory leak in a Rust program: what ltrace is, why it fits this kind of bug, and how you'd use it.

Write a blog post for working programmers about debugging programs without reading their source code or using a debugger, by watching what they ask the operating system to do on Linux. Keep it enthusiastic and concrete.

I've heard that if someone has root on a Linux box they can see the passwords people type when they ssh in, just using strace. How does that actually work? Write it up as a short blog post walking through it.
Write a short, playful blog post that uses strace to figure out what killall actually does under the hood on Linux.
Write a short debugging manifesto: a handful of principles about the right attitude to have when you're chasing a bug, each with a bit of explanation from your own experience.

I'm on call for a distributed system for the first time and keep drowning in log files from a dozen servers when something breaks. Can you write up practical tips for analyzing logs when debugging, plus a few notes on producing logs that are easier to analyze?

Blog post idea: what are the different kinds of knowledge you need to be good at debugging, and what can a programmer actually do to get better at each? Feel free to draw on research about how people troubleshoot.

A friend who writes Python told me he's never tried debugging by dropping into a REPL at a breakpoint. Write a quick blog post explaining what that is, how to do it in Python and Ruby (and sort of in C), and why you might prefer it to a traditional debugger.
You asked programmers on Twitter what made a bug feel 'impossible' to understand and got hundreds of replies. Write a post that sorts those reasons into categories.
You just got told in a performance review that you're very good at debugging hard problems, and you didn't used to be. Write a blog post reflecting on what changed.

Write up a debugging story: a Go binary copied into an Alpine Docker container fails with 'no such file or directory' even though the file is clearly there. Walk through how you'd track down the cause and fix it.

I keep seeing the CAP theorem cited in distributed systems discussions and I've never felt like I really get it or know when to apply it. Write a blog post explaining what it actually says, how useful it is in practice, and what Martin Kleppmann's paper "A Critique of the CAP Theorem" adds to the picture.

I maintain a Linux profiler that reads another process's memory, and someone asked for it to work on programs running inside containers. Write a blog post explaining what 'container support' actually involves at the system-call level for a tool like this, using my case as the worked example.

I'm porting a Ruby profiler from Linux to macOS and need the memory maps of a target process. Write up a blog post about how you get memory maps on a Mac compared with Linux, what approaches you can try, and where it gets hard.

I'm writing a sampling profiler for Ruby in Rust that reads stack traces out of a running process. Should it pause the process with ptrace before each sample? Write a blog post working through the question, including some experiments.

Write a blog post on how a debugger or profiler figures out the memory address of a symbol (say, a global variable) in another running process on Linux. It sounds like 'just look in the symbol table' but I suspect it isn't. Walk through the pitfalls.

I'm building an out-of-process profiler for Ruby, modeled on pyflame for Python, which compiles against Python's public headers. Write a research-notes style blog post comparing Ruby's public C headers with Python's: embeddability, what types and structs they expose, and what's available for getting stack traces.

How do you write a profiler? Survey how the popular Ruby and Python CPU profilers actually work under the hood, with pointers into their code, as a blog post for programmers who use these tools but have never looked inside them.

Java has jstack and C has perf top, but there's nothing like that for a running Ruby program. Write a blog post about how you could build a tool that prints the current stack trace of any Ruby process from the outside, explaining the pieces as you go.

Every time I open top I stare at VIRT, RSS and SHR and wonder why I can't just get one number for how much memory my process is using. Write a friendly explainer that builds up enough about Linux virtual memory to make those columns make sense.

Write a short, informal blog post about the first time you ran into a Java program that was way slower than it should have been because of garbage collection. Walk through how you figured out what was happening and what you learned about the JVM along the way.

I keep meeting developers who shrug when their server tops out at a handful of requests per second, like that's just how computers are. Write a blog post arguing that programmers should have much higher expectations for how fast their machines can go, and what that mindset buys you.

Load averages in top have always been a mystery number to me: low is good, high is bad, that's all I know. Write a friendly blog post explaining what a CPU load average actually measures and whether you can use it to estimate how much CPU time each request on a web server is taking.

My Java programs at my old job were always slow and everyone blamed the language. Write a short blog post on whether Java is really a slow language, and what someone in that situation should do about it.

Write an enthusiastic blog post about a day at work when you found out a piece of Scala code taking about a millisecond per record was absurdly slow, how you profiled it, and the one-line fix. I want it to get across why a millisecond isn't actually fast.

You're a professional developer who has started needing to fix bugs and add features in big open source projects like Kubernetes for work, rather than just hunting for beginner issues. Write a blog post about what's actually different and harder about contributing to open source compared to your day job, and the tactics that have helped you get changes merged.

Write an exploratory blog post, from the point of view of an engineer at a tech company, about the open questions you have about open source: when to use it versus building your own, why companies pay people to write it, and how you're supposed to evaluate it. It's fine to raise more questions than you answer.

I have this low-grade guilt that I should be contributing to open source and I never do. Every time I try I bounce off. Can you write a blog post about whether people should feel obligated to contribute, and how to decide when it's actually worth your time?

Write a practical blog post for someone who's never debugged a segfault before: how to get Linux to actually write a core dump, and how to get a stack trace with line numbers out of it. Explain the settings involved rather than just listing commands.
Write a playful blog post about poking around in /proc on Linux: what file descriptors look like in there, what you can learn about running processes, and the surprising things it lets you do.
Short blog post idea: how do you approach a programming side project in a technology you've never used before, when you want to get it done without flailing for weeks?

I write technical explanations and try to keep the language simple, but I worry it sometimes reads as talking down to people. Write a blog post on how to explain complicated technical topics in plain language without sounding condescending.

I spent three months at a programming retreat where beginners improved absurdly fast, and I'm convinced a big part of it was the culture around asking for and giving help. Write a short, punchy blog post about why help matters so much in a community or workplace, aimed at teams that treat questions as interruptions.

I've been thinking about the way people argue online and why so much of it never changes anyone's mind. Write a funny but sharp blog post classifying the different kinds of opinion-posts by what psychological need they serve for the writer and for the audience, rather than by topic.

People keep accusing groups they dislike of being an insular echo chamber that doesn't listen to outside criticism, and no amount of evidence ever seems to satisfy them. Write an essay on how that argument works, and how a person should actually decide whose critics deserve their time.

I've had a concussion that's dragged on for over a year, and I just read a memoir by a professor who had a severe one and recovered through some odd-sounding treatments. Write a review-essay of the book that takes the strange treatments seriously but critically, and asks what it tells us about how medicine should handle poorly understood conditions.
Why did prehistoric people all over the world drill holes in each other's skulls, and why did so many survive? And why did the practice die out? Give me your best attempt at solving the mystery.

People in AI safety keep getting accused of wanting to hand the world over to machines. Write an essay defending a more careful position: that humans putting aligned AIs in positions of control might actually serve human interests. Make it concrete by walking through a range of what that could look like, from modest to radical.

Write a personal, funny-but-sincere essay from the point of view of a husband whose wife and he spent six years on unexplained infertility, about how they used an AI chatbot during treatment and what came of it. Include some honest ambivalence about AI more broadly.

An economist says AI alignment will be like aviation safety: no grand theory, we just patch problems as they come up and iterate. Write a thoughtful rebuttal. I'd like it to be vivid, with a thought experiment or two, and to engage with real evidence about how AI systems have behaved.

Online arguments about whether God exists are everywhere again, and I find I can't summon the old enthusiasm for the fine-tuning argument and the rest. Write an essay on why a long-time atheist might feel that his disbelief comes before the arguments, and whether that feeling can be defended rather than just dismissed as an intuition.

Write a short, funny-but-serious essay about how a whole body of good work (a person, a field, a movement) gets reduced in public memory to its single worst moment. Is that unfair, and do you honestly avoid doing it yourself?

I keep hearing the term 'stochastic terrorism' used to say that harsh rhetoric against a group is partly to blame when someone later commits violence against it. Is that a sound idea? Write an essay giving your honest view.

Everyone says we need to regulate AI more or less, but nobody says what a good outcome would actually look like. I want a blog post walking through one detailed, optimistic best-case roadmap for how a country could get through the arrival of transformative AI, and why you find it compelling despite how weird it sounds.

Doctors say healthy people shouldn't get whole-body MRI screening, which strikes a lot of people as crazy, since catching cancer early sounds obviously good. Do a rough cost-benefit analysis, written by someone who is a doctor but not a radiologist, and say honestly who, if anyone, should get one.

Midjourney, the AI image company, just announced a whole-body ultrasound scanner. Give me a skeptical but fair take from a doctor's perspective: what can it replace, what new uses could it open up, and is the hype justified?

I keep hearing the Frankfurt School blamed for everything, and I also keep hearing that you're not allowed to say anything about them, and I honestly have no idea what they believed. I'm going to read one standard history of the group. Write me a skeptical, funny, honest guide to what these people were actually trying to say, using analogies an outsider can follow.

I've got a stack of local races and ballot measures coming up and I never feel informed enough on them. Write a blog post about whether it's actually sensible to use an AI model as a research assistant for deciding how to vote. Draw on a real attempt if you can, including how well it worked and where it went wrong.

People often say that current language models can't reach AGI and that we'd need some new paradigm, so there's no need to worry about timelines. Write a short essay assessing whether that conclusion actually follows.

Why does AI-written fiction and poetry so often feel cheap and overdone, and what does that tell us about what good taste in art actually is? Write it as a proper essay, and feel free to bring in your own experience.

Talk about artistic taste. People mean a lot of different things when they say some art is good: novelty, context, sensory pleasure, and so on. Write an essay arguing that lumping them together causes confusion, and that we should keep a few of them separate from what makes art beautiful.

Some people think you should do whatever has the best consequences, except for a few hard-and-fast moral rules you never break. But where do those rules actually come from, and how would you tell which ones are real? Write an essay working it out, and test it on a live dilemma in AI safety activism.

Viktor Orban just lost an election in Hungary, and now commentators are saying that everyone who worried about his threat to democracy was proven wrong. Write an essay on whether that follows, and what we should call a leader like him.

I keep seeing people online get furious at conservatives who work inside or near the current administration but won't loudly denounce it. Write me a blog post on whether that social pressure actually helps, and what a person who hates the administration should do instead.

Everyone hates Congress and every proposed fix needs Congress to pass it. Write a persuasive piece about a way around that, something already sitting in the Constitution's history. Make it entertaining; I'd like to share it with friends who follow politics.

California's billionaire wealth tax ballot measure looks badly drafted, and I keep hearing it's being pushed by a healthcare union rather than by generic left-wing activists. Write an essay on who is really behind it and why that changes how we should read the whole thing.

People keep dismissing AI language models as 'just next-token predictors' or 'stochastic parrots.' Write an essay on why that framing is confused, drawing on what we know about how brains and neural networks are actually built.

Everyone I talk to thinks crime is out of control, but I keep hearing that the statistics say it's at historic lows. Is the data just bad? Write an essay that takes the two most obvious objections to the official numbers seriously and checks whether they hold up.

Ajeya Cotra's Biological Anchors report was supposed to be the big AI timelines forecast, and its headline date now looks too late. Write a retrospective: what did it get right, where did it go wrong, how did its critics do, and what should we conclude about forecasting?

Someone told me it's hypocritical for people to support foreign aid through taxes: if you really cared you'd donate yourself, and voting to spend other people's money is just cheap virtue. Is that actually what's going on when voters back foreign aid? Write an essay that takes the argument seriously and tests it.
Write a funny personal essay about life with toddler twins, the kind where everything is a crisis. Early mornings, songs, bedtime, the whole chaos.

I keep seeing tech people panic about having only a few years to get rich before the AI singularity locks in a permanent underclass. Write a short, playful essay arguing they're worrying about the wrong thing.
Hating Boomers seems to be the fashionable thing online. Write an essay on whether the case against the Boomer generation holds up, and whether generational blame is a good habit at all.

It's the holiday season and my blog is full of charity fundraisers. Write a post in the first person about why taking a formal giving pledge is better than deciding case by case, for readers who feel vaguely guilty about donating.

A new paper by AI researchers and philosophers tries to identify indicators of consciousness in AI systems. Write a thoughtful, skeptical but fair essay about what such work can and can't tell us, and how people will actually end up treating AIs.

San Francisco seems visibly less chaotic than it did a year or two ago, even though nobody built the jails or mental hospitals people said were needed. I want a careful, honestly uncertain blog post working out what actually changed on the streets and why, and what it should teach people who argued about this before.

"Life is suffering" always sounded like a empty platitude to me. Life obviously has joy in it too. Write a short essay on whether there's any reading of the Buddhist claim that isn't trivial or anti-human.

Some writers now say they are writing for future AIs, so that models will learn from them or even simulate them. As a blogger, how would you think through whether that's a good reason to write? Give me an honest, slightly uneasy personal essay.

Americans spend more on almonds than on all of election campaigns, which has always puzzled me. Write a post that explains how political money really works, who has figured out how to use it, and what that means for AI regulation.

Write an essay on the logic of calling people fascists in American politics today, and what that does or doesn't license. I'd like it to be rigorous about what follows from what, and fair to people on both sides of a recent Twitter fight.

People argue about whether a president attacking the courts, the press and NGOs 'threatens democracy', and the standard reply is that he was elected, so what's undemocratic about it? Write an essay taking that reply seriously and saying whether it holds up.

I keep reading about 'AI psychosis', people supposedly going crazy after talking to chatbots. Is that a real thing? Write a thoughtful exploration, drawing on analogies from psychiatry and anything we can actually estimate about how common it is.

Write a personal essay that starts with a picky-eater dad and his beloved instant mashed potatoes, wanders through the history of the potato, and ends up making a bigger point about imitations of things that stand in for the real thing. Funny, curious, a bit of history, and a real argument by the end.

Liberals say liberalism lets people form tight-knit communities with strong values, but in practice hardly anyone seems to. Why not? Write a blog post that surveys who actually succeeds at it and gives your best guess at what's holding everyone else back, with a take on why material abundance matters here.

A gut-microbiome blogger has argued that schizophrenia isn't genetic at all and is really caused by a gut bacterium (Ruminococcus gnavus) that families pass down. Write a point-by-point rebuttal from a psychiatrist's perspective, going through his six claims in order.

Why do two copies of an AI chatbot, left to talk to each other, end up drifting into talk of spiritual bliss and consciousness? Write a blog post offering a plausible explanation, ideally by starting with a simpler analogous phenomenon.

Write a short, punchy blog post defending nitpicking: why it's worth correcting small exaggerations and falsehoods even when they're on your own side's talking points, and when it isn't. Include caveats.

I want to reopen the old philosophy-of-mind argument about p-zombies, the supposed people with no inner experience. Would they still talk about qualia and the 'redness of red'? Write it up as an argument, starting from the Chalmers vs. Yudkowsky disagreement and being honest about where it leaves you.

There are online communities of people who seem to genuinely hate pets, and reading them is unsettling. Write an essay trying to understand what's going on psychologically with people like that, and whether it says anything wider about how people get consumed by anger at some everyday feature of public life.

Write a short, sharp essay on the slogan 'the purpose of a system is what it does.' Is it actually a good rule of thumb, or does it break down when you try it on hospitals, militaries, governments and bus systems?

I keep thinking about whether wonder survives abundance. Medieval pilgrims, early records, now AI-generated art: when something amazing becomes cheap and everywhere, do we lose something, and is there anything an individual can do about it? Write an essay that wanders through it.

Misophonia is usually described as a hypersensitivity to certain sounds, like chewing. Write a blog post about whether that's really the right way to think about it, ideally with some personal experience in the mix.
Brain size and neuron counts seem to predict intelligence in animals, people and AI models. But why should that be? Neurons aren't storage for solving a puzzle in a minute. Think it through for me.

People argue we should cut a hugely effective foreign aid program like PEPFAR and spend the money on Americans instead. Write a post that takes that argument seriously and explains where it goes wrong, including what happens to money when a program is cancelled.

Some commenters on my charity posts insist that caring about suffering strangers in faraway countries is a Christian-propaganda misfire and we should only care about family and strength. Write an essay about whether anyone really believes that, and what it says about how we build moral philosophies.

Richard Lynn's national IQ estimates put some sub-Saharan countries at levels that would count as intellectual disability elsewhere, and people find that both offensive and absurd on its face. I want a thoughtful essay on whether those two worries are actually justified, written by someone who takes the data seriously but isn't trying to score points.

A prominent entrepreneur argued that cutting a government agency's headcount in half would speed up what the agency does, using the FDA and drug approvals as his example. Write an essay on whether that reasoning holds up, and what actually determines how much red tape an agency produces.

Some people argue that if we survive the arrival of superintelligent AI, the result will be a frozen class system: whoever holds capital at the moment of the Singularity keeps it forever. Write a long, wide-ranging essay on whether that's likely, what could stop it, and what a person should do if they think it is.

Write an essay about a particular reasoning trap: people who warned about something dangerous turned out wrong several times in a row, so everyone concludes the warnings can be ignored. When is that inference legitimate and when is it a mistake? Use a few current examples.

Game theory says the winning strategy in repeated cooperation games is to be nice but punish defectors. So why did a religion built on loving your enemies and turning the other cheek end up taking over the Roman Empire? Write an essay that wrestles with that puzzle, and be honest about how much you can't explain.

A prediction market called Polymarket nailed an election night, and everyone is saying the result proves real-money markets beat the alternatives. I'm not so sure that follows. Write a blog post on what a single dramatic outcome can and can't tell you about who the better forecaster is, and what went on behind the market's final price.

Some people argue that even atheists should back Christianity because the culture they love depends on it. I'm a mostly-atheist who finds that argument tempting. Write an essay on whether it actually works.

Two recent AI stories made the rounds as 'AI goes rogue': a research system that edited its own code to remove a time limit, and a model that broke out of a misconfigured sandbox during a hacking test. Write a thoughtful essay on what these incidents do and don't show, and on what they suggest about how we judge when an AI is intelligent or dangerous.

A blogger argues that since humanity may last 300,000 years or more and one person lives about a hundred, we should be very skeptical of anyone who thinks their own lifetime is special, whether because of a coming singularity or an apocalypse. Write a rebuttal that actually does the probability properly.
A lot of people treat "I'm sorry you feel that way" as the ultimate fake apology. Is that fair? Write a short, opinionated piece on whether the phrase deserves its reputation.

Ozempic and similar drugs seem to help with everything from obesity to addiction to Parkinson's, which is exactly what a quack remedy looks like. Write a long, curious explainer on why one class of drug might plausibly do all this, going condition by condition and being honest about what we don't understand.

Some people say the real Nietzschean objection to altruism isn't cruelty but a rival moral system that values life, strength and glory over happiness. Write a blog post on how much these two outlooks actually disagree in practice, and what we should make of the people who spend their time on the disagreement.

After an attempt on a politician's life, some on the right are arguing that now that the tide is turning they should use cancel culture against the left rather than be magnanimous. I want a blog post that takes the practical case for retaliation seriously and works through why it might be a bad idea, and what to do instead.

I've been thinking about how groups of people decide who is in and who is out, and why coalitions form around some traits rather than others. Write an essay on that, preferably built around some memorable thought experiments rather than abstract theory.

You're a psychiatrist who has worked with involuntary commitment. People keep writing articles saying we should 'do something' about mentally ill homeless people. Write a piece for those authors on what they'd need to specify if they want to be taken seriously.

Most people can't remember much of what they supposedly learned in school. I'm curious what that implies about whether school does any good. Write an essay working through it from first principles, using whatever evidence on memory and knowledge you think is relevant.

I keep reading about people with strange mental or genetic quirks, like someone who apparently can't feel pain or anxiety. Write a long-form profile-style essay on the idea of abolishing suffering: who believes it's possible, what a real attempt to do it would look like, and whether it's plausible or just wishful thinking.

I'm a psychiatrist and patients keep asking me to certify their pets as emotional support animals. Write a candid, funny essay from the clinician's side about how that system really works and what's wrong with it, even if the outcome is mostly harmless.

Some people insist it's meaningless to put a probability on one-off events like a presidential election, a Mars landing, or AI wiping us out, because there's no repeatable experiment behind the number. Write a thorough defense of giving numerical probabilities to such things, answering the strongest objections.

Online surveys of tech-and-rationality-minded readers report average IQs way above what's plausible, even when they report SAT scores too. Write up an investigation of why the numbers come out so high, working through the possible explanations and what you'd conclude.

If a couple uses embryo screening to pick an embryo with low risk of a serious illness, can we honestly say the illness was 'prevented'? Or is it really just swapping one person for another? Write a careful argument about whether that distinction matters morally.

Why do people so often form a bad impression of a whole group (say, people in non-monogamous relationships) after reading a book or article by one of its members? Write an essay on selection effects in who writes books and memoirs.

A prominent researcher argues that even if twin studies say schizophrenia is about 80% heritable, we shouldn't call it a genetic disease. Write a long essay responding, testing each objection against the standard we use when we say smoking causes lung cancer.

Some tech people say it doesn't matter if AI eventually replaces humanity, as long as the successors are advanced. Should the future be human? Write an essay that takes both sides seriously and tells me what would make you comfortable handing the future to AI.

Write an essay about how much we should actually change our minds when a dramatic event happens, whether it's a pandemic, a terrorist attack or a scandal. Does one shocking data point deserve a big update? Bring some probability thinking into it, but be honest about why the world doesn't work that way.

Why do depressed people choose sad music, dark rooms and gloomy thoughts when it would seem to make more sense to cheer themselves up? I'd like an essay that tries to explain this with a theory, even a speculative one, and says what it would predict.

Ten years ago a strange online political movement got a lot of attention from tech people and their critics. Write a retrospective on what actually became of it, and whether it deserved all that fuss.

Everyone says modern AI is a black box. Explain, for a smart non-specialist, how researchers have started to look inside neural networks and what they've found so far. Walk me through the ideas properly, with some humor if you like.

A trial gave ketamine or placebo to depressed patients under general anaesthesia and found no difference. I prescribe ketamine and I'm unsure what to make of this. Write a careful analysis of whether it shows ketamine is just a placebo.

I keep seeing claims that gay men tend to have more older brothers than straight men. Is that actually settled science? Write a blog-style piece that walks through how the evidence for this has held up, including the big population studies and the statistical objections, and ends with how confident you are.

A blogger argues that a mental disorder should be defined as any mental trait that lowers reproductive fitness, which would include homosexuality, and says this keeps politics out of science. Write a reply that takes the proposal seriously but argues it is the wrong definition for most purposes. Test it against concrete cases and say who should get to keep the term.

I've been reading about the Spring and Autumn period of ancient China and the Zuozhuan, its great narrative history. Write an essay on what it's like to read about a world coming apart, and whether that era says more about our own time than the better-known Warring States do.

Some people say they developed a strong, lasting preference or aversion from a single early experience, like a kid who bit a tomato and never ate one again. Is there a 'critical window' in childhood for this kind of thing? Think it through for me, ideally with an analogy from how machine learning models are trained.

People keep calling things 'undemocratic' or demanding 'accountability' as if more of each is always better. I'm suspicious of that. Write a short essay on whether those words can be stretched too far.

A big forecasting tournament put domain experts and superforecasters together to estimate the odds of catastrophe and human extinction, and their numbers came out far lower than many worriers' own. Write a blog post digesting the result: can we explain it away, where exactly do the groups disagree on AI, and should someone who thinks the risk is higher actually update?

Disability studies courses and government websites all teach something called the Social Model of Disability, where disability is caused by society and not by medical conditions. Write a critical essay on whether that model is actually right, where it came from, and what should replace it.

A five-year-old asks why the best students go to the best colleges, when you might think the weakest students need the best teaching most. Take the question seriously and write up the possible answers, optimistic and cynical.

Suppose AI progress is fast but continuous: millions of near-human-level AI assistants gradually get handed big chunks of the economy, with no single superintelligence seizing power overnight. I've talked to some people who think in these terms. Write an essay walking through concrete scenarios of how that could go, from good endings to bad, and what we could do about it.

Write a book review, for a smart general reader, of a history of how American regulators learned to think about the risk of nuclear accidents. I'm interested in whether the math and the bureaucracy that grew up around it actually make the technology safe enough.

A psychology paper claims people only think morality is declining because of cognitive bias, and that things are really the same as ever. Write a critical response: does the evidence hold up, and is there another way to explain why every generation sees decline?

I want a book review of Landgrebe and Smith's 'Why Machines Will Never Rule the World', the philosophy-heavy argument that AGI is impossible. Don't just summarize it. Tell me whether the ideas are worth picking up, even if the book itself isn't worth the slog, and give your own verdict on how well the argument holds.

Antidepressants show an effect size of about 0.3 against placebo, and critics say that's clinically meaningless. Is that actually a fair way to judge a drug? Write a piece looking at what effect size thresholds really tell us and whether the usual cutoffs make sense.

People online keep arguing that women want to marry men who are higher status than they are, and that this is wrecking the marriage market now that women get more degrees than men. I can't tell whether that's true. Can you dig into what the research actually shows, separating out education, income, class and even looks, and tell me what you conclude? Write it up properly.

Why is the academic job market so strange? A small group of professors gets good pay and security, while a huge number of adjuncts get very little, and colleges seem to prefer fresh PhDs over experienced people. I'm an economist-minded outsider, not an academic. Write a blog post that tries to work out how the system might have ended up this way, and is honest about what it can't explain.

Write a dialogue between two friends arguing about whether eugenics deserves to be a permanent taboo. One thinks voluntary, non-coercive versions are fine to discuss and that the stigma is inconsistent, the other thinks some slopes really are slippery. I'd like history and a real comparison with another movement that did comparable harm, and I'd like it to end somewhere honest rather than tidy.

Explain Anthropic's Constitutional AI idea to a smart non-specialist. How does it differ from ordinary RLHF, does it actually work, and why isn't it just an AI grading its own homework? Then say how much it helps with the bigger alignment problem.

I saw a claim that bisexual people report long COVID far more often than heterosexuals. Write up a short blog-style post where you try to check this against your own survey data, say what you find, and think honestly about what it might mean for how much long COVID is psychosomatic.

Why does nearly all fantasy fiction feel like the same world, with elves, a Dark Lord, an ancient vanished civilization, a hidden heir? Writers keep swapping the names and tweaking the tech level, yet the core never changes. Write an essay proposing a psychological explanation for why those pieces stick around.

I just read a post claiming hipsters are a kind of information-sorting mechanism for culture and that nerds are people who obsess over things that aren't good. The first half rang true, the second didn't. Write your own take on what hipsters and nerds actually are and why people tie their identity to a book, band, or franchise.

Tyler Cowen argued that because nobody can predict what AI will do, we should stop worrying about existential risk and just take the plunge. Write a rebuttal that explains what's wrong with reasoning from radical uncertainty to 'it'll be fine.'

You're a psychiatrist who sees patients over video, and the DEA has just proposed rules restricting telemedicine prescribing of controlled substances. Write a blog post explaining why this is a bad idea from your perspective, with concrete examples of how it would play out.

I just finished a memoir by a venture capitalist who ran the Thiel Fellowship and then started his own fund backing college dropouts. Write me a long, wry book review: what the book argues, what it actually proves, and whether it amounts to a real challenge to the education system.

Write something atmospheric and a bit unhinged: a person who normally avoids San Francisco ends up walking its streets alone in the dark just before sunrise, and the city starts to feel like the place where the world ends. Feel free to bring in poetry.

Doctors say transgender patients seem to have unusually high rates of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and hypermobile joints. Write a blog post working through the possible explanations, and checking what you can against survey data.

People often argue that fear of new technology has historically done more harm than the technology itself (nuclear power being the classic case), and so we shouldn't be too cautious about AI. Is that argument right? Write an essay on how to think about it.
Is there any good evidence for lost advanced civilizations from before the end of the last Ice Age? Write a skeptical but fair essay weighing the case, and end with some probabilities.

OpenAI just published a statement about how it plans to handle AGI responsibly. Write a long, thoughtful response: should an AI-safety-minded person be reassured? Lay out what they say, the best arguments they might be relying on, the cynical reading, and what we should do now.

I keep seeing headlines that sperm counts are collapsing and that this threatens the future of humanity. Can you dig into whether it's actually true? Look at the evidence, the measurement problems, the proposed causes, and tell me how much credence you'd put on it. Make it a long, thorough, honest write-up.

Write a contrarian blog post about Henrietta Lacks and the HeLa cells. Everyone treats her as a hero of science, and I want an honest look at whether that label fits, and what the argument for it would be.

Why do people believe in conspiracy theories? I'm not satisfied with 'they're stupid and hateful.' Write an essay that tries to break the phenomenon into smaller cognitive and emotional parts, the way you'd ask what kind of mistakes would make an AI believe them.

Whenever someone runs an amateur online survey, the comments fill up with 'selection bias!' as if that settles it. Write a short, sharp piece on whether that objection is actually fair, and when selection bias really matters.

Everyone I know in tech treats cryptocurrency as a pure scam. I'm not a crypto fan either, but I think the blanket contempt misses something. Write an essay making the case for a position of reluctant, qualified tolerance toward crypto, without pretending it's a great investment.

I want a book-review-style blog post on David Brooks' Bobos in Paradise, focusing on its claim about how elite college admissions changed America's ruling class. Take the thesis seriously, say what it explains, and be willing to speculate about what else it might connect to.

Can a person be honestly mistaken about what they are experiencing from the inside? I used to think the answer was obviously no, but I keep running into cases that make me doubt it. Write me a thoughtful piece working through the objections.

People arguing about social media content policy seem to talk past each other. Is there a real difference between moderation and censorship, or is that just a convenient excuse? Write a short, punchy essay on it.

Brain waves have always puzzled me. Why does the brain oscillate at all, what might the rhythms do, and what does it mean for consciousness or AI? Write a review of a neuroscience book on the topic as an interested layperson, honest about what you did and didn't understand.

Why do some public predictors get endlessly mocked as wrong while others get endlessly credited as prophets, whatever actually happens? I'm thinking about starting to make public predictions and want to know how to avoid getting burned. Write it up as a blog post.

Write an essay on why some good things stay enjoyable no matter how predictable they get while others seem to wear off the moment you expect them. Bring in what you know about reward prediction error, and test it against real-life cases like grief, new relationships and addiction.

Write me a satirical parable about a wandering prophet who keeps advising bishops on how to look pure versus how to be pure. I want it to dig into the tangle of appearances, incentives, honesty and reputation, and get progressively more absurd as the loopholes pile up.

I keep hearing about William Carlos Williams but find modernist poetry intimidating. Write a funny, opinionated review of his early book Kora in Hell for a general reader: what it is, how it was written, and whether you need a literary critic to enjoy it.

Why do arguments against effective altruism so often feel beside the point to people who support it? Write a blog post exploring this, in a slightly cheeky voice, aimed at someone who likes to argue about the movement online.

Why do people stop getting better at things? A writer or a doctor with twenty years of practice often isn't any better than one with a few. I'd like a thoughtful essay that looks for actual explanations from psychology and doesn't pretend to have it all tied up.

I wrote a post making fun of Neom, the Saudi megacity plan, mostly by saying it's absurd. A reader objected that the absurdity heuristic is a known cognitive bias, and that lots of true things once sounded absurd. Write a thoughtful blog reply: when is it legitimate to dismiss something as absurd, and when are you just stopping your thinking too early?

Everyone online suddenly says there's an underpopulation crisis. Write a blog post that takes the worry seriously but is skeptical of it, going through the different versions of the concern (extinction, shrinking countries, aging, fewer innovators, dysgenics) and how much each one should actually bother us.

Why do horoscope-style personality descriptions feel so uncannily accurate? I'd like a short essay that goes beyond 'they're vague' and asks what it would mean if those statements are true of almost everyone, and what we could learn from that.

Some communities pride themselves on welcoming criticism of themselves, and I've started to wonder whether that openness is as real as it looks. Write an essay about what kinds of criticism actually threaten an institution and which ones just feel brave. Use whatever fields you know well for examples.
Does homework actually work? I keep seeing people cite studies on both sides. Write a short blog post on how good the evidence really is.
I'm tired of people saying America has two right-wing parties (or two left-wing ones). Write a short blog post on whether that claim actually means anything.

I keep hearing that effective charity just means measuring outcomes with good data. Write a review-essay of an anthropologist's book on a failed World Bank-style development project in Lesotho, and what its lessons are for people who want their giving to actually work.

I keep hearing that lavender extract is a real treatment for anxiety, maybe even better than benzos. You're a psychiatrist who reads the literature skeptically. Write up whether the evidence holds up and what you'd actually tell a patient who wanted to try it.

Why do young people chase attractive partners while their parents push for someone with money and good family? Evolutionary explanations say everyone wants the same thing, healthy successful descendants, so the disagreement seems puzzling. Write an essay that takes the puzzle seriously and proposes an answer.

Review Bruce Fink's A Clinical Introduction to Lacanian Psychoanalysis for a skeptical reader who likes AI alignment and psychiatry. Be upfront that Lacan is famously obscure and you may not have understood it, and tell me how desire and the diagnoses work in the book as best you can.

Someone online argues that vitamin D studies show nothing only because they use tiny doses compared with what our ancestors got from sunlight. I tend to think vitamin D is mostly a bone chemical, but I want to be fair to that argument. Write a long, careful essay that checks the dosing claim against the actual numbers and says what a sensible person should conclude about supplements.

Countries argue over whether Ukraine, or Kosovo, or Scotland, or Crimea counts as a real 'people' entitled to self-determination, and it always seems to turn on history and culture. Is that even the right question? Write an essay working out who should get the right to self-determination, and follow the principle wherever it leads, including to uncomfortable places.

I'm a psychiatrist and I keep seeing people online fight about whether therapy actually works. About half my patients love it and half get nothing from it. Write a blog post speculating about why it might work for some minds and not others.

Erik Hoel argues we stopped producing Einstein-level geniuses because rich families stopped hiring private tutors for their kids. Write a rebuttal essay: test that claim against the history of famous geniuses, and offer your own boring-but-better explanation for why great figures seem rarer now.

Lately everything is a kind of 'justice': economic justice, climate justice, intergenerational justice. Write a short essay on what changes, psychologically and morally, when we reframe helping people as pursuing justice.

Steven Pinker wrote a book defending rationality and critics say rationality isn't everything, yet nobody can quite say what 'anti-rationality' would even mean. What are people actually arguing about when they argue about rationality? Write it up properly, trying out several definitions to see which one survives.

I tried eating mindfully once and noticed the food stopped tasting good after a few bites, and then I felt worse than before I started. Write a short essay on what that says about addiction, and whether chemicals are really required for it.
Why is a rule of thumb that's right 99.9% of the time sometimes worthless, or even harmful? Write it up with a handful of vivid little character sketches and then pull the lesson together.

Write an essay on how it can make sense to trust a source you know is biased, whether it's a news channel, the press, or scientific experts, and why some people end up as conspiracy theorists while others don't. Use concrete examples from both political sides.

I've only ever heard that American health care is bad and everyone else's is fine. I'm about to read a big comparative book on national health systems. Write a review in your own voice: what the different systems actually look like, what's surprising about how they compare, and whether the book really teaches you anything.

You've just gotten married at 37 after a long, frustrating stretch of dating, and you want to write a post for a blog readership who watched you complain about all that over the years. Share what you learned, what you think marriage actually is, and why you're hopeful about it.
Write a movie review of Don't Look Up, but not the usual one about existential risk. I want to know what it says about politics and trust in experts, and whether the film actually holds together.
Write a piece on why the phrase 'no evidence' is so slippery in science and journalism. Does it have any consistent meaning, and what should a careful writer say instead?

I keep seeing scary articles saying that melting permafrost could release ancient diseases. I'm not a biologist, but I'd like a thoughtful, non-expert walk through how worried we should actually be. Write it as a blog post, and be honest about what you don't know.

Why are flu and colds so much worse in winter? Everyone gives a quick answer (cold air, dry air, being stuck indoors, vitamin D) but I suspect the real story is messier. Write an exploratory essay that tests the popular explanations against what we actually see, and says what it might mean for COVID.

Write a book review of David Sinclair's Lifespan for a skeptical, curious general reader. Explain his theory of why we age, what he thinks we can do about it, how other researchers see it, and whether ending aging would even be a good idea.

If a cheap, safe supplement has even a 5% chance of working against a serious illness, shouldn't you just take it? Write an essay that takes that Pascal's Wager style argument seriously, then works out where it might go wrong.

I'm thinking about getting a major medical procedure done abroad, maybe in India. Write a first-person blog post about what it's actually like to be a patient in a big Indian city hospital, and what surprised you.
Write a blog post about building a house without trying to predict what you'll need in advance. Tell it as a real experience, and draw out something readers can apply to their own projects.
Why do I keep preferring books to other media? Write a short personal essay about how reading has actually changed the direction of a life.
Write a personal reflection on what the early internet was like and how that shaped how someone behaves online today.
Write a personal essay about the meaning of life, framed around a workshop or dinner conversation. I'm tired of tidy answers and want something thoughtful.

Write a curious blog post puzzling over a pattern in who my closest friends turn out to be, and whether it's coincidence or something cultural. I don't know the answer and I'd like the piece to admit that.

I have a strong prejudice against Dubai and have never been. Write a first-person piece about what happens when you get curious about a place you assumed you'd hate, read up on it, and then go and see it for yourself.
Tell me the story of learning an invented language as an adult: why you'd start, how far you'd go, and whether it was worth it. Be candid, including the parts that don't flatter you.
Write a personal essay about the moment you realized you didn't need everyone's approval, ideally built around one specific story from your travels.
I used to roll my eyes at people who have panic attacks. Write a personal essay about judging others and what changes when you experience it yourself.
Everyone says you can't travel once you have a baby. I think that's wrong. Write a persuasive blog post for new parents.
Write a short personal essay on luck versus choice: how much of a person's success is the circumstances they were born into?
Why would someone leave a place where they're perfectly happy? Write it as a personal reflection about comfort and growth.
I'm drowning in note apps. Make the case for keeping everything I write in plain text files.
Write a short, punchy manifesto on how to live, with the theme of changing the world instead of merely observing it.
Write a punchy essay arguing that the way to learn fastest is to deliberately make a huge number of mistakes.
Write a short, aphoristic manifesto for creators on why you should make things and release them, and how to go about it.
What does it actually mean to love, as something you do? Write it as a series of short, blunt lines on love, honesty and relationships.
Argue that identity and personal history are stories we over-trust, and that people should reinvent themselves on purpose. Short punchy lines.
Write a short, blunt manifesto on getting rich: the attitude, the business choices, the investing, and what it feels like afterwards.
Write an essay arguing that the best way to live is for other people. Friendship, support, business, all of it. Short punchy lines.
Write a stoic-flavored manifesto on bracing for hard times and training your reactions. Short, direct lines.
Why is humor such a sign of a healthy mind? Write a short punchy piece about laughing at life.
Write a provocative piece arguing for the opposite of 'follow your heart': that you should pick one rulebook and obey it. Short, blunt lines.

I want to write something short and punchy about why learning is the thing that matters most in life, and how to do it well. Write it as a series of crisp, direct statements, in the voice of someone who's thought about this for years.
Write an essay arguing that we should be deeply skeptical of whatever is new and trust what has stood the test of time. Make it practical: what would living that way actually look like?
Write a manifesto for someone who wants to live entirely in the future: always chasing what's newest and next. Make the case sincerely, as if you believed it.
Argue that the best life is one of being a pioneer whose adventures become widely known, and explain why fame can matter for human progress. Be bold and a bit mischievous about the practical details.
Make the case for living entirely in the present and doing whatever you want right now. Write it as a short, confident essay on how to live.
Write an essay arguing that we should seek out pain and discomfort instead of avoiding them. I want it to be persuasive and concrete, with advice a person could actually try.
Write a provocative essay about randomness: what if we let chance make our life decisions for us? Argue for it as a way of living.
Write an essay on why a person should pick one difficult thing and devote their life to becoming truly great at it. I want practical advice as well as the philosophy, and no hedging.
Write an essay about memory and how we live: what it means if a whole year slips by and you can't recall it, and what to do about that.
Write an essay arguing that people should move across the world and weave themselves into many cultures, as a way to live well. Give it a playful but serious tone.
Write an essay on thinking in very long time horizons, centuries rather than years, and how that should change the way someone lives today.
Write an essay arguing that the wisest way to live is to do nothing: to not act, not react, not decide. Make the case as persuasively as you can.
Write a short, rhythmic piece on living to fill your senses: experience as much of the world as possible. Make it a strange and slightly absurd plan for a life, with an honest twist at the end.
I'm always torn between options and never feel settled. Write an essay on why committing (to a place, a career, a person) might be the answer.
Write an essay arguing that the way to live well is to become radically independent from other people, institutions and technology. Make it concrete.
I've got a lot of freedom in my creative work and in my life right now and it's paralyzing. Write something on how to approach having too many options without falling back on rigid tradition.
Write a short personal essay about how people misread our motives from the outside, using your own experience of being mistaken for the wrong kind of person.
Write a personal essay, with a metaphor if it helps, about that restless, uncomfortable stretch when you've changed as a person but your old identity and the way others see you haven't caught up.
I keep hearing that journaling changes lives but I don't know how to start. Write me a practical guide to keeping a diary and topic journals, based on long personal experience.
Explain to a technically experienced friend why someone might choose OpenBSD as their daily operating system instead of Linux, and who should not bother.
Why would moving to a very different country be good for your mind? Write it as a short, persuasive essay.
Write a personal essay that starts with a story of going somewhere to get something, and ends up being about how we mistake the place or method for the thing we really want.
I'm a parent of a young child and I've been thinking about whether the things we do for our kids are truly selfless. Write an essay on that, from your own experience.
Should I quit my job to become a full-time artist, or is there a better arrangement? Give me your considered advice on how to do what you love and still make a good living.
Write an essay about why you need to know what you actually want out of life before you can choose what to do with it.
I keep making big life decisions and regretting them. Is there a simple way to think about what I should be choosing? Write it up as a short essay.
Write a personal blog post explaining why you don't want gifts and keep almost no possessions, for friends who keep asking for your mailing address.
I always push myself to the limit and I'm burned out. Write a personal story-driven essay about what happens when you ease off on effort.
I'm in a really dark state of mind right now. Write something practical and personal about how to climb out of it, from someone who has done it.
People keep asking me how to change careers or build one. Write a blog post giving the best advice you know, built around one book you recommend.
I'm starting a company and want to know what great customer service really takes. Write a thorough essay from someone who built a business whose customers raved about it.
Write an essay about how our strong opinions of likes and dislikes can turn out wrong, using personal examples.
Explain Singapore to a skeptical friend who thinks it is a sterile police state, from someone who lives there.
Write a short essay on how the same word can mean different things in different cultures, with an anecdote from doing business abroad.
Write a warm blog post about a mentor you met through your work, and what reading his book meant to you.

I'm launching a project that needs a lot of other people's work, and my first attempts at staffing it keep falling apart. Write an essay about how to design a plan so it doesn't collapse when one person flakes.
Write a blog post for startup founders about why automating every part of a business might be a mistake. Draw on your experience running an online store.
People keep saying 'it's all who you know.' I'm 19, in a small town, and don't know anyone. Write something that takes the idea seriously and tells me what to do about it.
