Should I put my energy into my local community or into reaching people worldwide? Write an essay on that trade-off, from your own experience if you have it.
Write an essay about deliberately pushing yourself into unfamiliar situations, and what happens to your sense of what's comfortable over time.
A friend of mine is moving to Los Angeles next month and has only heard bad things about it. Write up the advice you'd give someone who spent years there and loved it.
I want to start a business but have no idea what kind. Write an essay with your honest suggestion, using what you've actually done.
Write a cautionary essay about a founder who tried hard to empower his employees and it went badly wrong. What does good delegation look like?
I just started a company and everybody assumes I want to be a big-shot CEO and grow as fast as possible. I'm not sure I do. Write an essay for me about this.
Why do some people insist on doing things themselves when hiring an expert would be faster and cheaper? Write an essay exploring that, with real examples.
Write a piece for small business owners about the tiny, human touches that make customers fall in love with a company, with concrete examples from an online shop you ran.
I have a big business idea but everyone says I need funding first. Write an essay on whether that's true.
Write an essay arguing that having no investors can be an advantage for a young company, drawing on the dot-com years.
Tell the origin story of how a musician selling his own CD online accidentally started a business. Write it as a blog post.
Write an essay about how people project meaning onto things that have none. Start from something small like language or songs.
Write a short essay about how living abroad makes you see your own culture for the first time.

I run a small business and I'm doing everything myself. I know I need help but training someone feels like it'd take more time than I have. Write me an essay on getting out of that trap, ideally with a real story from someone who lived it.
Write a first-person account of the time you had to deal with a giant tech company on a deal that mattered enormously to your small business, including the part where it got tense.
Why do so many talented artists and musicians struggle to make money? Write a blog post for a musician friend who's frustrated, with practical directions they could take.
I want a blog post about a bad hotel experience that taught you something about how to work with other people. Keep it grounded in the story.
You've hired around a hundred people over the years. Write practical advice for someone who wants a job at a company they admire but who isn't advertising any openings.
I have an idea for a web app but I'm not technical. Explain, step by step, how I'd go about finding and hiring a programmer to build it.
Write a personal essay about the idea that some people are just born with a talent and others aren't. Use your own experience of trying to get good at something you were told you'd never be good at.
Tell the story of how you landed a gig as a young musician with a famous artist, and what you took from it.
Why do people say such awful things to strangers and businesses online? Write a short essay with a couple of true stories.
'It's all who you know' always felt like a door slammed in my face. Write an essay that looks at that saying differently, from the point of view of someone who started with no connections.
Explain why someone would sell a successful company and give nearly all the proceeds to charity instead of keeping it. Write it in the first person, as the person who did it.
Write about a teacher who changed your life in only a few lessons. I want to give it to some of my students and their parents.

After a year of reading dozens of business and psychology books I feel dumber than when I started, and I'm struggling to start my new venture. Write an essay about this problem, from someone who's been there.
How do you know when it's time to sell your company? Answer with your own story rather than a checklist.
Write a reflective personal essay about organizing your whole life around maximizing freedom, and what happens once you actually get it.

I've always believed you should never be desperate, that confidence comes from having options. But I've been reading about entrepreneurs who deliberately put themselves in do-or-die situations and thrived. Write something exploring whether desperation can actually help, or whether it's a trap.
Why do so many people seem to crave drama in their lives, even when nothing dramatic is going on? Write a short piece, ideally with an anecdote from someone who thought hard about stories.
Write a short blog post about the gap between how effortless great performances look and how much work lies behind them, and whether it matters if the audience ever finds out.
I'm thinking about adding a referral bonus to my business so customers get paid for recommending us. Write me an essay on whether paying people for favors or recommendations is a good idea.
Write a blog post about a small-business idea for people who want self-employment: how reading a couple of good guides can be turned into a service for busy people.
Explain why giving customers more options can reduce sales, and where that idea stops applying. Practical advice for someone running an online store or showcasing their work.
People keep pitching me business plans that try to do everything at once. Write a blog post for would-be founders about why that's a mistake and what to do instead.
Write a blog post about a personality dimension that explains more about how people behave than introversion versus extroversion does.
Write a first-person story about a costly mistake a founder made in the early days of a small business by not paying attention to paperwork and structure.
Write a personal story about working as a young man for a cranky, famous old songwriter, and something strange that happened afterward.

A 19-year-old guitarist from Alabama emailed me wanting to become a session musician. He's eyeing an expensive music school in Hollywood but is scared of decades of debt. Write the reply you'd send him, with real advice on how to actually get there.
Write a practical piece on how to get real value out of attending a music industry conference, for someone who's about to go to their first one and tends to waste these things.
You're giving a short talk to incoming first-year students at a music college on the first day. Write the talk: what you wish you'd known when you started, built from your own experience there.

I'm a working musician and I keep hearing that the college market is a good way to make a living. I want a long, honest, practical guide from someone who actually did it: how it works, what it's really like, and what's worth paying for.

I run a company with a big, ugly legacy codebase, and everyone keeps saying we should rewrite it all in whatever framework is fashionable. Write a candid first-person post from someone who tried a big rewrite and what they concluded about it.

I've been writing for years and have a form that works, but I'm trying to move beyond it and for months everything I make falls apart, even though I'm full of ideas. Write a reflective essay on being creatively stuck when you're trying to change how you work, and how long that can reasonably last.

Write an essay about how the things we do repeatedly to evaluate our own work end up shaping us. I'm thinking especially of keeping a journal and rereading it, and how that might change what and how you write.

Write a personal essay about what happens to a long relationship when one partner changes in a direction the other doesn't share, and what it means to love someone while they keep becoming someone new. Use your own marriage and a move to a remote farm as the setting.

I want a blog post about a formative trip from my teenage years, and what it taught me about trusting strangers and the way the world opens up when you go out into it. Make it personal, with friends who pushed me out of my shell.

How do some people manage to do things that seem impossible by normal standards, like making a feature film for a fraction of the usual cost? Write an essay on the mindset behind that, with concrete examples, and how someone could develop it.
Why does doing what feels right to you, even when it risks social pushback, deepen some relationships and end others? Write an essay on this, drawing on stories people have shared with you.

I live somewhere rural and have become fascinated by the obscure local artists who worked for decades with almost no recognition. Write a reflective essay about why some people feel compelled to make things regardless of money or fame, told through one particular artist and a place.

I just finished a big political biography and realized my school-taught picture of how power works is basically a cartoon. Write an essay on how real political operators actually accumulate power, and what that implies for the rest of us.
Why do so many people (and writers, and artists) start out wild and interesting and then slowly become repetitive and safe? Write a blog post on staying creative over decades, and what it costs.

I recently reread my old university diaries for the first time and it was strange seeing patterns I couldn't see then. Write a personal essay about what looking back at your younger self can reveal, and what actually lets a person change.
Describe how you read when you want a book to actually change how you think: how you choose books, how you read them, and how you make time. For someone who reads a lot but retains little.

You and your wife spent years turning an overgrown farm into a garden, and somewhere in that process you learned something about how to deal with messy, complicated decisions. Write an essay about what you learned about solving hard problems.

Your daughter is turning eight and you wish you could hand her a book about living freely and getting things done. Write that essay: what does 'agency' really mean, what does it look like in the lives of people who have it (a filmmaker, perhaps), and what held you back from it for so long?
Write a short essay on why unpublished writing, like diaries, notebooks and fragments, can be more rewarding to read than the polished books their authors wrote on purpose.
A reader asks: 'How do you filter problems worth solving from problems worth quitting?' Answer her in a blog post, drawing on your own experience of getting distracted by things that don't matter.

I have a feeling that some people I wrote off years ago might have been wonderful friends if I'd looked harder. Write an essay about misjudging people, and what it takes to see someone properly. A story from your own life would help.

A friend of mine is a talented artist who feels stuck and keeps doing what he thinks he's supposed to do, even though it clearly isn't working. I suspect he's making his life harder than it needs to be through how he frames his options. Write an essay about how our unexamined assumptions about what a good life or career must look like limit us, and what to do about it.

I've lost my sense of curiosity lately. Nothing feels interesting, even though I'm not burned out. Write a personal essay about what it means to be curious, why it can dry up, and how you tell what is actually worth pursuing.

Is following your gut really the best way to be true to yourself? Write an essay exploring authenticity, the role of emotion and intuition versus reason and writing, and how a person might actually figure out what fits them.
You spent a few years running an art gallery on a small island while also writing. Write a reflective essay on the lessons about agency, work, money and seriousness that you took from the job.
Write a short essay about generosity and the feeling of connection to other people. Is it something we have to receive, or something we can make ourselves?
What does it mean to be perceptive, and why are some people better at seeing what's really going on than others? Explain what's happening in the brain and what a person can do to get better at it.
Write an essay about pseudonyms and online identities, and whether wearing a mask can make you more honest and more capable rather than less.
There's a design rule that you should pave the paths people wear in the grass. Write something that pushes on that idea, thinking about writing and about making things for other people.

Everyone says writing helps you think, but when I write I mostly just produce tidy paragraphs that confirm what I already believed. Write a long essay on how to actually think on the page: the specific moves that make your ideas better rather than just clearer.

Should I read serious, grown-up books aloud to my small kids instead of only children's books? Write a blog post from a parent's perspective, including what you think it does for reading comprehension.

I keep hearing that you are the average of the five people you spend the most time with. It feels too crude. Write an essay on how the people and books around us shape who we are, and what it means to take care of that surrounding context, including what authenticity could mean.

Write an essay about a poet who stayed true to his own sense of what mattered while the literary world around him demanded something else. Tomas Tranströmer is the one I have in mind. Make it personal and quote the poems where it helps.

I just moved my family somewhere new with no job lined up and no idea what comes next. How should I decide what to focus on? Write an essay, and feel free to use ideas from probability or machine learning if they help.

I've been watching a friend burn out on dating apps, and it got me thinking about how we go about choosing people in general, whether partners or colleagues. Write a short, personal essay on a different way to approach meeting and evaluating people.

Write a personal essay about how audiences shape what a writer (or any creative person) is able to say. Can writing for other people and writing for yourself ever be compatible, or does an audience always distort you?

I want a blog post about reconnecting with old friends when your lives have drifted apart, and about finding new ways to talk that go beyond nostalgia. Maybe bring in the idea that a person is made of parts.

You've been with your partner for ten years and built a life together from almost nothing. Write an essay about what makes a relationship a place where both people can change and become themselves, drawing on how you actually set up your first home.

Write a short essay about the difference between attacking a hard problem head-on and taking the slow route, with some thought on what happens in your mind when you stay with a problem for a long time.
Write a short essay about a piece of music that makes you feel more human: Shostakovich's eighth string quartet. Give me the history behind it and what you hear in it.

Everyone says bloggers should publish constantly and not overthink each piece. I've started to doubt that. Write a blog post on whether slow, effortful writing or high-cadence writing actually grows an audience faster, using your own experience.

Someone wrote to a famous songwriter saying she didn't know who she was and so couldn't make art. He told her she didn't need to know. Write an essay on whether self-knowledge matters for creative work, and how people actually come to know themselves.

Write a long essay on the mental state in which genuinely new ideas appear: why solitude seems to matter so much for creative people, what it feels like, and the techniques people use to protect it. Use real examples from mathematicians, filmmakers and writers.

I have a five-year-old and I keep wondering how I'll ever explain the internet to her, and honestly how I should be using it myself. Write a thoughtful blog post on using the internet well, as something you get better at over time rather than something that just happens to you.
Everyone says AI tutors are about to revolutionize education. Write an essay on whether that's actually going to happen, and what might stand in the way.

Why has a small country like Sweden produced such a disproportionate share of the world's pop hits? Write it up properly, with the people and institutions involved, not just the usual theories about long dark winters.

Two friends have just asked me for dating advice, which is funny because I'm a nerd who doesn't know much about it. I'd like to write a personal essay about how I actually found the person I'm married to, and what I'd tell someone searching for that kind of person. Can you write it, with real stories rather than tips?

I want a blog post about what happens when you keep written notes on your recurring conversations with particular friends or your spouse, so you can return to topics later. How does it change the conversations themselves? Draw on your own experience with a couple of people.

You've been blogging for years and one essay suddenly connected you with a bunch of people who shared an obscure obsession of yours. Write an essay about what writing online is actually for, and how your words find the right readers on the internet. Make it personal and a bit strange.

How do people become great at a craft like writing? I'm interested in the role of influences: what you read or watch, how you find the best examples, and why simply studying the canon doesn't always work. A story or two would help.

My daughter was just born and I keep thinking about how a person becomes who they are. Write an essay about how the people and ideas around us shape us, and whether we can deliberately choose that environment. Bring in some historical examples.

Christopher Alexander just died. I know him vaguely as the architect behind A Pattern Language, but I'm more interested in what his ideas could mean for how a society passes knowledge between generations. Write a personal, reflective essay on that.

Schools get all the attention when people talk about how knowledge spreads, but most of what people know they picked up elsewhere. Write an essay about what it would mean to treat learning as a self-organizing system rather than something to be managed from above, and what policy might look like if we took that seriously.

I'm a programmer about to sign a stack of paperwork for a new job and some NDAs. Which clauses should I push back on, and how much leverage do I actually have? Write it as a blunt piece of advice from someone who has signed a lot of these.
You've worked at a famously successful software company and then at a smart but miserable one, both full of talented people. Write a blog post about what made the difference in how they were managed.
Write a blog post telling two stories from your career as a programmer that show the difference between a well-managed tech company and a badly managed one. Make it vivid and a little angry.
I'm thinking of quitting my tech job to take a year off with no plan. Write a personal post about why a self-funded sabbatical can be a good idea, drawing on your own experience taking one before.
Why do so many software teams refuse to hire dedicated testers? Write a punchy piece that goes through the usual excuses and explains why each one is wrong.

I just read a magazine column telling startup founders to skip the private offices and the free soft drinks. Write a rebuttal essay for people who run small tech companies, arguing about how to treat the people who build your product.
I'm about to start a company and can't tell whether to raise a pile of money and grow as fast as possible or build slowly on revenue. Write me a proper essay on how to think about that choice.
Every software CEO I know says they simply can't find good programmers. I think that's wrong. Write an essay on how to hire them, aimed at founders.
Write an essay on what it takes to win customers away from an entrenched competitor. I want the strategy angle: what actually keeps people from switching?
Write a blog post giving a quick, irreverent checklist for judging how good a software team is, with a sentence or two of justification for each item.

Software teams keep arguing about who should write the spec and who should own product design. Write an essay about where that job should sit in an organization, who to hire for it, and who not to, drawing on any big-company experience you have.
Explain what a daily build is and why a software team should have one. I'd like it to start from why fast feedback loops matter and end with practical advice on how to set one up.

Why do the biggest IT consulting firms often turn out mediocre work, and why do the exciting young ones go downhill as they grow? Write a blog post, and feel free to find an unexpected analogy from outside software.
People love to complain that modern software is bloated. Write a piece arguing with that complaint, and with the idea that vendors should just ship a lite version with the features most people use.
I'm a working programmer and I'm tired of grand architecture talk and hype around every new platform. Write an essay on why smart people drift into over-abstraction and why it's mostly noise.

Is fixing every bug in your software actually the right goal? Write an essay for a small software company owner on how to decide which bugs are worth fixing, with practical ways to find out about them and put a number on it.
How long does it really take to build great software, and what business mistakes come from not understanding that? Write it as a blog post for startup founders.
Tell the story of a weekend spent fighting a third-party library while building a product, and use it to reflect on how a programmer's day-to-day work has changed over the last decade.

Everyone says reusing other people's code is good and reinventing the wheel is bad. Is that actually true? Write a blog post on when a software company should build things itself versus buy or outsource.

I want an essay about the unglamorous work of making software run on every kind of computer out there: testing on odd configurations, strict versus forgiving APIs, and what it costs. Draw on real experience if you can.

I'm a junior programmer on a team with no bug tracker, no schedules and no source control, and I can't just leave. Write something on how someone with no authority can still improve a dysfunctional engineering team.
Write a short blog post on refactoring an old codebase one safe step at a time instead of rewriting it, including what you do about tests.

Your team has a messy, fragile codebase that began life as a prototype, and people are itching to throw it out and start over. Tell the story of an alternative: how a careful cleanup went, with the pros and cons.
Write an essay about those days when you just can't get started working, and what actually helps. Personal and honest, from a programmer's point of view.
Why do non-technical managers and customers misjudge how far along a software project is? Write an essay for programmers on how to communicate with them.
Some programmers say you can skip up-front design and just write code and refactor. Write a blog post arguing your side on whether you should design a feature before implementing it.
How should a software team decide when to ship, and how often to release? Write a thoughtful piece that covers small teams, shrinkwrap products and big platforms.

I'm a developer and I keep reading books and articles about 'how software should be built' that seem to describe a completely different job from mine. Write an essay about why advice on software methodology so often doesn't transfer between kinds of projects.
Why would giant, profit-minded companies pay programmers to work on free open source software? Write it up as a proper essay, using some basic economics, for a technically literate reader.
Write a short essay about what goes wrong when companies try to measure and reward the performance of knowledge workers.
Write a blog post for software people about platforms: what makes a platform succeed or fail, and why platform vendors so often sabotage themselves.
I run a small bug-tracking product and customers keep asking for custom fields. I'm torn. Write me a candid blog post thinking through whether to add them.
Explain, for programmers, why higher-level tools never quite spare us from understanding what lies underneath them. Start from something concrete like how the internet moves data reliably.
Write an essay on why becoming a really proficient programmer keeps getting harder even as tools get better, and what that means for hiring and for picking technology for a new project.
Tell me the story of a week when everything went wrong at a small software company at once: servers, backups, phone lines, even the heating. And what you'd take away from it.
Should a software company talk publicly about products it hasn't shipped yet? Write an essay giving your honest view.
Write a short essay on how optimizing a single metric can quietly damage a business, using a well-known computer maker as the example.

I run a small software company and our website has been hosted off a line in our office. I'm told that's a bad idea but I don't really understand the alternatives. Can you write a behind-the-scenes post about moving a site to a proper data center, what you learn about how hosting actually works, and what the move was like?

Write an essay about building online communities: how the small design decisions in discussion software shape what kind of place it becomes. Use a discussion forum you built yourself as the case study, and take the sceptical questions people ask about its design one at a time.

Windows and Unix can do basically the same things these days, so why do programmers on each side seem to think so differently? Write a thoughtful essay on the cultural divide between the two camps, where it comes from, and whether either is simply right.

I'm about to start applying for summer internships. You've read hundreds of applications from a hiring manager's chair. Write me a candid post on what makes a résumé and cover letter get tossed, and what helps.

I'm about to run a beta test for a packaged software product that will go out to lots of users. What do I need to know about how many testers, how long it takes, and how to actually get feedback out of them?

I've been asked to write a foreword for a friend's book that helps programmers grow from writing code to actually developing software. I want it funny and a bit self-deprecating, and about how little developers know about what they don't know. Can you write it?

Usability gets all the attention in software design, but some very successful products have awful interfaces. Write an essay about what matters once the UI is right, especially for software that connects people to each other.

I'm hoping you can write some career advice for computer science undergrads, in the voice of a veteran programmer who runs a small software company and is openly self-mocking about whether anyone should listen to him. Cover what to study, what to do in the summers, and whether the offshoring panic matters.

Write a short foreword for a book about managing software projects and tracking bugs. I'd like it to open with something from everyday life rather than software, and argue for why careful, unglamorous attention to what goes wrong is what separates great products from merely good ones.

I've been thinking about what separates a junior programmer from a senior one, and it seems to have something to do with noticing things that aren't strictly errors. Write an essay about how code can be written so that mistakes are easier to spot, including whether naming conventions are worth the bother.

Is it actually true that some programmers are far better than others, or is that just something hiring managers tell themselves? Write a blog post from the point of view of someone running a small software company, making the case for paying for the best people.

Why do movie tickets cost the same whether the film is a hit or a flop, when basic economics says prices should vary with demand? Write a short, opinionated piece, and bring in what it might mean for how digital music gets priced.
Why are the most iconic products in each category so often ones with obvious flaws? Write an essay about what it takes to be number one rather than merely good.
Write a blog post about what design actually is, for software people who think it's about making things look nice. Use everyday objects and gadgets to make the point.
I want a blog post kicking off a series on good design, starting from a personal gripe about how hard modern gadgets have become to use. Funny and a bit self-deprecating.

You run a small software company and have just received hundreds of applications for a handful of summer internships. Write a blog post about how you sort through them and defend the process against people who call it elitist.
Write a cranky blog post about trying a bunch of new web calendar apps and finding that none of them do what you need. Include a theory about why so many of them exist.
Explain usability to a software team in the simplest way you can. If you could only give them one rule, what would it be and why?
A friend who wrote a book about starting a software business has asked you for a short, funny foreword. Write it, starting from something personal rather than from advice.

Tell the story of your first big review meeting with the most powerful person at the company, when you were a young program manager on the spreadsheet team. Make it funny and let a technical detail matter in the end.
Why doesn't paying people bonuses for specific results work well for managing knowledge workers? Write an essay for new managers who just took an economics class.
Write an essay on why military-style command and control management works poorly for software teams, and why the military uses it anyway.
Write a short blog-style book review of Bruce Tate's Beyond Java, framed around why veteran programmers are slow to jump on every new language and what makes a genuine advance in programming tools.
Take the shutdown menu in Windows Vista and use it to write a short essay about what too many options does to people, and how you'd design your way out of it.

A blogger argues that when a sales emergency interrupts a developer's planned two-week iteration, a good manager should shield her from the context switch. Write a response from someone who thinks that argument is missing something about what agile is for.

A management consultant just emailed me about 'benchmarking developer performance metrics'. Write a funny, cynical blog post about how software productivity consulting really works and why the metrics are worthless.
Companies keep sending free laptops and trips to bloggers and reviewers. Is it ethical to accept them if you disclose it? Write a blog post taking a position, and be honest about your own record.

Everyone says simple products win and that software should do fewer things. Write a blog post pushing back on the cult of simplicity, from the point of view of someone who runs a small software company.
Write a book review of Scott Rosenberg's Dreaming in Code, about the Chandler project, that uses it to talk about why ambitious software projects fail to converge. Open with something unexpected.

I run a small bootstrapped software company and we've been doing our own customer support because we can't afford staff yet. It's eating my time but I suspect there's something to learn here. Write an essay on how to do customer service well enough that customers actually talk about it.
Explain the history of Visual Basic for Applications in Office, why Microsoft built it the way it did, and what it says about how backward compatibility and lock-in work as a business strategy.
Why do text on a Mac and text on Windows look so different on screen? Write a blog post about the two philosophies of font rendering and why people argue about which is better.

I'm a software developer about to ship my first real product and I keep wondering what separates software that merely works from software people love. Write me a blog post about that, ideally starting from some everyday story.
Should blogs allow comments? Write an opinionated post arguing your position, for people who run their own sites.

A spreadsheet bug made 77.1 times 850 display as 100,000 instead of 65,535. Can you explain what is actually going on, including how floating point numbers work, and answer the obvious questions people would ask about whether it matters?

Write a strategy essay arguing that web application development is repeating the history of desktop software, and that this tells us what kind of platform will win. Use old software history to make the case.
Write a blog post about the time you approved every step of a design project and then hated the final result. What went wrong with incremental polishing?

Why are software schedules so hard to predict? Write an explanation of the phases of a software project and how each one should be scheduled differently, for a manager who has been burned by slipping deadlines.

Developers hate making schedules, and the schedules they do make are usually fiction. I run a small software company and want a practical method that gets honest ship dates without turning everyone into a timesheet fanatic. Write it up as a blog post for other software managers.

Write an essay about why customers pay for solving the hard, unpleasant parts of a business, and what that means for small startups that stick to the fun parts. Feel free to draw on a job you once had.

Our hosted service went down at 3:30 in the morning and our sysadmin had to rush into the city. Afterwards we argued about whether to promise customers a formal uptime guarantee. Write an essay on what uptime guarantees do and don't tell you, and what to do instead.
Microsoft just published the Office binary file specs and they look insane: hundreds of pages for Excel alone. Explain why these formats got so complicated, and whether it reflects bad engineering.
Write a cranky blog post about big software companies that keep building grand 'platform' products nobody asked for, and what that does to the rest of the industry.
I'm a college senior about to start interviewing for jobs. Give me some honest advice about the pressure tactics recruiters use on students when making offers, and how to handle them.

Write a short, irritated blog post about the flood of popular books and columns that string together amusing anecdotes and pass them off as science. Why does it bother you, and are you guilty of it too?
You run a small software company. Tell the story of a time you realized you'd approved something and then forgot you had, and what that says about how managers should treat their own advice.
Explain what a program manager does on a software team, why most teams lack a good one, and what makes the role work or fail. Write it as a practical guide from someone who held the job.

I've been reading an interview book with famous programmers and one of them strikes me as the kind of person who just gets things shipped, no matter how ugly the code. Write a blog post about that type of programmer: what they do differently, why teams need them, and where the style goes wrong.

Why does WiFi work so badly at tech conferences, even ones full of engineers? I'm helping organize an event for a few hundred people and want to understand what actually goes wrong and what to ask the venue. Write it up conversationally.

You've run a small software company for nearly a decade and only now figured out what it is actually about. Write a blog post on how a company finds its real mission, using your own company's history as the example, and why a fill-in-the-blank tagline can be a useful test.

Do software teams really need dedicated testers, or can programmers and automated tests cover it? Write a short blog post for a manager deciding how to staff a team, including what kind of person makes a good tester.

You've spent years preaching slow, profitable, bootstrapped growth, and now you're about to take venture capital for a new company. People are shocked. Write a post explaining how you decide whether a business should or shouldn't raise VC.

I run a small software startup and we have nearly all engineers and almost no sales or marketing staff. Is that the right mix? Write an essay on how the ratio of developers to sales and marketing people should change as a software company matures.

Write a blog post in which you admit you were wrong about distributed version control like Mercurial and Git. Explain what finally made you understand why it matters, in terms someone who only knows Subversion could follow.
Does it matter whether coworkers eat lunch together? Write a short essay about lunch at work, from the point of view of someone running a company who has strong feelings about it.

You've launched two products at startup conferences like TechCrunch Disrupt. A founder asks whether it's worth applying to launch at one. Write a thorough blog post giving your honest answer, covering what the conferences really deliver and what they don't.

Your company has only ever sold tools to software developers, and you've just launched a simple team-coordination app meant for everyone. Write a blog post about what it means to build a 'horizontal' product versus a 'vertical' one, and what you learned about why the great general-purpose apps succeed.
I run a small software company and our projects always seem to drag. Write an essay applying ideas from manufacturing to how software teams work, and what to do about it.
Write a blog post for programmers who are fed up with bad software patents: why so many get granted, and whether an ordinary developer can actually do anything about it.
I'm a developer at a software company and I want to start a side project on weekends. Does my employer own it? Explain how this really works, in plain language.
I quit Twitter and Facebook this year and feel much better. Write a personal essay about why these feeds make people unhappy, from someone who designs social software.
Write a blog post about why online programming Q&A communities have so many strict rules, and how welcoming beginners fits with that.
Write an essay on how a reputation points system works in an online Q&A community, why people care about the points, and where it goes wrong.
Tell the story of how a free programmer Q&A site came to exist, including what the internet was like for developers before it, and what the founders were really after.
Write an essay on what it will actually feel like to live through the arrival of superintelligent AI over the next decade or so. I'm tired of both the doom and the hype.
I'd like a short piece laying out a few observations about the economics of AI, and what they imply for work and society if they keep holding.
You've watched thousands of would-be founders ask where startup ideas come from. Write a blog post answering that properly.
Write a short essay arguing something counterintuitive about which startups are easier to get off the ground.
There's tons of advice for founders but hardly any on being a good startup investor. Write a practical essay on how to do it well, from someone who's invested in a lot of companies.
Write a long blog post of practical advice on how to achieve outlier success in your career or in building something, drawing on what you've seen in thousands of founders.
People keep asking me how I stay productive. Write up your own productivity advice in one place, including the unglamorous stuff like sleep and lists.
Write an essay on why a culture's tolerance for heretical ideas matters for innovation, with a view from the startup world.

People in tech love to argue about the year humans and machines will 'merge' or get overtaken by AI. Write a blog post giving your own take on that debate: what the merge might actually look like, whether it has already begun, and what we should do about it.

You run a well-known startup accelerator and you've been thinking about wealth concentration and automation. Write a short post floating a policy idea for giving ordinary citizens a direct stake in national economic growth, and be honest about the open problems.
Something feels off about a lot of venture-backed startups lately, and it isn't just high valuations. Write an essay about what the real problem might be and how a founder can avoid it.

Why do so many promising startups stall a few months after finishing an accelerator, even after growing fast during it? Write it up for founders, from the point of view of someone who has watched hundreds of them.
I'm working on something early and people keep asking whether it's a 'real company' yet. Write an essay on whether it matters if an early-stage venture is thought of as a project or a company.

I just turned 30 and want to write down whatever life advice I've actually learned in the past decade, without it sounding hollow. Write that post for me: relationships, work, money, time, regrets, all of it.

Write an essay arguing for how governments should handle the development of superhuman machine intelligence. Cover why the topic gets so little practical discussion, what concrete regulation might look like, and the objections to it.

Write an essay arguing that people who work in or near tech should take the development of machines smarter than humans seriously as a risk. I'm especially interested in why smart people tend to wave the danger away, either as impossible or as very far off.

I'm a first-time founder and we just raised our seed round. Everyone says hiring is now the thing I should obsess over, but nobody tells me how. Write me a proper guide to hiring for an early-stage startup, from someone who has watched hundreds of them do it well and badly.

Write a blog post about how the current wave of software and computing is different from earlier technological revolutions, and which two social problems we are probably underestimating because of how the last revolution turned out.

Imagine a government official asks you what policy changes would most help a country innovate and grow its economy. You have a startup investor's perspective. Write up your answer as a numbered list of recommendations with the reasoning behind each.
Why does Silicon Valley work so well for startups, and can other cities copy it? Write a short piece for a general newspaper audience.

I'm a seed investor with a decent track record and I've been looking back at which of my bets paid off. Write a blog post on what the best early-stage investments tend to have in common, and what that means for founders stressing about how popular their round is.
Write a post for startup founders about how employee stock options are commonly handled badly, and what concrete changes would make equity fairer to the people who join early.

A lot of people I know would probably be good at starting a company but are scared to try, partly because the famous founders seem impossibly impressive. Write something to encourage and also level with them.
You've sat through hundreds of seed pitches and watched founders raise money. Write a post about the mistakes founders most often make when fundraising.
Why is hiring engineers so much harder than hiring anyone else at a startup, and what can founders realistically do about it? I'd like a blog post with practical, opinionated advice.
Write a short essay about the difference between feeling productive and actually creating value, aimed at ambitious people who spend a lot of time around the startup scene.

I want a blog post on what the founders of extremely successful companies tend to do differently in the early days, from someone who has watched a lot of startups up close. Personal observation is fine, exceptions acknowledged.
We're told we worry too much about unlikely disasters. Is there any tail risk we actually underrate? Write an essay arguing a position.
Startup founders obsess over fundraising and hiring, but what about keeping people once you've hired them? Write a piece on employee retention at early-stage companies.
I keep meeting non-technical founders who spend months hunting for a technical cofounder. Write a blunt blog post telling them what to do instead.
What actually makes things get done, in a company or in life? Write a short reflective post with your best theory and why it holds up.
A 19-year-old who wants to do something great asks you whether to stay in college, join a company or start their own. Write your honest advice as a blog post.
People argue about whether innovation has slowed down. Write an essay that takes the question seriously: where has progress been fast, where has it stalled, and why?

Write a funny piece in the style of a travel-guide or anthropology survey, describing three imaginary countries with strange systems of government, each one a clever twist on a real political idea. Let each one have an ironic downfall or loophole.

Two antidepressants from the early 2010s, vilazodone and vortioxetine, were designed from theory rather than discovered by accident. I'm a curious non-specialist: explain the pharmacology behind why drug companies thought they'd be better, and then whether they actually turned out to be. Be honest about the parts that don't make sense.

I find paywalled news articles weirdly infuriating, even though the standard economic argument says a business that offers a deal I can decline shouldn't be able to make me worse off. Write an essay working out why paywalls feel like a harm, and what could be done about it.

A survey says nearly half of one party's voters 'believe' a wild conspiracy theory, and people take that as proof that fake news is enormously persuasive. How much should we trust poll numbers like that? Write a blog-style piece on what such surveys actually measure.

Should news organizations spend so much energy debunking stupid or fringe ideas? Write an essay weighing the case for challenging them against the case for ignoring them, ideally using a historical example that tells us something.

I've heard that gout is oddly common among famous, successful people, and that there might be a real biochemical reason for it. Write a skeptical but curious blog post on whether high uric acid could actually make you more accomplished.

I'm a psychiatrist and I keep running into the ways our health insurance setup messes with my patients' lives, beyond the usual complaints about cost and access. Write a blog post making the case against tying insurance to employment, using the kinds of people you see in practice.

The Amish supposedly spend a fraction of what the rest of us do on health care, and have no insurance companies. Is that actually true, how do they pull it off, and could any of it be copied by everyone else? Write it up properly, skeptically, with real numbers where you can find them.
Why are depression and a poor sense of smell linked? Go through the evidence, work out which way the causation probably runs, and say whether it suggests anything about treatment.

Write a humorous piece describing seven invented countries, each with a bizarre legal system built around some clever idea about fairness or incentives. Play out the strange consequences of each, as if for a blog about thought experiments in law.

Why is it important not to treat a learner's persistent, sometimes hostile-sounding questions as a challenge to your authority? I'm thinking about teachers, and also about how people react to curious questioners online. Write an essay on it.

I want a blog post about a self-experiment: I tried a sleep supplement, thought it was working wonders, then ran a proper blinded trial on myself to check. Write it as the experimenter, including what went wrong with my first impression and what I actually learned.

Write a blog post that uses a review of a book on Chinese preschools as a jumping-off point to ask whether strict, discipline-heavy schooling builds the self-control that creative, self-directed adults need, or just crushes motivation. Look at what evidence we actually have, and be honest when it runs out.

Most doctors seem to think they're better than the average doctor, which can't be true of everyone. I'm a psychiatrist and I catch myself doing it too. Write a blog post working out why it happens, from the inside.

People keep telling me that psychiatric labels like depression or autism are useless because each one lumps together many different causes. Is that actually a good objection? Write an essay on whether a diagnosis can be useful even if it doesn't match any single underlying cause, and what we should do about the heterogeneity.

I've been reading about how therapy and psychedelics supposedly change deep emotional beliefs that plain evidence can't touch. Write an essay on why the mind seems to keep some of its beliefs walled off from each other, what that says about mental illness, and whether it also explains why smart, informed people fail to change their minds.

I'm a psychiatrist who has read a lot of psychotherapy books and keeps feeling uneasy about them. Write a skeptical essay on what these books have in common, and why that should make a thoughtful clinician cautious about believing them.

People say a theory that can't be tested isn't science, so multiverse ideas are out. Write something that builds intuition for why that's too glib, using a few short fables rather than abstract philosophy.

Write a candid book review of Bessel van der Kolk's The Body Keeps the Score from the point of view of a practicing psychiatrist: what it taught you, where it left you unconvinced, and what you'd actually change in how you treat patients.

An article in Aeon argues that multiverse theories are 'post-empirical' pseudoscience because they can't be tested. Write a response from a non-expert who thinks the argument proves too much. Build the case slowly with examples, without claiming special authority.

Several famous Buddhist teachers who were widely regarded as enlightened have been caught up in sex scandals. Write a short essay on what, if anything, that tells us about what enlightenment actually is.
Write a book review of James C. Scott's Against the Grain, for readers who know his earlier work. I want your honest take on whether his story about the origins of early states holds up.
Everyone complains about how much money is in politics. Write an essay arguing about whether that's even the right way to look at it, and what the amount of political spending really tells us.

I keep reading that the opioid crisis was fueled by a made-up medical concept, and that doctors fell for it. I'm a psychiatrist-adjacent skeptic and suspect the story is more complicated than the headlines. Write an essay that takes the media and Senate version of this idea seriously and tests it against how medicine actually works with patients who ask for drugs.

Psychedelic users sometimes report lingering visual changes afterward, and the estimates of how common this is range from a few percent to basically nobody. I've got some survey data from a few thousand readers about this. Write a blog post that works out why the estimates disagree and what it might say about how differently people perceive the world.

Walk me through the predictive-coding theory of how psychedelics work, the idea from Friston and Carhart-Harris about relaxed priors, as if you were leading a journal club. Explain it clearly, say where you think the authors are convincing, and where you'd push back.

Whatever happened to the big public conversation about superintelligence and AI risk from ten years ago? I'd like a thoughtful book-review-style essay that also looks at an alternative picture of how advanced AI might develop, and whether the old worries still hold up.
I just saw a newspaper piece arguing we shouldn't run experiments to test whether we live in a simulation, in case it gets the universe shut down. Write a short, funny-but-serious rebuttal.

Could parasites that hijack animal behavior have shaped how our brains and bodies work, including why psychiatric drugs so often stop working? Walk me through a recent academic paper on this, how plausible it is, and what it would mean for biology if true.

Write a blog post about trying to replicate a psychiatry study that claimed a certain snack food could trigger manic episodes, using data from a big reader survey. Be honest about what the data can and can't show.

I keep hearing about Ken Kesey and the Merry Pranksters but never got around to reading Tom Wolfe's book about them. Can you write a book review of The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test that tells me the story and also tells me what you make of it, especially what it says about psychedelics?

I'm a psychiatrist and I'm puzzled by the gabapentinoids. Write a post comparing gabapentin, pregabalin and phenibut: what's actually different between them, what seems like it should explain it, and what remains a mystery.

Rationalists love to say you should correct for your biases, and yet 'you're only saying that because you're biased' tends to wreck conversations. Write an essay on why bias arguments so often go nowhere, and whether there's any good way to use them.
I've noticed words like 'lie' and 'abuse' getting stretched to cover more and more. Write a post arguing about whether it matters when we broaden the meaning of a word like that.

Write an essay about a puzzle in medical statistics: a drug class that studies keep linking to higher death rates, even after researchers say they've controlled for everything, and what it would mean if a newer study with a very different method turned out to be right.

Did cultural evolution produce sexual purity taboos, including taboos on promiscuity and homosexuality, partly as a defense against sexually transmitted infections? Go through the evidence for and against and tell me how far you think it gets.

Philip Morris says it's going smoke-free and Tyson is selling plant-based chicken. Should we buy from companies that spent decades doing the harm and are now selling the fix? Write a short, thoughtful blog post weighing it.

I want a book-review style blog post about the Baumol effect as an explanation for why health care and education keep getting more expensive. Lay out the case, then say honestly what still bothers you.

Write an essay on the idea that careful rational argument can sometimes lead people further from the truth, not closer. Start from everyday examples and work up to how societies reason about big questions, and end with what we should practically do about it.

Everyone is excited about psychedelics as a treatment for depression and trauma right now. Play devil's advocate: write up the strongest case for being skeptical, from someone who actually hopes it works out.

A candidate gene for depression spawned hundreds of studies, a mechanism story, media coverage and even commercial genetic tests, and then a giant sample found nothing. Write an essay on what that episode should make us worry about in science and medicine.

I'm a psychiatrist and my patients can't find buspirone anywhere, and meanwhile insulin is absurdly expensive even though it's off-patent. Why do drug markets behave so differently from markets for bread or chairs? Write a blog post working through it, with some honesty about what you don't know.

Economic growth used to look like it was racing toward infinity, and then around the middle of the twentieth century it stopped accelerating. Why? Write a long speculative essay on what drove the old trend, what broke it, and what it might mean for the future.

A survey finds that around 40% of Americans support some mild form of eugenics, yet any politician who said so would be shouted down. How can a view be both popular and taboo? Write a short essay with a good analogy.

Elephants have bigger brains than we do, and yet we're the ones writing the books. What actually makes some animals smarter than others? I'd like an essay that looks at what biology tells us about intelligence, including the oddity of clever birds, and what it might imply for AI.

I find Karl Friston's free energy principle and predictive coding almost impossible to follow, but perceptual control theory makes immediate sense to me. Write a post arguing about how these two frameworks relate, and whether one is a better way of talking than the other.

The FDA just approved a nasal-spray version of ketamine for treatment-resistant depression. You're a psychiatrist who has wanted to prescribe ketamine for years. Write a blog post on why this approval is more disappointing than good news.

I just read an exposé about how awful it is to work as a Facebook content moderator. You run a blog with a big comment section and have worked in a psychiatric hospital. Write a reaction to the piece, including what the reporting leaves out about why these rules exist.
Write a short essay on how we should judge brilliant thinkers who are also sometimes spectacularly wrong. When someone smart says something dumb, how much should that change how we read them?

I keep seeing two contradictory stories about how fringe, low-status people affect a cause. Sometimes they seem to pave the way for respectable people to join in, and sometimes they seem to poison it. Write an essay thinking through both stories and whether there's any way to tell which one applies.

I want a blog-style book review of Peter Thiel's Zero to One, focusing on what he says about monopoly and whether competition is really as good as economics textbooks say. Skeptical but fair, please, with your own counterpoints.

Write a short piece about a thought experiment that reframes how we think about government and the things that govern us beyond laws and elections. Use it to explain a few real-world puzzles, like why nation-building fails and what libertarians actually want.

I keep seeing a particular kind of bad argument in debates where someone who says 'we should do some of Y too' gets treated as though they claim 'only Y matters.' Can you write a short blog post naming and explaining this pattern, with several examples and some sympathy for why it happens?
Is schizophrenia somehow the opposite of autism? Write a blog post working through the case for and against that idea, and be honest about how strong the evidence really is.

Research output keeps growing exponentially, yet measured progress in things like chip density, crop yields and economic growth seems roughly constant per year. Is science slowing down? Write an essay giving your own take on how worried we should be, and what the right baseline expectation even is.

Some activists argue that nobody alive is morally acceptable, since we all benefit from some structural harm. I find that both compelling and paralyzing. Write an essay on where the bar for being a 'good person' should be set, and how to think about it.
Write a blog post about the newest evidence on how ketamine works as a rapid antidepressant, and what it might mean for psychiatry and for how we think about drugs and addiction.

You're a psychiatrist who wrote a long post years ago about whether SSRIs are barely better than placebo. Write the follow-up: what you've changed your mind about since, and how you reconcile the trial data with what you see in the clinic.

A few years ago you did a rough cost-benefit analysis of marijuana legalization and ended up undecided. Now several states have legalized and data is coming in. Write the follow-up, honestly, including where your earlier prediction turned out wrong.

I used to be sure that preschool programs were a waste of money because they don't raise test scores. Then I learned about evidence of long-run benefits. Write a post about changing your mind on this, owning the error, and working out what it implies for other things you believe.

People often assume that anyone who believes in "desert" must secretly want bad people to suffer. I don't think that's the real intuition. Write an essay that tries to give the most sympathetic version of what it means to say someone deserves a bad outcome, using concrete cases where it clashes with utilitarian arithmetic, and be honest about whether the intuition survives scrutiny.

Why should smart drugs even exist? If a pill can make you learn better, why wouldn't evolution have left us on that setting already? Write a speculative piece on how cholinergic drugs like nicotine and piracetam might work, what they might trade off against, and flag where you're out on a limb.

Write a blog post using a piece of folklore as a metaphor for how the mind decides which thoughts reach consciousness, and what that might explain about intrusive thoughts and anxiety. You can draw on your experience as a psychiatrist.

A recent economics paper claims that each researcher is far less productive than decades ago, since scientific progress stays roughly constant while the number of researchers grows exponentially. Is science slowing down? Write an essay giving your own take, including whether we should even find this surprising.

Use a thought experiment about a town founded by people who hate late-night noise to think through when a community has the right to restrict what its members do, and then apply it to the housing and NIMBY debate. Write it as a long, exploratory blog post with a libertarian-ish flavor, ending with a practical proposal.

Write a blog post for a general educated audience about the earliest stage of schizophrenia, the so-called prodrome. Is it worth intervening aggressively that early, and is there any good reason, in terms of how the brain works, to think delay makes things worse? Be honest about how uncertain the evidence is.

I finally got around to reading The Black Swan, years after everyone else. Write me a book review that engages with the ideas rather than summarizing them, including where you think Taleb is right and where his advice might be dangerous. Some humor welcome, since reviewing him seems like a risky business.
Genetics went from hopeless to productive in a couple of decades. Write an essay on what happened there and whether sciences that still seem stuck, like psychiatry, can learn anything from it.

Write a short essay on whether bureaucratic hassle is ever deliberate, a feature rather than a bug. Use a concrete example from health insurance or similar, and be honest about where the idea stops working.

A headline is going around saying a new study proves trigger warnings are harmful to college students. Write a blog post for a skeptical general reader on whether the study shows that, and what you'd actually do about trigger warnings.

Someone told me there's a neat historical explanation for why drugstore melatonin pills are many times stronger than what research suggests you need. It involves a university patent. Write a short blog post weighing whether that story is believable, and how much to trust a famous expert's account when it sounds too perverse to be true.

A common view says disagreements come in two kinds: factual ones we can resolve, and fundamental value differences where the other side is just an enemy. Write an essay questioning how real and how clean that divide is, and what it means for how we treat political opponents.

Rationalists once pitched rationality as a martial art, a trainable skill, but people say that's the part of the movement that's stalled. Where does a blog that mostly argues about whatever controversy is in the news fit into that? Write a short, candid reflection from a blogger's point of view.

I keep hearing the Fermi Paradox is 'solved' by a recent paper about the Drake Equation. Can you explain what the paradox is, what's wrong with the way people used the Drake Equation, and whether the dissolution is convincing? Blog-post style, from someone who found it exciting.

Write a blog post from a psychiatrist's perspective: imagine you quit your job and tried to fight rising healthcare costs by running the cheapest possible practice. Do the math, then wonder why nobody does this.

Bryan Caplan argues that it's arbitrary which atrocities and scandals people get outraged about, like sexual harassment versus an abusive boss, or chemical weapons versus conventional ones. Write a response arguing there might be a rational explanation.

A psychiatrist treated a patient who took LSD once and has hallucinated ever since. Write an essay on how a drug that leaves the body in hours could cause permanent changes, and what that might say about other lasting side effects.

I'm a psychiatrist and I just read a blog post arguing that my profession is negligent for not routinely testing depressed patients for environmental poisons like lead. A story about one doctor's patient who turned out to be lead-exposed is making the rounds. Write a thoughtful response from a practicing clinician's point of view: is it reasonable that we don't test more, or is the critic right?

A newspaper profile of a loose group of anti-political-correctness commentators set off a debate: people say you can't claim to be silenced if you have millions of listeners and a lucrative Patreon. Write an essay examining whether something can really be both popular and silenced, and what the popularity argument misses.

Write a blog post about the difference between a single recommendation and a full set of guidelines, using medicine as the starting point, and why so few other areas (diets, supplements, self-help) have anything like it.

It's April Fools' Day and also Passover, which strikes me as the right moment to speculate about God. Write a playful but serious essay that pulls together ideas from decision theory, AI alignment and physics to ask whether anything like a God could fall out of them. Assume the reader knows some rationalist jargon but explain each idea as you go.

I want a book review of Jordan Peterson's Twelve Rules for Life from someone who went in expecting to mock it. Say what actually works about the book, what doesn't, and what kind of thing it really is.
Is it actually unethical to download scientific papers from a pirate site like Sci-Hub? Work through the strongest arguments on both sides and tell me where you land.

I've read a bit about predictive coding and I'm curious how it's supposed to explain mood and depression. Can you walk me through the idea that emotions are about confidence in your predictions, what mood would be on that view, and then tell me honestly whether the theory holds together?

Everyone says Karl Friston's free energy principle is a big deal in neuroscience, and almost nobody seems to understand it. You're a psychiatrist with no special math background trying to make sense of it. Write up your best attempt, including what's convincing and what isn't.

Is the placebo effect actually real? I keep hearing it's one of the most powerful forces in medicine, but I've also seen claims that it's overblown. Write up what the evidence really says and how you'd make sense of it.

I read an article arguing that stories about good guys fighting bad guys are a modern invention, basically a product of nationalism, and that ancient myths like the Iliad weren't like that at all. Is that right? Write an essay weighing the claim and offering your own account of why modern stories look the way they do.

I keep seeing startups that want to put dating on the blockchain, and I can't tell whether any of it is serious. Take a crypto dating site's white paper seriously and go through it claim by claim, half-jokingly but with real scrutiny: what might actually work, what looks like a scam, and what the blockchain is even doing there.

A well-known sci-fi author wrote that fears about superintelligent AI are really just Silicon Valley capitalists projecting their own nature onto machines. Write a sharp rebuttal. I'm interested in whether 'this resembles that' counts as an argument at all, and what's wrong with explaining away a risk by psychoanalyzing the people who worry about it.

Oregon bans self-service gas stations and people there get outraged at the idea of pumping your own. Everyone else laughs. Write an essay that starts there but asks what it should make us worry about, about how we decide what's absurd and what's sensible.

Write a deadpan, absurdly over-researched piece of fan scholarship about what became of the Silmarils after the end of The Silmarillion. Treat it as a serious detective problem, use whatever pop culture you like as 'evidence', and keep a straight face throughout.

A small pharma company's experimental antidepressant failed its main trial, then put out a press release months later saying it worked after all, and the stock jumped. I'm a psychiatrist who badly wanted it to be real. Write a blog post working out whether to believe the new results, and why the market might believe them anyway.

Write a provocative essay arguing that public conversation about sexual harassment is too one-sidedly gendered, and that this costs everyone, including the people it claims to protect. Bring in data, and use analogies from other areas of social debate.
It's my birthday and I'm wondering whether getting older really makes you wiser, or whether the things I think I've learned are something else. Write a candid, self-skeptical essay on that.
Write an essay about the idea that you can be missing an entire concept, an emotion or an idea, and not realize it, and what that should mean for how we treat ideas that seem pointless or confused.

Why is explaining a hard idea so different from explaining something simple? Someone told me there are already experts who explained it better than I could, so why bother writing my own explanation? Write a blog post addressing that.
Rat Park is usually cited as proof that addiction is caused by misery and deprivation. Write a skeptical essay examining whether that story holds up.
New Atheism went from cultural force to being widely despised, even by people who agree that God doesn't exist. Why did that happen? Write an essay with your own theory.

People say the Church never burned scientists for their science, only for heresy. Suppose that's true. Is there still something to learn from it about what happens to curious people under an orthodoxy, and what a sensible person should do about it? Write an essay, and feel free to range from medieval Europe to the Soviet Union.

Write a journal-club style blog post about a paper that tries to make sense of what serotonin actually does in the brain, focusing on how two different receptor types might fit together. Be skeptical where it's warranted, and keep it readable for a non-neuroscientist.

I just read a magazine piece that sorts futurists into four quadrants by optimism and belief in a singularity, mostly by their gender, race and class. It annoyed me. Write a rebuttal blog post: what's wrong with it, and what should writing about the future be doing instead?

Why do people living in the same city, even doing the same job, report such wildly different experiences of how other people treat them: some say everyone is kind, others say everyone is awful? Write a thoughtful essay, drawing on your psychiatry background if you like.

You've spent years defending IQ research against people who call it meaningless. But readers keep writing in panicking about their own low scores. Write a post explaining why IQ can be hugely important for science and still not worth agonizing over personally.
Why doesn't the brain just spiral into endless bliss the moment it feels something good? Write a short blog post on that puzzle, and bring in whatever you know about advanced meditation.

I'm a doctor with no time and a lot of skepticism about meditation. Write a long book review of a no-nonsense, practical guide to Buddhist meditation and enlightenment written by an ER physician. I want to know what it actually claims, what the path looks like, whether it's worth wanting, and whether any of it connects to modern brain science.

Suppose the brain is basically a machine for making and checking predictions. Is there a way to explain depression in that framework, and sadness and happiness too? Speculative is fine, just flag where you're guessing.

If the brain builds all its concepts from scratch out of sensory data, how can evolutionary psychology claim that genes make us attracted to specific things like particular body shapes? Write a piece working through that tension and say what you'd make of it.

Is moral offsetting okay? Like flying and then paying to clean up the carbon, or eating meat and donating to an animal charity. Most people think that works for emissions but obviously not for murder. Write an essay trying to find a principled line instead of just saying 'trivial vs serious.'

You just got back from a big effective altruism conference in San Francisco, as a sympathetic but skeptical outsider (you're a doctor who's been dodging the career coaches). Write up what it was like: the polished spreadsheet people, the very strange fringes, and what you think actually holds the whole thing together. Keep it personal and a bit wry.

A friend of mine is thinking about buying one of those all-in-one 'brain boost' supplement stacks. I'm a psychiatrist who knows the field. Write a blog post explaining why you're wary of branded combination nootropics, even the well-made ones, and what you'd do instead.

The First Amendment is a clean bright-line rule, but social norms about free speech (who can criticize whom, who can get fired for what) seem hopelessly incoherent. Is there any principled way to think about them? Write an essay working through it, and be honest about where your own position gets fuzzy.

Someone with a big platform retweeted a stranger's offensive joke so his future employers would see it, and her defenders said that isn't doxxing because he posted it publicly under his own name. Write an essay on whether 'just signal-boosting' public statements to get people fired is something we should be okay with.

Friends at a party insisted that the pharaoh Djoser was the real inspiration behind both the god Osiris and the Biblical Joseph. Write up what you'd find if you actually dug into whether either connection holds up.

A lot of people blame the Supreme Court's Griggs v. Duke Power decision for why employers demand college degrees for jobs that don't need them. Is that a fair diagnosis? Write a short essay testing it.

Every few weeks another magazine publishes an article attacking meritocracy, which sounds weird since the word seems to just mean the best people getting the jobs. I want an essay that works out whether these critics have a point and whether meritocracy is worth defending.

I just read a magazine piece arguing that humble technologies like barbed wire and warehouse software matter more than flashy ones, and it ended by saying we should perhaps fear mundane software more than superintelligent AI. Write an essay responding to it, about what's wrong with that kind of move and what sort of caution we should actually want.

Why do people ask 'what are you reading?' when they really mean 'can I join you?' Why not just say what they mean? Write a piece that takes a viral social-rule post and tries to explain why ordinary conversation is built this way.

Depression research seems to have a dozen unrelated leads at once: stress hormones, inflammation, serotonin, ketamine, folate, shock therapy. Is there any single mechanism that could tie them together, and how much should we trust it? Write it up as a curious non-specialist who reads the papers and is honest about what still confuses him.

Why do street drugs like ketamine and MDMA keep turning out to be better psychiatric treatments than what pharmaceutical companies produce on purpose? I want a speculative blog post that tries a few explanations and says honestly where they might fail.

Laszlo Polgar claimed he could raise any child into a genius, and his three daughters became chess prodigies. Does that prove education can beat talent, or is something else going on? Write a thoughtful, skeptical but playful piece, weighing genetics, practice, and the objection that such a childhood is cruel.

Write a deadpan satirical piece in the style of the hot takes that blame everything on late capitalism and 'modern pathologies', except applied to things that are very obviously ancient. Pick a handful of absurd targets and make the fake-critical argument with a straight face.

I saw a headline saying a third of newly approved drugs end up recalled or with new safety warnings, and people are saying the FDA is too lax. Is that actually what the number means? Write it up properly, as someone who prescribes these drugs.

People keep claiming polyamory is just polygyny in disguise, where a few high-status men end up with all the women and everyone else loses. Write a blog post that actually tests that claim against whatever data you can find, and is honest about the data's limits.

I'm interested in reducing mass incarceration but everyone gets stuck on 'which criminals do you release?' Is there a lower-hanging fruit? I've heard bail might be one. Write an essay looking at what bail does, whether it does any good, and whether charities that pay it are worth donating to.

Everyone is using a ridiculous overpriced startup product as proof that Silicon Valley is vapid and shallow. Write a blog post giving a reality check on that: is the stereotype fair, and why does it feel so true to so many people?

After an election loss, everyone says the losing party should be more emotional, more tribal, less wonky. Write an essay about the hidden risk in that advice: what happens to a party's own thinking when it adopts the style that wins votes?

A journalist argues that conservatives abandoned shared institutions like the press and universities for their own echo chambers. I think the story is more complicated, and the dynamics are worse than either side admits. Write a long essay responding, as a liberal who works in a hospital and reads both sides.

Is there a biological explanation for why people with anorexia can't just regain weight once they decide to? Speculate about it using what we know about obesity and the body's weight set point. Flag clearly that you're not an expert.

Walk me through a recent psychiatry study on whether childhood abuse lowers IQ, and tell me what you make of it. I'm interested in how it fits with twin-study findings about family environment, and how much we should trust it.

Some students plan to promote free speech on campus by inviting the most controversial speakers they can find. Write a short essay on whether that actually helps the cause of free speech, or whether there's a hidden cost to how we invoke principles we care about.

I'm a psychiatry resident and have to present an interesting case at a conference next month. I'd like to see how someone might write up a case where the explanation ended up mattering more than the treatment. Can you write it as a thoughtful blog post, with a real patient story, the physiology behind it, and what it says about how psychiatry works?

Write an essay about consent for people who can't give it in the usual verbal way, like long-term institutionalized patients or the severely intellectually disabled. Can they ever have a sexual life? I want something honest about how hard this is, and I don't want a tidy answer.
