Write a pastiche of G.K. Chesterton arguing about AI risk. He should answer the standard skeptical objections (it sounds like a fairy tale, a smart machine would have rich motives, the worriers are self-indulgent and ignore real problems like malaria) in his usual paradoxical, epigram-heavy style.

I keep hearing about an obscure psychology book from the sixties that claims the brain is built out of control systems like thermostats. Can you write a candid review of the idea: what's convincing, what's a stretch, and whether it's useful? Please be upfront if you only partly understand it.

I'm a non-technical person who just got invited to a big conference on the risks and benefits of AI, full of researchers, economists and philosophers. Write up your impressions of what such a gathering is actually like and what ideas people are chewing on, as a loose, honest blog post.

A big news site just ran a takedown of a hyped psychology theory, and it reads as very convincing. You think the theory may well be wrong, but you're uneasy about the article. Write a blog post on what makes a debunking trustworthy and where this one falls short.

I just got my medical board exam results back and it got me wondering: why do average scores on standardized tests seem to level off after a few years of training? Dig into what we actually know and what might explain it.
Write an essay about the danger of drawing firm rules of thumb from one or two memorable cases, with a few examples from tech forecasting, politics and anything else that fits.

A president-elect keeps getting credit for companies announcing they will keep jobs in the country. Write a blog post on why those announcements might be misleading, and what the incentives behind them look like.

Explain the idea that mental disorders might be networks of mutually reinforcing symptoms rather than single underlying diseases. Why would anyone think that, what would it explain, and where does it break down? Write it for a curious reader with some psychiatry background.

I keep reading amazing stories on Reddit threads about spooky coincidences and past lives, and part of me can't dismiss them. Write a piece on why the most compelling things we read online should often be treated as lies, and why that's so hard to actually believe.
Write a blog post investigating whether altitude affects obesity, and whether rising atmospheric CO2 could be fueling the obesity epidemic. Weigh the evidence honestly, even if the theory is fun.
Do experts actually beat smart amateurs at predicting how experiments turn out? Walk me through what a study of this would find and what we should and shouldn't conclude from it.

I'm a doctor who has avoided the famous novel about medical internship for years because I assumed it would be cliché. Write a review of The House of God that explains what it gets right about medicine and whether it mattered beyond being a good read.

It's the day before the 2016 US election and the race looks close. I'm worried everyone will draw sweeping conclusions about the country from whichever way it falls. Write a short essay on how we should think about what the result will mean.
I saw a claim that the Great Pyramid's coordinates encode the speed of light. Is that a real coincidence, and what can it teach us about statistics in actual science? Write it up properly.

I know almost nothing about the technical side, but I've been following the AI risk debate. Do the recent advances in neural networks change how we should think about superintelligent AI as a goal-maximizing agent? Write an exploratory essay.

Do people end up attracted to partners who resemble their opposite-sex parent? I'd like a skeptical, evidence-weighing write-up that covers the animal research, the human studies, and what twin studies say about how we choose mates.

There's a theory that autism and schizophrenia are failures or overshoots of human 'self-domestication', like the changes seen in tame foxes. Write a critical but fair assessment of whether it holds up, and what, if anything, is worth salvaging.

A newspaper story just revealed that the sugar industry quietly paid for research blaming fat for heart disease, and people are treating it as proof that sugar was the real villain all along. Write a short piece putting that kind of revelation in context.

I keep reading that the brain is basically a prediction machine. Can you write a speculative essay on how that idea might connect to what's going on neurochemically in conditions like schizophrenia, hallucinogen use and autism? Be upfront about what's shaky.

Someone shared one of those 'you're more likely to be killed by your own furniture than by a terrorist' articles. Something about the statistics bugs me but I can't put my finger on it. Write a blog post on what's wrong with reasoning like this.

A news site just argued that EpiPen prices jumped because drugs aren't regulated like chairs and mugs, i.e. not enough regulation. I think that's backwards. Write a funny but pointed blog post making the opposite case.

Write a speculative essay about the replication crisis in psychology: is there a pattern in which famous findings are collapsing, and what might it say about how much power the unconscious mind really has? Mark clearly that you're guessing from a handful of examples.

I'm a psychiatrist-in-training and something about drug tolerance has always confused me: why do some drugs stop working, some keep working forever, and some make things worse than baseline? Write an exploratory essay about this puzzle, admitting what we don't know.

Write an essay on what actually makes one group an outgroup for another. It's not simply difference or hostility. Then use it to explain how American political tribes and online arguments have shifted around 2016, and make some predictions.

Write a short blog post about two kinds of goals, the ones where you want something and build a plan, and the ones where you already have the plan and must find a reason to fill it. Why do the second kind feel off to you?

I'm a psychiatry resident about to start my final year and want to write a funny, honest, slightly rueful blog post about what a year of training changes: the tricks you pick up, the supervisors, the moments of doubt, the things that scare you. Write it as a series of short numbered sections, in a wry first-person voice.

I keep seeing press releases saying a new study proves something surprising about fathers and sons. Take a recent one like that, look at the actual paper, and write up what you find. I'd like a skeptical statistician's view on what to believe.

Write an essay arguing against the habit of reading hidden coded messages into politicians' offhand remarks. Use a few recent examples from the 2016 campaign and British politics, and say what you think is lost when 'offensive' gets treated as the same thing as 'bigoted'.

A new study just showed ketamine's antidepressant effect comes from a metabolite, not the mechanism everyone assumed. I'm wondering what that says about how trustworthy psychiatric research is. Write a blog post digging into how the field behaved before it corrected itself.

Write a speculative essay about an economy that slowly drifts out of human control: companies run by algorithms, owned by algorithms, selling to other algorithms. Could that actually happen, what would stop it, and why should we worry?

Write an essay about why we tend to sympathize with people in a bad job situation only when we've seen it up close, and whether being personally affected makes someone a better or worse judge of whether they're being treated fairly. Feel free to be honest about your own inconsistencies.

I'm trying to make up my mind about whether junior doctors who strike over their working conditions are justified. You trained in a medical system outside the US and have worked in the American one. Write something honest about what you saw and where you land, including your doubts about labor disputes in general.

A biologist argues that you can't engineer smarter humans because every gene touches many systems, so optimizing for intelligence must cost you health or other traits, like a car built only for speed. Is that objection actually right? Write it up carefully, with the evidence and your own uncertainty about the genetics.

I run an online forum and keep getting asked why I ban people who try to publicly shame others, since shaming can be a legitimate social tool. Write an essay on when meanness, if ever, is excusable, and what principle I could use to decide.

Many of the scientists who ran the first psychedelic experiments in the 1950s and 60s went on to hold some extremely strange beliefs. Write an essay speculating on why that happened, and what it might tell us about the drugs. Be upfront about how speculative you are.
Where does religion come from? I'm tired of the usual answers about hyperactive agent detection. Write an essay with a different angle, one that takes ancient religions seriously on their own terms.

Groups like nations, religions, fandoms, parties and online communities all seem to share some common machinery, whatever they claim to be about. Write an essay on what that shared thing is, why people value belonging to these groups despite the obvious dangers, and why almost any shared activity seems to drift toward becoming a social club.

I've read plenty of self-help success books and never trust them. Someone told me to look at Trump's 1988 book The Art of the Deal, as a how-to on persuasion and success. Write a book review: is there anything to learn from it, and what does it reveal about the man who wrote it?

Twin studies are always summarized as '50% nature, 50% nurture,' and people take the 'nurture' half to mean parenting, schools and friends. Is that reading right? Write a post on what the non-shared environment term in twin studies actually contains.

A Vox piece argues that prisons have become America's substitute for a gutted mental health system, since mentally ill people in prison outnumber those in state hospitals ten to one. As a practicing psychiatrist, write a rebuttal that checks the statistic and the story behind it.

Online communities that prize open debate seem to get stuck re-fighting the same few arguments forever. Why does that happen, and what can a community do about it without giving up on honest disagreement? I'd like a thoughtful blog post.

You're a psychiatrist reflecting on your own habits. Write an essay on the two broad stances a doctor can take toward what patients say they want, taking them at their word versus looking for the real problem underneath, and which one you lean toward and why.

A study came out claiming that women's contributions to open source projects on GitHub get judged differently depending on whether their gender is visible, and the headlines are all about sexism in tech. I haven't read the paper. Can you go through what it actually found, how far the evidence goes, and whether the coverage is fair? Write it up like a blog post from a skeptical statistics-minded reader.

Write a book review of Philip Tetlock's Superforecasting for a blog audience that's already interested in rationality and cognitive biases. Explain what the book claims about people who predict the future unusually well, what to make of it, and how much a reader who knows the field already would get out of it.

Write a blog post about the link between smoking and schizophrenia. I've seen claims that smoking causes psychosis and others that it protects against it, and I'd like someone to dig into how good the evidence on each side actually is, and what researchers should do when studies disagree.

I work as a psychiatrist and I keep feeling like the world is far more miserable than most people around me seem to think. Help me write an essay on how much hidden suffering there is, why we don't see it, and whether I can check my impression with some rough numbers.

OpenAI has just launched with the promise to make advanced AI research open source and widely available. Is that actually a good idea for safety? Write a thoughtful critique that takes the risks of superintelligence seriously.

I just finished a popular-science book arguing that a country's average IQ matters far more for its wealth than any one person's IQ matters for theirs. Write a thoughtful review: lay out the book's case fairly, then say where it's convincing and where it leaves you with questions.

You're a psychiatrist who does couples therapy, and a couple comes in with a conflict that looks genuinely zero-sum: one partner wants to be allowed something the other can't bear. Therapeutic neutrality says you can't take a side, but a friend would. Write an essay on how we should decide who is right in disputes like this, and what that says about the role of culture.

My uncle insists we need college because it teaches you to think critically. Does the evidence actually back that up? Go through what the research shows, how much to trust it, and what we still don't know.

I've been a critic of a certain political movement for years from the margins, and now big mainstream outlets are suddenly piling on with the same complaint. You'd think I'd be pleased. Write an essay about why having the powerful take up your side can be a reason for unease rather than celebration.

Write an essay on developmental psychology for adults: the idea that some ways of thinking, like seeing that other people have different minds, are skills people may never fully pick up rather than stages everyone passes through. What milestones might some adults be missing, and how would you even tell?

Every few months a headline says some food is as bad as smoking or raises your mortality by 20%. Write a piece on how to make sense of those numbers, using the processed-meat scare as the worked example. I want to know how much it actually matters.

Why is it that generic drugs, which are supposed to be the cheap, competitive part of the pharmaceutical market, so often end up weirdly expensive? A drug company just jacked up the price of an old drug 5000% and I want to understand how the system lets that happen. Write it up as a blog post by someone who prescribes these things.

I think animals have moral value and I also eat meat, and I'm tired of pretending that's not awkward. Write a blog post for fellow meat-eaters about practical ways to cut down the harm we do without going full vegetarian.

Write an essay on whether effective altruists should get involved in 'systemic change' and political causes, as critics keep demanding. Take a cautious view if you can make it, and let it work through the objections, maybe as a conversation between two voices.

Write an essay on how journalists and activists can make any group look terrible using only true anecdotes. Maybe try demonstrating it on a profession that doesn't deserve the reputation, and then explain what's wrong with the technique.
A professor wrote in the New York Times that psychology's replication failures are no cause for alarm, just ordinary science at work. Write a response arguing whether that reassurance holds up.

A paper just claimed a blood test can predict suicide risk with 92% accuracy and the press is running with it. I'm a psychiatrist-ish skeptic. Write a blog post picking the claim apart, both whether the study shows it and whether it would matter if true.

Write a speculative essay linking hallucinations, paranoia and mystical experience. Is there one cognitive mechanism behind why a broken brain sees things that aren't there and why meditators and prophets report cosmic understanding?

People keep telling me you can't assign probabilities to things when you have no model, like first contact with aliens or a risky long-shot bet. I think that's wrong. Write a piece arguing about whether we can and should use probability without a model.

Write a long essay on overconfidence: how sure people say they are versus how often they're right, what saying 'one in a million' really commits you to, and what it should change about how we argue and treat people who disagree.

I've been getting defensive online lately and a friend asked why. Write a candid piece explaining, from the gut, why criticism that aims to make a group disreputable can doom it, and why that makes someone jumpy.

A critic says the case for funding existential-risk work depends on made-up probabilities that you can shrink by adding zeroes until the argument fails. Write a response on when it is legitimate to put tiny numbers on things and why the zeroes aren't free.

Why do people who turn out to be right against the scientific consensus so rarely get credit for it, while cranks get dismissed loudly? I'd like a thoughtful essay on telling real contrarians from crackpots, and what happens to the contrarians even when they win.

I keep noticing that some careers (medicine, academia, big law) are all-or-nothing while others like programming are smooth ladders. Write a blog post about what makes a field like that, whether it's unhealthy, and where else the pattern shows up.

Is there such a thing as being generally good at getting answers right, across unrelated controversial questions, independent of IQ or just agreeing with experts? Write it up as an essay for a rationalist-leaning blog, considering what evidence would show it and why it matters.

Libertarians like to say that competition between private communities, each trying to offer the best rules, will protect freedom better than government can. The internet looks like a real-world test of that idea. Write an essay on whether it actually has, especially for unpopular speech.

Cognitive-behavioral therapy seems to work less well in recent studies than it did in the 1980s. I'm a psychiatry trainee reading a CBT self-help book full of dramatic success stories, and the results I see in real life look nothing like them. Write a speculative, thinking-out-loud blog post about why the effect might be shrinking.

People increasingly appeal to 'cultural evolution' to argue that traditions we inherited must be doing something useful, even if we can't see what. Write an essay on whether that argument actually holds up, and what different things the phrase can mean.

I just read a news story about a woman who says she was wrongly committed to a psych ward for claiming a famous person follows her on social media. You work as a psychiatrist. Write a blog post giving the view from inside the system on whether this was as outrageous as it sounds.

I'm a psychiatry resident and just hit the halfway mark of my four years. Write a reflective blog post about what I've learned working inpatient, what the work does to you, and what I'm wondering about as I move to outpatient.

Write an essay about whether making college free is the right response to the way degrees have become required for everything. I'd like you to use an analogy or a story to get at the problem, and bring in some real examples from jobs people actually do.

A journalist ran a deliberately bad diet study and got the press to report that chocolate helps you lose weight. Everyone online is drawing big lessons from it about science, statistics and the media. Write a blog post sorting out which of those lessons are right and which are overreactions.

I've noticed that when I compare political candidates or weigh up causes, I tend to treat every issue as equally weighty. Is there a good metaphor from how the US Congress is built for what's wrong with that kind of reasoning? Write it up as a short essay.

Imagine that in ten years, machine-learning filters let everyone block anything they don't want to see online, down to whole categories of speech. Write an essay thinking through what that would do to public argument and to who holds power. Draw on today's tools like keyword blockers and shared block lists.

I'm a psychiatry resident and I've been poking around online drug-review sites, where patients rate their medications. Write a blog post about what you might learn by comparing patient ratings with doctors' ratings and with how often drugs get prescribed. Be honest about what could be confounding the numbers.

Why do doctors avoid prescribing drugs with rare but dramatic side effects, even when the alternatives hurt more people in quieter ways? Write it up as a blog post by someone working in psychiatry, with concrete examples and some rough numbers.

I want a blog post about how to read a scientific paper skeptically when the abstract sounds too good. Use a recent psychology study on student mindset interventions as the worked example, and show how an impressive abstract can hide weak results.

Academics from privileged backgrounds often seem eager to blame their own group for the world's problems, which looks odd. Write a short essay proposing a psychological explanation that is charitable rather than cynical.

Two well-designed experiments on whether academic hiring committees favor men or women just came out with opposite results, and each side is citing its own. How should a sensible person think about that? Write it as a blog post, and be willing to speculate about why the studies differ.

Someone told me superintelligent AI can't be dangerous because it's just software on a computer with no way to touch the physical world. Write an essay answering that objection. Assume a skeptical but smart reader.

Lately it's fashionable to say psychiatry lied to the public with the 'chemical imbalance' theory of depression. You're a psychiatry resident who thinks that charge is mostly unfair. Write a long essay defending your profession and explaining what the phrase actually meant and why it was said.

A TV personality got into trouble for describing a grotesque hypothetical to make a point about atheists and morality, and everyone's outraged. As someone with a philosophy background, how do you think about extreme, disturbing thought experiments in general? Are they just morbid, or is there a real method to them? Write it as a blog post.

People keep claiming that environmentalism, social justice, transhumanism, even Apple fandom is 'really a religion'. Is that a meaningful claim or a cheap rhetorical move? Write an essay working out what, if anything, is going on.

Some psychology studies claim huge, lasting effects from tiny interventions, while expensive multi-year social programs barely move the needle. What should we make of that gap? Write a short, skeptical blog post.

Why do small online communities and hobby groups so often get stuck at the same size no matter how hard they recruit? Write an essay drawing on personal experience, and be honest about how much you trust any neat theory of it.

I want a blog post about what happens when you take utilitarianism seriously at a meetup and someone pushes you on animal welfare. How do you stay sane while still being honest about your own inconsistency?

Genetics people say childhood interventions barely matter; psychiatrists say they matter hugely. Take one good randomized trial of early intervention and tell me what to make of it, both scientifically and as policy.

Everyone assumes doctors who take drug company money are shady. Write a funny, honest piece from a psychiatry resident's perspective on how pharma influence actually works on people who think they're ethical.
Could the long decline in testosterone help explain why crime fell? Look at the evidence, poke holes in the idea, and say what data you'd want.
Write a piece about psychiatric hospital work from a resident's view: the kinds of patients who really show up, and one case that made you rethink what we spend money on.

Headlines say drug testing welfare applicants found almost no drug users. Dig into whether those numbers mean what the media says, and what it says about honesty in journalism when you're on the right side of an argument.

A magazine article says polyamory has a problem because black people are underrepresented in it. Write a response from someone in the poly community, thinking about why any group might be demographically skewed and what the framing does.

Write a satirical New York Times style op-ed from the year 2065 where a smug bioethicist declares that refusing a certain universal medical enhancement for your kids is child abuse. Make it read like real moralizing editorial prose.
Use basketball and height to think clearly about intelligence and talent. What does the NBA height distribution teach us about innate ability versus practice?

Newspapers love to point out that places like Denmark and Finland have high antidepressant use and suicide rates, as if that proves they are secretly dysfunctional. Write an essay on what depression and suicide statistics can and can't tell us about how well a society works.

Why does society keep finding new groups it's apparently fine to mock, and why does it seem like each new kind of evil is invisible until it's too late? Write a blog post exploring this, with an idea that ties the two together.
Is weight gain really just 'calories in, calories out'? Write something that takes the thermodynamics seriously but also looks at what the research says about metabolism, genes and willpower.

I keep noticing that a lot of conversation seems to carry no information at all, small talk, the same radio rant every week, stock interview answers, therapists' stock phrases. Write an essay on what that kind of talk is for, and why some people find it comforting and others infuriating.

You know how people buy carbon offsets for a flight? Write an essay pushing that idea as far as it will go: when, if ever, can you cancel out something ethically dubious by doing more good elsewhere? Test it on awkward cases.

Write a book review of G. K. Chesterton's What's Wrong With The World from a modern, skeptical but admiring reader who works as a psychiatrist. I want honest praise and honest objections, not a summary.

I feel guilty that I don't engage more with political causes online, but I also feel the standard of 'you can never do enough' is paralysing. Write an essay on how to think about moral obligation without either giving up or drowning in guilt.

Write an essay about why the causes that campaign hardest for attention so often seem to sabotage themselves, picking the most divisive examples to rally around. Use a few contemporary cases, and think about what incentives the media and the activists are each responding to.

Why is it a bad idea to trust any single study, and why can even a long list of studies, meta-analyses and expert surveys still mislead? Write it up properly, with examples from medicine and from a contested policy debate, and end with what a reader can actually do about it.
Write a book review of Kerouac's On the Road. Make it funny and opinionated, quote the book where it helps, and say what you think the novel is really about and whether it holds up today.

I'm a psychiatry resident and I know of a website that gives patients far better information about psychiatric drugs than the handouts we print out, but I'm reluctant to point anyone to it. Write a blog post exploring why a resource can be excellent and still not something a clinician can safely recommend.

I just saw a headline claiming psychiatric treatment might increase suicide risk, based on a study showing treated people die by suicide far more often than untreated people. Write a piece on what's wrong with reading causation into numbers like that, with a sense of humor if you can manage it.

I read a book arguing that genetics explains almost everything about how kids turn out and parenting barely matters, and the divorce example convinced me. Then I wondered whether it holds up. Write a post about checking that claim: does divorce actually harm children, or is it just that the parents who split pass on bad genes?

I'm about to turn thirty and keep wondering what actually changes between being a teenager and being an adult, beyond the obvious. Write a reflective essay on what we lose and gain as we grow out of youth, maybe drawing on a poet or two.

Argue a case that people should be allowed to sign away their own rights in contracts, even though that is usually seen as something that helps the powerful exploit the weak. If you can, ground it in a real profession's experience rather than abstractions.

Explain the 'motte and bailey' fallacy for a general reader, with plenty of examples, and say how it relates to other debating errors like straw-manning. What should you do when an argument keeps shifting under you?

Suppose we had a perfectly reliable oracle that could tell countries how any war would turn out. Would that end war, or would countries still fight? And if no such oracle exists, what's the closest real-world substitute? Write it up as a thoughtful, slightly wry blog post.

Write an essay about a moral dilemma I keep coming back to: why do people find it so much easier to help the suffering they can see than suffering they've been able to avoid noticing, and what does that do to utilitarianism?

I'm asexual and polyamorous, and a lot of what I value in relationships is physical closeness that isn't sex. Write a personal blog post about cuddling, why it matters, and whether whole communities can make it normal.
Why is there almost no scientific research on nerds? Write a curious, skeptical blog post that asks whether 'nerd' is a real category or just a stereotype, and what might explain it if it is.
Write a blog post criticizing a common design flaw in psychology experiments, using the debate over violent video games as the starting point. I want it to be skeptical but fair to the researchers.

I just finished a book about Soviet economic planning and the mathematicians who tried to fix it. Write a long, thoughtful review that goes beyond the plot to what it teaches about planning, incentives and who ought to run a country.
I keep hearing that ADHD is wildly overdiagnosed, and then in the next breath that it's badly underdiagnosed. Both can't be true, can they? Write a short piece sorting this out, with numbers.

People say the rich have captured government and bend it to their interests. But doesn't collective action get in the way of that? Write an essay thinking through whether class interests can actually be coordinated.

I read a short introduction to Marx hoping to find a more sympathetic picture than the one I grew up with. Write a book-review style essay on what a skeptical, curious non-expert might come away with, including anything that surprisingly holds up.
Hegel dominated philosophy for a century and is now mostly a punchline. Write a blog post about what to make of a thinker whose reputation swung that far, and what it might mean for our own thinking.
There's a stereotype that the left thinks problems are social and fixable while the right thinks they're biological and fixed. Write an essay arguing about whether that gets things backwards.

Contractualism says morality is what selfish agents would agree to, but the veil of ignorance is a fiction. Write an essay exploring a toy model with agents of unequal power and see where cooperation breaks down.

A newspaper article claims an old doomsday forecast has been vindicated because the data have tracked its predictions for forty years. Write a critical essay about whether that kind of track record is actually evidence, bringing in some philosophy.
Write a book review of a popular-level book on quantum computing from the point of view of someone who isn't a mathematician and only half understood it, but still came away with one big picture.

I work in a hospital, and a patient reported another patient for breaking the rules, and I caught myself thinking less of him even though he did exactly the right thing. Why do we instinctively dislike people who tell on others, and what does that say about promises and when you're allowed to break them? Write it up as a thoughtful essay.

Write a blog post from a psychiatry resident's perspective on why medicine in the US seems to ignore drugs that have been used for decades in other countries, and how perfectly sensible individual incentives can add up to something that looks insane.

Write an essay from a psychiatrist's point of view about patients who feel like a burden on the people around them. What can you honestly say to them, especially when the feeling isn't entirely a cognitive distortion? I'd like it to be compassionate but not sugar-coated, and to get into what society owes people who can't keep up.

I keep noticing people who are scrupulously rigorous about the claims they dislike and totally relaxed about the ones they like. Write a funny but serious essay about that habit, ranging from philosophy to politics to science, and what a fair standard of rigor would look like.

When someone hits you with a wall of statistics to prove a common-sense category isn't real, and you can't follow the math, what can you do? Use the debate over whether race exists as the worked example, and write it as a blog post.

You're a non-mathematician with strong views in philosophy and social science, and sometimes someone buries you in sophisticated math to say you're wrong. How should you respond without just dismissing the math or being steamrolled by it? Write an essay, with stories.
Why does 'just be yourself' work for some people and fail for others? I'd like a short, personal essay about confidence, social awkwardness and the way the same behavior can mean opposite things.
I feel like I only ever think the same thoughts. Write a blog post on where original ideas actually come from and how to deliberately go looking for them.
Why is coming up with genuinely new ideas so hard, and why do so many of them show up in dreams or by accident? Write a short, speculative blog post.
Write a post about the hidden assumptions that make online arguments go sideways, the unspoken questions about what a speaker is actually trying to do when they say something.
People say technological progress has stalled since the moon landing. Write a witty essay pushing back, and also explaining why futurists' cool predictions so often fail to materialize.
Write a short blog post about psychiatric drugs and base rates. Something about how surprised we should or shouldn't be when drugs from unrelated fields turn out to affect the brain.

Why do social movements like libertarianism, feminism or atheism end up as a loose cloud of NGOs rather than anything like a Church? Write an essay on how you would design an organization to capture a movement's energy, what the Catholic Church gets right, and why almost nobody copies it.

I've been reading Bostrom's Superintelligence and got stuck on the idea of a hyper-competitive Malthusian future full of digital agents where consciousness might get optimized away. Write something speculative about whether anything meaningful could survive in that kind of economy, and where it might hide.

Congressional voting data gets turned into a left-right scale without anyone telling the algorithm what left and right are. Could something like that work for morality? Write an essay exploring whether you could discover what 'good' means statistically from ordinary life decisions.

Write a funny but serious blog post about why a doctor will happily prescribe a $300-a-month drug that is basically a supplement you can buy for $30. Is the pharmaceutical industry just greedy here, or is something else going on?

Someone argued that rationality is a scarce resource you have to budget, and a commenter countered that it's more like weightlifting. I think both metaphors miss something. Write a blog-style piece on what it actually takes to be rational at the moments when it matters most.

I want a blog post about a thought experiment: you discover that your deepest, most obvious beliefs were planted to test whether you'd conform to a crowd. Which beliefs would survive, and what does the exercise reveal about moral reasoning?

Write a long blog post defending trigger warnings from a psychiatrist's point of view, answering the usual objections: that they're censorship, that they get politicized, that research shows avoidance makes trauma worse.

Everyone seems to read the Great Filter as proof that humanity is doomed. Write an essay on whether that's right: which candidate explanations for the Fermi paradox actually hold up, and how scared should we be?

A big media outlet recently argued that the wealth white Americans enjoy today is basically compound interest on what was stolen from Black Americans, and called anyone who doubts it unserious. Is that actually a good argument? Write an essay that digs into what the evidence says about whether wealth really passes down and compounds across generations.

I work with addiction patients and noticed something odd about money and motivation. Write a short, candid blog post that starts from a clinic anecdote and ends up explaining why someone who is always 'too busy' for obligations still finds time for the thing they love.

Write a playful, wandering essay about how certain trigger words or names can carry emotional charge that bypasses argument, and how that might make political disagreement so unproductive. Feel free to bring in fiction, psychology experiments and a few current-events examples.

I never got pep rallies, patriotism or group rituals and always assumed I was just wired without the ability to feel that kind of belonging. Write a personal essay on whether that's really true of people like me.

Write a thoughtful essay on why Kant's moral philosophy, which is usually mocked as rigid rule-following, might deserve a second look. Include the notorious murderer-at-the-door example and some modern applications, and be honest about where it still doesn't work.

Why do people so often get defensive when someone criticizes 'some members' of a group they belong to, even when the criticism clearly doesn't apply to them? Write an essay that tries to explain this, using a few examples from online arguments and religion.
Write an essay about moral debts that have no natural limit, like what we owe our parents or our society. Where do such obligations come from, and how should anyone live with them?

I just came across the idea of governments contracting private companies to fix social problems and paying them only if it works. Write a blog post exploring what's interesting about this, whether it's a good idea, and what it says about how we might harness profit motives for public goods.

Science has a huge problem with bad studies, biased researchers and unreplicable results. Imagine a fictional utopian society that had designed its whole system of doing and funding science from scratch to avoid those failures. Describe how research works there, in an engaging essay.

A big study just made headlines claiming childhood bullying causes terrible adult outcomes decades later, even after controlling for confounders. I'm skeptical of 'controlled for confounders' as a method. Write a blog post on whether we should believe results like this.
Why do close friends insult and threaten each other as a way of bonding? Write a short piece using real examples from your own life, and include one where it went wrong.
A bankrupt city is debating selling the masterpieces in its art museum. Write a short, hard-nosed economic argument about whether it should, and what that says about thinking quantitatively.

Two political science findings seem to contradict each other: one says policy outcomes track what the wealthy want rather than what ordinary voters want, another says money barely moves votes in politics. Write a blog post that takes both seriously and tries to reconcile them.

I keep reading that kids of older fathers have higher rates of psychiatric disorders. Is that really a biological effect of parental age, or could something else be going on? Write it up like a blog post, with a bit of personal flavor if it fits.

You're a psychiatry resident who just heard a prestigious speaker give a stock answer to patients who ask 'You don't believe me, do you?' Write a reflective essay on how you'd actually want to answer that, and the related 'Do you think I'm crazy?'

Write an essay about what's wrong with how the rationality community talks about homeopaths, creationists and moon-landing skeptics. I suspect it does more harm than good, but I want it argued properly.

Write a speculative essay (flag it as crackpot if you like) about emotional feedback loops in the brain: why we don't spiral every time we feel something, what happens in anxiety and OCD when we do, and whether our modern emotional vocabulary makes it worse.

A new study says people who use e-cigarettes are no more likely to quit smoking after a year than people who don't, and maybe less likely. That seems off to me. Write a short blog post on how a study like that could produce a misleading result even if nobody did anything wrong.

Write an essay about advice. A lot of it comes in opposite pairs (be harder on yourself / be kinder to yourself), and the people who go looking for a given kind of advice may be exactly the ones who least need it. What should that do to how we take advice?

I've been wondering how many people go their whole lives missing some ordinary human experience without ever noticing, because everyone around them talks as if it were metaphor. Write a blog post exploring that, with real examples.

Why does re-reading an idea that once changed your mind often feel obvious and boring, when forgotten facts never feel that way? And is giving a name to a pattern always a good thing, or can it do harm? Write it as a thoughtful blog post.

Write a reflective post for the fifth anniversary of an online rationalist community: how much did its members learn without noticing they were learning it, and what does it feel like to look back and see how far you have moved?

A friend gave me a copy of a popular paleo-ish diet book. Write a candid, funny, evidence-minded review from someone with medical training: what does it get right, where does it mislead, and would you recommend it?
Genes, technologies and business practices that give an advantage tend to spread until everyone has them. Do productivity tricks and life hacks ever do the same? Write an essay working through this.

Write an essay about why it's so hard to find a real bargain, whether in college admissions, politics, or self-improvement tricks. When almost everything on offer is a tradeoff, how would you ever find something that isn't?
Can you actually teach doctors to communicate well with patients? Write a blog post from the perspective of a medical resident who has opinions about this.

I just found out some online forum members pool money to synthesize experimental drugs and try them on themselves. It's obviously reckless, yet I feel weirdly pleased it exists. Write a short blog post making sense of that mixed reaction.
Write a creepy but informative blog post about the strangest and scariest sleep disorders, written by a medical trainee who has just read a sleep medicine textbook.

I'm a medical student and our communication-skills classes feel strangely fake: role-plays, checklists, scripted phrases. Write me a thoughtful essay on whether you can teach doctors empathy, and what the difference is between seeming empathetic and actually being so.

Write an essay about the far future where technology has made everything effortless, and whether a civilization of beings who just sit in permanent bliss is a dystopia or a utopia. I'd like it to poke at why my gut reaction to that image might be unreliable.

A friend shared a slick infographic rating supplements by how strong the evidence is, and everything on it looked reassuring. I'm a doctor and I'm skeptical. Write a blog post on why mass-produced evidence ratings for supplements can mislead, and how to read them critically.

There's a study where telling elderly people they carry an Alzheimer's risk gene made their memory scores worse. Write a blog post that looks at whether the conclusion, that genetic testing itself can harm people, actually follows.

It's January and I'm in a cranky mood about internet culture. Write a funny, opinionated blog post listing the habits, words and jokes you would most like to see disappear from the internet this year.
Is bipolar disorder a culture-bound syndrome, or is it the same across history? I'm curious whether an ancient physician's description matches a modern screening questionnaire. Write it up.

People love to say that the First Amendment only restricts the government, so a boss firing someone for something they said isn't a free speech issue. Legally that's right, but it feels like it misses something. Write an essay on whether free speech means anything beyond what the law requires, and what a healthy norm of disagreement looks like.

I want a blog post about how petty and vicious online communities get, from fandom feuds to hobbyist forums, and what that says about people in general. Feel free to draw on personal experience of getting too invested in some absurd internet subculture as a teenager.

Do public awareness campaigns actually change behavior? Everyone seems to have a pet example of one that worked and one that flopped. Write an essay that tries to make sense of the pattern, and be honest about how much you can really conclude.

I went to a secular solstice event with a bunch of nerds and loved it, even though plenty of people call that kind of thing cringeworthy. Write a blog post about why strong communities, religious or not, so often seem to depend on being a little embarrassing, and what that means for atheists trying to build one.
Write a blog post on a recent study that tested how well doctors understand statistics (p-values, mammogram probabilities). I want a funny but fair look at what it shows and what it doesn't.
The Pope just got named Time's Person of the Year. Write a short, wry blog post on how you feel about the way people react to his humble gestures.

Write an essay arguing for a political position that mixes free-market tools with real concern for the poor and for minorities. Use concrete policy examples and explain why taxes and subsidies might beat bans and mandates.

Some political writers claim democracy tends to spiral ever leftward until it ends in a bloody reign of terror. Write an essay evaluating that claim against the actual history of revolutions and terror regimes. You can start with an analogy if it helps.
Write a darkly funny blog post that retells the Thanksgiving story (Squanto, the Pilgrims, the plague) as though it belonged to a different genre than the one it's taught in.

I'm a psychiatrist in training and my work is making me terrified of having kids. Write a candid, personal essay about why, covering what I've seen in medicine and psychiatry and what it's done to my thinking about parenthood and discipline.

A friend on Facebook said anti-rape awareness campaigns aimed at men have been proven to work, citing one city's crime numbers after a poster campaign. Write a careful but entertaining post on whether that evidence holds up.

I'm a medical student and something about a sleep drug called ramelteon bugs me: it mimics a hormone you can buy for pennies at any drugstore. Write an essay on what that says about how medicine decides which treatments get used, with a story from clinical practice if you have one.

A new randomized trial found Freudian-style therapy did about as well as cognitive behavioral therapy for depression. I'm a psychiatry resident and I was taught that psychoanalysis was debunked. Write a blog post on what to make of this and how we ended up believing what we believed.

You're a junior doctor and something went sideways at work: a patient fell after a drug you gave, a miscommunication blew it up, and now you've been told not to say 'I'm sorry.' Write a reflective essay on what apologies actually mean, why they're so hard to get right, and what it takes to give and accept them well.

Write an essay about what happens to promising-but-unproven medical ideas: some get tested and killed, some get ignored, some get proven but still never reach patients. Use a few concrete examples from medicine, and be honest about what you don't understand about the process.

A popular article argued that military intervention is a wasteful way to help foreigners because the same money donated to a top charity would save more lives. I think the argument is flawed. Write a rebuttal that actually does the cost-effectiveness arithmetic.

Opponents of euthanasia often cite Dutch statistics showing thousands of people killed without consent. Write a careful, skeptical piece that traces where those numbers come from, what they really count, and what better data show. Keep a sense of humor.

Write an essay about people who invoke 'consent' as a reason to ban things like euthanasia, BDSM or prostitution. Are they really motivated by concern for consent? Explore what's going on underneath, with some humor and a thought experiment or two.

I'm a layperson who is puzzled by how highly heritable traits like intelligence can be spread over thousands of tiny genetic effects. Write a blog post in the voice of a curious, self-deprecating amateur working through that confusion, and the other genetics ideas that don't quite add up for them, and asking readers to set them straight.

Two psychology studies came out in the same month with results that seem to pull in opposite directions about whether stress is bad or good for you. Write a wry blog post about what the pair tells us about how we explain results in psychology.

People accuse scientifically minded folks of 'scientism' when they weigh in on philosophy, morality or religion. Write an essay that takes the accusation seriously, works out what is really going on, and says whether the charge is deserved. Feel free to take a side.

I'm bad at math and just don't find it interesting, and every time I say so people try to talk me out of it. Write a personal essay about why people react that way to a lack of interest, and what it means to be fascinated by some things and not others.

I'm a medical resident, and I want to write something honest about what dying in a modern hospital is actually like, as opposed to the peaceful deathbed people imagine, and what I think should change about how we approach the end of life. Write it as a blunt, darkly funny, personal essay.

A lot of political arguments, about violent media, stereotypes, diversity training, rape culture and so on, lean on findings from social psychology. Write a skeptical but fair essay on how much weight those findings can bear, and try it by turning the usual arguments upside down.

Chesterton said he accepted Christianity because it was a 'truth-telling thing'. Write a blog post from an atheist's point of view on whether that holds up, and why believers often report that a religion makes everything 'click' and fit together.

A doctor learns that a patient sent an innocent man to prison, and a newspaper ethics column debates whether she should break confidentiality. Write a piece that looks at this dilemma from an unexpected angle, and at when saying nothing is a moral choice.

Why do people give each other opposite advice, 'be more selfish' and 'be less selfish', and each sound completely sure? I want an essay that explains why so many debates go in circles, with a few real examples.
Write a short personal essay about meditating while exhausted and where the mind goes, and what that has to do with why some big ideas feel so satisfying.

Does making contraception more available actually reduce abortion rates? I keep hearing both that it obviously does and that the data says the opposite. Dig into the evidence honestly and tell me what you conclude.

Some people say that if our good deeds are mostly driven by status and self-image, then humans aren't really good at all. I'm not sure that follows. Write a short, imaginative essay on whether people can be basically good even when their motives look selfish.

I keep seeing arguments of the form 'group X doesn't REALLY believe what they say, they just want Y' in politics, with abortion as the standard example. Write a long essay on why that style of argument is so tempting and why it usually fails. You can be pro-choice and still take the other side seriously.

I'm about to move away from a city where I found a community of unusually kind, smart people, and I'm sad about it. Write a reflective piece about what made that community work and whether it can be reproduced.

A friend swears by 'training your inner pigeon', using behaviorism on yourself by rewarding yourself when you do what you want to do more of. Does that actually work? Think it through skeptically, using what you know about conditioning.

Why do arguments about who is the brave dissenter and who is the conformist go so sour so quickly? Write an essay on this pattern in political and cultural debate, including why both sides can be so sure they're the underdog.
Write a deadpan, tongue-in-cheek essay that treats morality as if it were a physical force, with real-sounding calculations, and uses it to explain why we feel less obligated to distant strangers.
Some questions, like whether Mozart is better than Beethoven, seem neither purely subjective nor purely objective. Write a blog post proposing a way to think about this and a word for it.

I've been wondering why people think of atheists as loud and angry. Write a short blog post exploring whether that stereotype could come from how we notice groups, and whether it generalizes to other groups.
Many people object to putting numbers on things we can't really measure, like how bad North Korea is to live in or the chance your laptop dies. Write a post defending using made-up numbers anyway.

Write a skeptical but enthusiastic blog post reviewing a psychology paper that tried to use a reaction-time test to predict suicide risk, covering what it claims, what's wrong with it, and why the idea still matters.

In high school I helped start an elaborate online role-play of an imaginary world that ended up running for more than a decade. Write a reflective essay about what years of simulated politics and worldbuilding can teach a person, including the odd, half-serious lessons about leadership.

Write a short blog post praising a favorite debating trick: attacking an argument by showing it would also prove obviously false things. Explain why it's so effective in a time-limited debate and give a few examples.

Write an essay about why survey and poll results on weird or extreme beliefs are less trustworthy than they look. Use the headline claim that a few percent of Americans believe lizard people run the world as a starting point, and bring in a couple of other cases where noise or mischief corrupted the data.

I always found the history of philosophy frustrating because so much of what's taught is obviously wrong by now. Is there still a good reason to read old philosophers? Write a thoughtful piece on how to get value out of them.

Write a witty, critical review of Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue from the point of view of a utilitarian-leaning reader who found the book more confusing than convincing, while still giving it a fair hearing.

I've started to doubt utilitarianism as a foundation for ethics. Write an exploratory essay about whether it can really give morality an objective basis or whether it just formalizes our own intuitions, and what might take its place.

I recently started a polyamorous relationship, and what surprised me most is how ordinary it feels. Write a candid personal essay for skeptical readers about what that experience is actually like, covering the usual objections about love, jealousy, and sex.

I just got back from a talk on effective charity where one of the speakers argued that donors are mostly fooling themselves. Write me a blog post about what it's like to hear that, and whether the idea of investing your money now and giving it away later actually holds up. Do some back-of-the-envelope math.

When I was in college I devoured books on mysticism and the occult, and I think it did me more harm than good. Write an essay on the difference between learning about a field and actually learning it, and why that trap is especially bad for spiritual stuff.

A friend says the cure for youth unemployment is abolishing the minimum wage so everyone can find some job. Write a blog post taking that seriously and then arguing the strongest case you can for why it might backfire, especially as automation advances.

Do we pick partners who are genetically similar to us or different from us? Write it up as a curious, slightly meandering blog post: lay out the evidence on both sides, including the weird stuff, and be honest about where the explanation falls apart.

I've just finished Infinite Jest and I'm still puzzled. Write a long, funny, opinionated review for people who've read it (spoilers fine) that tries to say what the book is actually about and how its structure relates to that.

Why does society seem to drift gradually in one political direction over time, and what do 'left' and 'right' even mean such that they stay recognizable across eras and cultures? I'd like a proper essay that tests a few existing theories against the evidence and then offers one of your own.

I finally got an Amazon Prime account and it's changed how I buy things, which feels almost embarrassing to admit. Write a funny, self-aware blog post about how you decide what to buy and what it feels like when basic economics turns out to work.
Lots of geeks name-drop Cthulhu and make jokes about it without ever having read Lovecraft. Write a blog post on what you think pop culture gets wrong about him, and why it bothers you.

I keep hearing that 90% of medical research is false. Is that true? Write a careful piece that looks at where the number comes from, what the real statistics of medical studies say, and how much a reader or a doctor should actually distrust a published study.

I'm starting a blog with no single subject and want to open with a short statement of the attitude I'll bring to disagreement. Write that first post for me, with a bit of humor but a real point about how to treat ideas you think are wrong.
